story.title: Milo and Juno and the Glowing Brick
story.subtitle: A click-tastic trip through LEGO history!

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Billund, 1932
chapters.text:
Milo lay on his bedroom floor, snapping LEGO bricks together. He was building a tower taller than his elbow. Juno sat beside him, roaring like a dinosaur. Stomp, stomp, stomp went his toy dinosaur feet, careful not to bump the tower.

Suddenly, one brick on top began to glow. It glowed bright green, like a firefly caught in a jar. 'Whoa,' whispered Milo.

The brick started to hum. HMMMMMM. Juno leaned in close. 'It's singing!' he said.

Milo touched the glowing brick. WHOOOOSH! The whole room spun like a merry-go-round. When it stopped spinning, Milo and Juno were standing in a small wooden workshop. Sawdust floated in the air like tiny snowflakes. A kind man with a hammer looked up and smiled.

'Well, hello there!' he said. 'I'm Ole Kirk. I make wooden toys and ladders, right here in Billund, Denmark. The year is nineteen thirty-two.'

Juno looked down at a little wooden duck on the workbench. 'Quack?' he said. The duck did not quack back, but Ole Kirk laughed anyway.

'Not every toy has to make a sound,' said Ole Kirk. 'It just has to make someone smile.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Play Well
chapters.text:
Ole Kirk held up a blank wooden sign. 'I need a name for my little company,' he said, scratching his head. 'Any ideas?'

Milo thought about his favorite thing to do with LEGO: play. 'What about... Play Good?' he said.

Ole Kirk's eyes lit up. 'In Danish, we say leg godt,' he said. 'That means play well!' He grabbed his paintbrush and shortened it: L-E-G-O. 'LEGO!' he announced proudly.

Juno clapped his hands. 'Lego, Lego, Lego!' he sang, hopping in a circle.

Ole Kirk hung the new sign above his door. It read LEGO, nineteen thirty-four.

'Here's a funny thing,' Ole Kirk added, winking. 'In a very old language called Latin, the word lego means I put together. Nobody is sure if that's why we picked it. But it fits pretty well, doesn't it?'

Milo grinned. 'It's like it was meant to be!'

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Wobbly Brick
chapters.text:
Years flew by in a blink. WHOOOSH! Milo and Juno landed in a buzzing factory. A big machine squirted melted plastic into brick shapes.

'This is our new plastic machine,' said a worker. 'We got it in nineteen forty-seven. Now we can make toys out of plastic, not just wood!'

By nineteen forty-nine, the factory was making little studded bricks called Automatic Binding Bricks. Milo picked one up and pressed it onto another. It sat there, wobbly. He gave the tower a tiny poke, and the top brick toppled right off.

'They don't stick very well,' Milo said, catching the falling brick before it hit the floor. 'They need something extra.'

Juno peeked underneath a brick. 'It's just empty in there,' he said, 'like a little cave.'

The worker nodded, surprised. 'You're both right. We're still figuring it out.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Click Heard Round the World
chapters.text:
A tall young man burst into the room, pencil behind his ear. 'I heard you two found a problem,' he said, smiling. 'I'm Godtfred, Ole Kirk's son.'

Milo pointed at the hollow bottom of a brick. 'It needs something inside here,' he said, 'to hold onto the bumps on the brick below.'

Godtfred's eyes went wide. 'That's exactly it!' He grabbed his pencil and drew little round tubes inside the bottom of the brick.

Juno pressed two new bricks together. CLICK! He pulled. It held tight. He pulled harder. It still held.

'IT CLICKS!' Juno shouted, bouncing on his toes.

'On January twenty-eighth, nineteen fifty-eight, we made it official,' said Godtfred, patting the brick like an old friend. 'And here's the best part: a brick made today will always click with a brick made way back then.'

Milo thought of his own LEGO tower back home, waiting for him. 'So my bricks at home would fit right in?'

'Every single one,' said Godtfred.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Park Made of Bricks
chapters.text:
WHOOOSH! Next they landed outside a giant gate built entirely from LEGO bricks.

'Welcome to LEGOLAND!' said a voice. It was Godtfred again, older now, with a big smile. 'We opened this park right here in Billund, in nineteen sixty-eight. Right next to where it all started.'

Milo gasped at a LEGO model of a castle, taller than his dad. 'Could you build a shark out of bricks?' he asked, hopeful.

Godtfred chuckled. 'With enough bricks, you could build almost anything.'

Juno spotted a tiny LEGO dinosaur peeking out of a flower bed. He pointed and gasped, but kept his hands to himself. 'Dino!' he whispered happily.

'You found him!' said Godtfred. 'Good eyes, Juno.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Bricks for Little Hands
chapters.text:
Juno tried to pick up a tiny brick, but his fingers were too small. It slipped and rolled away across the table.

'Hmm,' said Godtfred, watching. 'What if we made some bricks just right for little hands?'

In nineteen sixty-nine, the company made big chunky bricks called DUPLO. Godtfred handed one to Juno. It fit perfectly in his small fist.

Juno pressed it onto a regular LEGO brick. CLICK! It fit right on top, snug and tight.

'They still work together!' Juno cheered, holding his new tower high above his head.

Milo high-fived his little brother. 'Now we can both build, even when your hands are small.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Little Yellow People
chapters.text:
A box tumbled open, and dozens of tiny yellow figures spilled out. They had little round heads and arms that could move.

'These are our newest idea,' said Godtfred. 'We made them in nineteen seventy-eight. You can swap their heads and their hats!'

Milo picked one up and gave it a pirate hat. Then he swapped it for a tiny shark-fin hat he found in the pile. 'Now he's Shark Captain!' Milo announced.

Juno found a tiny green minifigure and gave it a party hat. 'He's Dino Dance Party!' he giggled, wiggling it side to side.

Godtfred laughed so hard he nearly dropped the box. 'I don't think we ever imagined that combination,' he said, 'but it works.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Bedroom Floor
chapters.text:
The tiny minifigure in Milo's hand began to glow bright green. 'Oh!' said Milo. 'I think it's time to go home.'

Godtfred waved. 'Before you go, one more thing. My son Kjeld grew up playing with these very bricks. He took over leading the whole company in nineteen seventy-nine. And guess what? Our family still runs it today, right here in Billund.'

WHOOOSH! The room spun again. Milo and Juno landed back on their own bedroom floor, right where they started.

Milo looked down. His LEGO tower was still standing tall. And right on top sat a tiny yellow minifigure wearing a shark-fin hat, one they had never owned before.

Juno yawned a big dinosaur yawn. 'Best brick ever,' he mumbled, snuggling into his blanket.

Milo tucked the little shark-hat figure next to his pillow. 'Goodnight, LEGO,' he whispered. 'Thanks for playing well with us.'

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: Ole Kirk Christiansen started his company in **Billund, Denmark**, in **1932**, making wooden toys and ladders.
In **1934**, he named his company **LEGO**, from the Danish words leg godt, which mean **play well**.
The word lego also happens to mean **I put together** in an old language called Latin — nobody's sure if that's why it got picked, but it's a fun match.
In **1947**, the company started using a machine that made toys out of **plastic** instead of wood.
By **1949**, they were making little studded bricks called **Automatic Binding Bricks** that didn't hold together very well yet.
On **January 28, 1958**, Godtfred added tiny **tubes** inside the bricks so they would click together and hold tight.
A brick made in **1958** still clicks together perfectly with a brick made today.
The first **LEGOLAND** park opened in Billund in **1968**, right next to where it all began.
In **1969**, LEGO made bigger bricks called **DUPLO**, just the right size for little hands — and they still click onto regular LEGO bricks.
The first tiny LEGO people, called **minifigures**, showed up in **1978** with arms that move and hats you can swap.
Ole Kirk's grandson **Kjeld** took over running the company in **1979**.
LEGO's headquarters is still in **Billund, Denmark**, right where Ole Kirk's workshop once stood.
The same family that started LEGO still owns the company today.

story.title: Theo and the Secret History of Video Games
story.subtitle: A journey from a glowing green dot to a blocky world, one glitch at a time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Dot That Played Tennis (1958)
chapters.text:
Theo was still awake at 10:47 p.m., hunched over his laptop in the blue glow of Roblox Studio. He wasn't just playing — he was building a stadium for a penalty-kick game, tuning the sliders that controlled gravity and bounce until the ball arced just right off the crossbar.

Then the screen flickered. Black, then green, then black again, scanlines crawling sideways like something out of an ancient TV. A tiny green dot blinked on the glitching screen and rearranged itself into a pixel face with a crooked grin.

"Name's Blip," said the pixel face. "Want to see the very first video game anyone ever played?"

Before Theo could answer, the screen opened like a doorway. **WHOOOOSH.** He tumbled through pixels and landed in a humming room full of machines the size of refrigerators.

A man in a white coat stood hunched over a small round screen, turning dials with both hands. Green lines formed a tennis court, seen from the side, with a net in the middle. A dot that was supposed to be a ball kept rolling flat across instead of arcing over it.

"Visitors arrive in ten minutes," the man muttered, "and my ball won't bounce."

Theo had tuned enough gravity sliders in Roblox Studio to spot the problem instantly. "That knob," he said, pointing to a small dial marked with an arrow. "Turn it up. You need more pull, not less."

The man — Blip whispered his name was **William Higinbotham** — turned the dial. The dot arced down, bounced off the net line, and sailed back. Perfect tennis.

"Well, I'll be," Higinbotham said, laughing. "A ten-year-old just fixed my physics."

"Theo, meet **Tennis for Two**," Blip said, "built in **1958** right here at **Brookhaven National Laboratory**. It ran on an **oscilloscope** — an old screen that draws glowing lines to show how something moves. This is the dot where it all began."

Theo watched the little green ball bounce back and forth. Sixty years before Roblox Studio, somebody was already arguing with gravity sliders too.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ships That Wouldn't Stop Spinning (1962)
chapters.text:
Blip's screen glitched again, dragging Theo into a buzzing room crammed with reel-to-reel tape machines and one enormous computer with blinking lights across its face — a **PDP-1**, basically a computer the size of a refrigerator wall.

Two college students were shouting at a round screen covered in white dots. "I pressed turn and it thrusted!" one yelled. Both their spaceship shapes spun in dizzy circles, bumping into each other instead of fighting straight.

Theo had built enough control schemes in Roblox Studio to know a keybind mess when he saw one. "You're using the same two keys for turning and firing," he said, leaning over the switch panel. "Split them. One switch, one job."

The taller student — Blip murmured his name was **Steve Russell** — rewired the switches fast. The next test run, the two triangle ships spun apart cleanly, each one steering exactly where its pilot wanted.

"THAT'S IT!" Russell shouted, and the room cheered like he'd scored a stoppage-time goal.

"Say hello to **Spacewar!**," Blip told Theo, "made in **1962** by **Steve Russell** and his friends at **MIT** — the first game a lot of early computer fans ever got hooked on."

Theo watched the two ships circle each other on the fuzzy screen, trading little bursts of light. It wasn't much to look at. But somewhere under all that static, he could feel the start of every Roblox battle arena he'd ever built.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Brown Box That Needed One Plug (Late 1960s–1972)
chapters.text:
The next stop smelled like solder and static. Blip set them down in a workshop where a man was hunched over a plain wooden box wired to a television set.

"Come on," the man muttered, smacking the box's side. "Work."

Nothing happened. Just a blank gray screen.

Theo crouched to look at the tangle of wires behind the TV — the same kind of mess he'd seen behind his own television plenty of times. One wire had slipped halfway out of its socket. He pushed it back in. **CLICK.**

The screen flickered, then lit up with two glowing white squares — crude paddles — and a square ball bouncing between them.

The man leaped back, grinning. "There she is!"

"Meet **Ralph Baer**," Blip said, "later called the father of video games. That plain wooden box is his **Brown Box**, built in the late 1960s — the first machine made to play games on a home television instead of a lab computer."

"And in **1972**," Blip added, "it became a real toy anybody could buy: the **Magnavox Odyssey**, the first home video game console you could plug into your own TV."

Baer shook Theo's hand like he'd just assisted on a winning goal. "Every kid who's ever played a game on a TV owes that loose wire a thank-you."

Theo laughed. He'd fixed plenty of glitches in Roblox Studio. He'd just never fixed one that led to an entire industry.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Machine That Choked on Quarters (1972)
chapters.text:
The next doorway dropped Theo into a dim arcade room that smelled like popcorn and spilled soda. In the corner sat a wooden cabinet with a black-and-white screen, two paddles and a bouncing square ball glowing on it.

A line of people waited to play, tapping their feet. Two men in short-sleeved shirts — Blip said they were **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** — were shaking the cabinet, trying to get it to turn back on.

"It's jammed again," one groaned.

Theo peered into the coin slot and saw the exact problem: quarters packed in so tight not one more could drop through.

"It's not broken," Theo said. "It's full."

He tipped the machine gently so the jammed coins slid loose, and the screen flickered back on. The waiting line cheered.

"That's the story, anyway," Blip said with a wink. "Nobody's totally sure one single machine really choked on quarters — but it's the kind of thing that *could* happen, because this game got popular fast."

"This," Blip went on, "is **Pong**, released by a brand-new company called **Atari** in **1972**. Simple paddles, simple ball — and it turned out to be exactly what the world didn't know it wanted."

Theo grinned, watching strangers lean in to play a game about two lines and a square. Sometimes the simplest idea was the one that broke the machine.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Box With a Thousand Games Inside (1977–1978)
chapters.text:
Blip's next stop looked like Theo's own living room, if it were decorated entirely in wood paneling. A boxy console sat under the TV, a long slot on top, plastic cartridges scattered across the carpet.

A frustrated engineer held two cartridges that looked almost identical. "If I jam the wrong one in, I could fry the whole system," he said.

Theo had swapped enough Roblox game templates to recognize a labeling problem. He flipped both cartridges over and spotted a tiny printed code on one edge. "This one matches the slot's notch," he said, holding it up. "Try this."

The engineer slid it in. The screen filled with rows of pixel aliens marching sideways, dropping slowly toward a tiny cannon at the bottom.

"That's the **Atari 2600**," Blip explained, "launched in **1977**. Before this, consoles only played the one game built inside them. This one let you swap plastic cartridges in and out — so one box could hold a thousand different games, as long as you had the carts."

"And that," Blip said, pointing at the marching aliens, "is **Space Invaders**, made in **1978** by designer **Tomohiro Nishikado**. It kicked off the first big arcade craze on the planet."

Theo watched the aliens creep lower, row by row, and felt the same itch he got building new levels at 11 p.m. — the itch to press play just one more time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Pizza, the Crash, and the Buried Cartridges (1980–1983)
chapters.text:
Next, Blip dropped Theo into a glowing arcade shop where a designer sat sketching a yellow circle with a wedge missing, like a mouth.

"I was staring at a pizza with one slice gone," the designer said, laughing. "Seemed like a good shape for a hero."

Theo squinted at the sketch. "That's... **Pac-Man**?" he guessed.

"Got it in one," Blip said. "Designer **Toru Iwatani** made him in **1980** — and that pizza story is the one he always tells, even if nobody can prove the pizza existed."

The scene shifted fast, the way dreams do. Suddenly Theo stood in a store aisle stacked with video game boxes, most looking cheap and rushed.

"Nobody can tell which games are actually good anymore," a shopper sighed, putting a box back down.

"This is **1983**," Blip said quietly. "Too many rushed, low-quality games flooded the shelves, and people stopped trusting games enough to buy them. The whole market shrank fast. It's called **the video game crash**."

Through the store window, Theo noticed a dump truck tipping load after load of cartridges into a dirt pit.

"Are they just throwing them away?" Theo asked.

"Including a famous *E.T.* game nobody wanted," Blip said. "Buried in a **landfill** — a giant dump where trash gets buried — in **New Mexico**. People didn't believe the story for thirty years, until diggers actually found the cartridges there in **2014**."

Theo stared at the pit. "So even video games have, like, a bad patch."

"Every great story does," Blip said. "Wait till you see the comeback."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Plumber and the Falling Blocks (1984–1985)
chapters.text:
Blip's screen flickered cold, dropping them into a gray computer center in Moscow full of humming machines. A scientist stared at a screen where blocky shapes fell from the top, stacking into a messy pile.

"They won't fit," he muttered, trying to cram a square sideways into a gap built for something thinner.

Theo had spent hours fitting blocks into tight spaces in Roblox Studio. "Rotate it," he said, nodding at a key on the panel. "Don't force it — turn it."

The scientist tapped the key. The piece spun, slid neatly into the gap, and a whole row vanished with a satisfying **FWOOMP**, the blocks above dropping down to fill the space.

"**Alexey Pajitnov**," Blip said, "built this puzzle game in **1984**, right here at a Moscow computer center. You know it as **Tetris** — falling blocks you rotate and fit together to clear lines. Still one of the most played games ever made."

The screen glitched again, and Theo stood in a bright toy store, boxes everywhere showing a mustached man in overalls leaping over a turtle.

"Nintendo needed America to trust games again after the crash," Blip explained. "So in **1985**, they released the **NES** — bundled with a brand-new game starring a jumping plumber."

"**Shigeru Miyamoto** designed him," Blip added. "**Super Mario Bros.** Probably the most famous character in video games, and he started as a free extra in the box."

Theo picked up a box with Mario mid-jump on the cover and grinned. "A free extra that took over the world. Not bad."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Faster, Fuller, and Linked Together (1991–1994)
chapters.text:
The next jump was fast — literally. Blip barely had time to say hello before a blue blur zipped past Theo's head, leaving a looping green trail of light.

"That's **Sonic the Hedgehog**," Blip said, catching his breath. "Released by **Sega** in **1991**, built to be faster than anything Nintendo had — their answer to Mario."

Before Theo could ask anything else, the scene swapped to a cluttered office stacked with gray computers wired together in a tangle. Two players sat back-to-back, grinning at separate screens showing the same maze-like level.

"The cable's not carrying signal," one said, frowning at a dead connection.

Theo had wired up enough multiplayer test servers for his own Roblox games to spot a loose network cable on sight. He traced the wire, found the disconnected end, and clicked it firmly into place.

Both screens lit up at once, now linked.

"That's **Doom**," Blip said, "from **1993** — one of the games that got people connecting computers together just to play with friends in the same room. People called those **LAN parties**: everyone brings their own computer and plugs them all together."

One more flicker, and they stood in a living room glowing with the colors of a brand-new disc spinning inside a sleek gray console.

"**Sony** jumped into consoles in **1994** with the **PlayStation**," Blip said. "It used CDs instead of cartridges, which meant games could suddenly have fuller sound and smoother video."

Theo watched the disc spin and thought about every online Roblox match he'd ever joined. People had been plugging computers together to play with friends since long before his parents were his age.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back to the Carpet, Blocks and All (2006–Tonight)
chapters.text:
The last doorway opened onto a living room where a grandmother stood holding a white remote, swinging it like a tennis racket at a screen showing a cartoon version of herself doing the exact same swing.

"I haven't played a game since Pong," she laughed, swinging again.

"This is the **Wii**," Blip said, "from **Nintendo** in **2006**. It used motion controllers — ones that could feel you moving your arm — and it pulled in people who'd never really gamed before."

Theo watched the grandmother line up another swing and thought it looked a lot like lining up a free kick. "Follow through, don't just tap it!" he called. She swung smoother, and the on-screen ball sailed clean. She whooped.

The scene shifted one last time into a world made entirely of chunky cubes — grass, stone, trees, all built from blocks.

"Recognize the shape?" Blip asked.

Theo laughed. Of course he did — half his own Roblox builds used the same blocky logic. "**Minecraft**," he said.

"Made by Swedish developer **Markus 'Notch' Persson**, released in **2011**," Blip confirmed. "It went on to become the best-selling video game ever made. Blocky worlds built one piece at a time — sound familiar?"

"Extremely," Theo said.

One final flicker brought them into a quiet museum hall, glass cases lining the walls with old cartridges, consoles, and a very familiar oscilloscope.

"The **World Video Game Hall of Fame**," Blip said, "opened in **2015** at a museum called The Strong, in **Rochester, New York**. Every game you've met tonight has a case here somewhere."

Theo looked down the long hall at decades of glowing screens, and grinned. "I've got a few builds that might belong here someday."

Then the museum dissolved into familiar black and green, and Theo landed back on his bedroom floor, laptop glowing softly beside him, Roblox Studio still open to his half-finished stadium. On the screen, small and easy to miss, a single green pixel blinked once before fading — Blip, signing off until next time.

Theo looked at his penalty-kick level, at the gravity slider he'd been fighting with for an hour, and nudged it exactly the way Higinbotham once had. The ball arced perfectly over the crossbar.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a whole stadium left to build.

true_facts.text: William Higinbotham built **Tennis for Two** in **1958**, showing it on an **oscilloscope** — an old screen that draws glowing lines — at **Brookhaven National Laboratory**.
In **1962**, **Steve Russell** and his MIT friends programmed **Spacewar!** on a giant computer called the **PDP-1**.
**Ralph Baer** built a wooden game machine called the **Brown Box** in the late 1960s, the first game made for a home TV.
Baer's box became the **Magnavox Odyssey** in **1972** — the first video game console anyone could buy for home.
Also in **1972**, **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started **Atari** and released the arcade hit **Pong**.
A fun story says one **Pong** machine jammed because it got stuffed with too many quarters — nobody's totally sure it's true, but it shows how fast the game caught on.
In **1978**, designer **Tomohiro Nishikado** made **Space Invaders**, which kicked off a worldwide arcade craze.
In **1980**, **Toru Iwatani** made **Pac-Man** — the story goes he got the idea from a pizza missing a slice.
In **1983**, too many rushed, low-quality games flooded stores, and the video game market shrank fast — people call it **the video game crash**.
Unsold cartridges, including a game based on **E.T.**, were buried in a **landfill** in New Mexico — and diggers actually found them there in **2014**.
**Shigeru Miyamoto** designed **Super Mario Bros.** in **1985**, starring the most famous character in video games.
**Alexey Pajitnov** invented **Tetris** in **1984** at a computer center in Moscow — falling blocks you rotate to clear lines.
**Sega** released **Sonic the Hedgehog** in **1991**, built to be faster than Mario.
**Minecraft**, made by **Markus 'Notch' Persson** and released in **2011**, went on to become the best-selling video game ever.

new_recurring.name: Blip
new_recurring.rule: A small glitching pixel figure who appears inside any screen gone black-and-green, pulls the child through to a real moment in history or science, and changes his own pixel style to match the era he's visiting.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Theo returned to his bedroom floor to find his half-finished Roblox stadium still open on the laptop, and used what he'd just learned to finally nail the gravity slider on his penalty kick.

story.title: Milo, Juno and the Brick Full of Sharks
story.subtitle: A swim through time with the fin-tastic fish of the sea

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Ocean Before Dinosaurs
chapters.text:
Milo lay on his bedroom carpet, snapping a grey LEGO fin onto a LEGO shark. Juno sat next to him, walking her dinosaur across the rug in little stomps.

It had been a whole week since the magic red brick last went **CLICK**. Milo almost forgot — until it started to glow.

"Juno! It's doing the thing!" Milo whispered.

The little red brick buzzed on the shelf, brighter and brighter, until the whole room filled with blue light. **WHOOOOSH!** The carpet melted into water, and the water melted into a wide, old ocean.

"Where are the dinosaurs?" Juno asked, looking all around.

"That's the surprise," said a bubbly voice. A small red brick with eyes popped up beside them, wearing a tiny snorkel. "Sharks were swimming in the sea for a **super** long time before any dinosaur ever took a step. A long, long time ago — before trees, even!"

Milo's mouth fell open. "Before trees?"

"Before trees," said the brick. "Want to go find one?"

Milo pointed at a shadow gliding past a rock. "There! I SEE ONE!"

Because Milo pointed first, the brick spun them gently toward the shadow, and the old grey shark swam closer, curious but calm.

"Good eyes, Milo," said the brick. "Sharks have been doing that swim for a long, long time."

Juno giggled and pretended to swim like the shark, wiggling her whole body side to side.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Bendy Bones
chapters.text:
The old shark swam a slow circle around them, and Juno reached out — then stopped herself, remembering to just look, not touch.

"Its bones look wiggly," Juno said, squinting.

"Sharp eyes again!" said the brick. "A shark's skeleton isn't hard like yours. It's made of something bendy called **cartilage** — that's the same squishy, bendable stuff that's in the top of your ear. Try wiggling your ear!"

Milo and Juno both grabbed an ear and wiggled it. "Bendy!" Juno shouted.

"Exactly," said the brick. "Bendy bones help a shark twist and turn fast in the water."

Milo watched the shark flex its whole body like a ribbon. "That's why it swims so wiggly!"

"You got it," said the brick, spinning happily. "Nice work, Milo."

The shark gave one more lazy wiggle and swam off into the blue, and the water around them began to swirl into a brand new color.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: So Many Kinds!
chapters.text:
The water cleared into a busy reef, full of shapes zooming every which way.

"Whoa," said Milo. "How many kinds of sharks ARE there?"

"Guess!" said the brick.

Milo thought hard. "Ten?"

"Bigger!" said the brick, bouncing. "More than **five hundred** different kinds of sharks swim in our oceans right now. Some are long, some are round, some are even tiny!"

Juno spotted something odd near the coral — a little shark walking on its fins like tiny paddles. "IT'S WALKING!" she yelled, stomping her feet just like it.

"You found the right one, Juno!" said the brick. "That's a walking shark. It uses its fins like little feet to climb over the reef, and it barely needs to breathe much air to do it."

Milo laughed. "A shark that walks better than it swims!"

"Some days," said the brick, "sharks surprise even me."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
A shadow the size of a school bus slid overhead, blocking out the light.

Juno froze. "Is it scary?"

"Let's find out," said the brick calmly, and they floated up beside the enormous shark.

Milo looked at its huge, open mouth. "That mouth is SO big."

"That's the whale shark," said the brick. "The biggest fish in the whole sea, longer than a school bus! But guess what it eats?"

Milo guessed first. "Seals?"

"Nope," said the brick.

Juno guessed next, scrunching up her nose. "Tiny, tiny bits?"

"Right, Juno! Teeny tiny floaty bits called plankton. This giant just gulps water and strains out the small stuff, like a soup strainer."

Milo grinned. "So it's huge AND gentle."

"Huge and gentle," agreed the brick, "and some whale sharks live over a hundred years — practically forever!"

Juno waved up at the giant shadow as it swam on, careful to keep her hands to herself.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Tooth After Tooth
chapters.text:
Something flashed white in the water ahead — rows and rows of pointy teeth.

"That's a great white shark," said the brick. "It can grow as long as a car, with teeth like little triangles, all in neat rows."

Milo leaned close, carefully, from a safe distance. "Why so many rows?"

"Smart question," said the brick. "Sharks lose teeth all the time, and new ones just slide forward to take their place. A shark can grow thousands of teeth in its whole life!"

Juno gasped. "THOUSANDS?"

"Like a never-ending tooth conveyor belt," said the brick.

Milo counted the rows with his finger in the water, not touching. "One, two, three rows!"

"Good counting," said the brick, "now let's go meet a tooth from a shark so big, it would make this one look small."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Giant from Long Ago
chapters.text:
The water turned murky and old-looking, like a photo from long, long ago.

On the sandy floor lay a single tooth as long as Milo's whole hand.

"Whoa," Milo breathed. "Whose tooth is THAT?"

"That belonged to Megalodon," said the brick, "a giant shark that lived millions of years ago. It's not around anymore — that's called **extinct**, which just means it isn't swimming in our oceans today."

Juno looked worried for one second. "Is it coming back?"

"No, sweet pea," said the brick gently. "It's long gone. But people found its teeth, like this one, buried in the ground — those old, hardened bits left behind are called **fossils**. Teeth are almost all we have, because bendy bones don't last that long underground."

Milo picked up the giant tooth — carefully, since it wasn't attached to anything swimming — and held it next to his own hand. "It's as big as my whole hand!"

"Great measuring, Milo," said the brick. "That's exactly how scientists do it too."

Juno patted the sand where the tooth had been, happy it was just a story from long ago and nothing to worry about.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Hammer-Head Helper
chapters.text:
A strange, wide-headed shadow swam by, shaped almost like a hammer.

"That shape looks silly!" Juno laughed.

"That's a hammerhead shark," said the brick. "Its head is wide and flat, with an eye on each end. Guess why?"

Milo thought about looking both ways before crossing a street. "So it can see more stuff at once?"

"Exactly right!" said the brick, spinning in delight. "Its wide head gives it an almost all-around view, so it spots things other sharks might miss."

Juno swam her hand like the shark, looking left and right dramatically. "I see EVERYTHING!"

Milo reached toward the shark's skin, then stopped and just looked instead. "Is its skin smooth?"

"Nope — rough, like sandpaper," said the brick. "Tiny little bumps, shaped almost like teeny teeth, cover its whole body and help it slide through the water smoothly."

"Rough AND smooth swimming," said Milo. "Sharks are weird in the best way."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Shark Lady
chapters.text:
The water lightened into a sunny shallow, where a kind-looking lady in a diving mask floated, watching sharks glide by with a notebook in hand.

"Who's that?" asked Milo.

"That's Eugenie Clark," said the brick. "Everyone called her the **Shark Lady**. She spent her whole life studying sharks and showed everyone that sharks are curious — she even taught some to do tricks, like pressing a target with their nose!"

Juno clapped. "Sharks can learn things? Like me and my dinosaurs?"

"Just like you," said the brick warmly.

Milo watched the Shark Lady wave gently at a shark swimming past, never reaching out to grab it. "She just watches. She doesn't touch them."

"That's exactly how she did it," said the brick, "and that's exactly how we do it too."

The water began to swirl, pulling them up, up, up, back toward a familiar blue glow.

**WHOOOOSH!**

Milo and Juno landed softly back on their bedroom carpet. Sitting right between them was a brand new LEGO piece — a tiny grey LEGO shark tooth, shiny and new.

"A souvenir!" Milo said, snapping it onto his LEGO shark's mouth. **CLICK!**

Juno yawned a giant dinosaur-sized yawn and curled up next to her toy dinosaur.

The little red brick dimmed to a sleepy glow. "Goodnight, you two. You swam very well today."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: Sharks were swimming in the ocean a long, long time before any dinosaur ever walked — even before trees!
A shark's skeleton isn't hard like ours — it's made of bendy stuff called cartilage, just like the top of your ear.
There are more than five hundred different kinds of sharks swimming in the ocean today.
One kind of shark can even walk across the reef using its fins like little feet!
The whale shark is the biggest fish in the sea, but it mostly eats tiny floaty bits called plankton.
Some whale sharks live more than a hundred years.
The great white shark can grow as long as a car and has rows and rows of pointy teeth.
Sharks lose teeth their whole lives, and new ones keep sliding forward to replace them.
Megalodon was a giant shark from long, long ago that isn't around anymore, and we mostly know about it from its huge old teeth.
Bendy shark bones don't last long underground, so old teeth are almost all we have left from ancient sharks.
The hammerhead shark has a wide, flat head with an eye on each side, so it can see almost all around itself.
Shark skin feels rough like sandpaper because of tiny bumps all over it.
A scientist named Eugenie Clark, nicknamed the Shark Lady, studied sharks for her whole life and showed that they can learn tricks.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Back home, a tiny LEGO shark tooth souvenir appeared on the carpet, and Milo snapped it onto his LEGO shark's mouth with a CLICK.

request.care_notes: Focus on the fascinating diversity of sharks across time and ocean habitats, their hunting adaptations, and their role in the ocean. Avoid graphic descriptions of attacks or killing; keep the tone of wonder rather than fear.

story.title: Theo and the World's Oldest Game
story.subtitle: A Roblox Studio build glitches into ten thousand years of soccer.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Oldest Kickoff (China, more than 2,000 years ago)
chapters.text:
Theo was supposed to be asleep an hour ago.

Instead he was hunched over his laptop, placing the last goalpost in his Roblox Studio stadium. It had been exactly one week since the glowing message from his last game: THE NEXT LEVEL IS YOURS TO BUILD.

He had built it. A whole stadium, crowd and all. He just hadn't expected the lights in it to turn green and start buzzing.

**BZZZT.**

A square of green pixels popped up on the screen, blinked twice, and grew legs. "Player One," squeaked Bit, "you left me loading for a WEEK."

"Sorry," Theo said, grinning anyway. "What's the next level?"

Bit's screen flickered to a dusty market square, older than anything Theo had ever built. Men in long robes kicked a stitched leather ball between two poles, trying to boot it through a small hoop strung with net.

"Where even is this?" Theo asked.

"**China**," Bit said. "This game is called **cuju** — it means 'kick ball.' People have been playing it for more than **2,000 years**."

Theo watched a player miss the hoop by a mile. "That net's tiny. No way I could hit that."

"Says the kid who practices penalties every Tuesday," Bit said.

Theo grabbed the ball that rolled to his feet — in the game, Bit was quick to point out, not in real life — and lined up his shot the way his coach had taught him: plant foot, strike through the laces, bend it.

**THWOCK.** The ball curled through the hoop.

The market square cheered. A golden coin popped out of the net and zipped straight into Theo's pocket.

"First coin," Bit said, eyes glowing. "One down. A LOT more history to go."

"Level complete," Theo said, and the market dissolved into green static, already loading the next one.

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Game They Banned (London, 1314)
chapters.text:
The static cleared into a muddy street crammed with shouting people.

A ball — more like a lump of stitched rags — bounced between fifty players at once. There were no teams Theo could tell apart, no goals he could see, and definitely no referee.

"This is **mob football**," Bit said. "Whole villages against whole villages. Through streets, over fences, across rivers."

"There's no rules at all?"

"Pretty much none. It got so wild that **King Edward II banned it in London in 1314**." Bit sounded delighted by this. "Too many broken windows."

Theo watched a man crash through a market stall chasing the ball and decided banning it made some sense.

A shout went up ahead — somebody had lost the ball completely, kicked clean over a wall into a stone castle's yard.

"That's not just any castle," Bit said, quieter now. "Look familiar?"

Theo squinted at the banner. "**Stirling Castle**?"

"Good eyes. Someone's about to lose a ball in there, and nobody finds it for centuries."

Theo thought about every time he'd lost a Roblox item in his own badly organized inventory. "If I built this castle, where would I hide something I didn't want found?"

He scanned the walls — not climbing them, just looking — and pointed at a gap behind a wooden beam, the kind of spot nobody checks. Bit zoomed the screen in. Tucked in the gap was an old leather ball, stitched shut around something soft.

"That," Bit said, "is a **ball made from a pig's bladder, maybe hidden here since the 1540s**. When people finally found it, hundreds of years later, it turned out to be the oldest football anybody's ever found."

"I found the oldest ball in the world," Theo said, "and I didn't even have to climb anything."

"Builder's eye," Bit said, and a second coin dropped into Theo's pocket.

chapters.heading: Level 3: One Rulebook to Rule Them All (London, 1863)
chapters.text:
Next came a tidy room full of serious men in suits, arguing over a single sheet of paper.

"Why does everyone look so grumpy?" Theo asked.

"Because every school and town had different football rules," Bit said. "Some let you carry the ball. Some let you trip people. It was chaos."

Theo thought about the time three friends tried to play his Roblox map with three different control settings, and nothing worked until he wrote one rulebook into the game itself.

"They need one rulebook," Theo said. "An actual official one. Everybody follows the same settings, or nobody can play together."

As if on cue, a man near the front stood up. A small plaque on the table read **Ebenezer Cobb Morley**.

"No carrying the ball," Morley announced. "Feet only."

A few men groaned. One, mid-argument, was literally holding the ball under his arm. He looked at Morley, looked at the ball, and dropped it, sheepish.

"That's it," Bit said. "The **Football Association was founded in London on 26 October 1863**, and that 'no hands' rule is still football's most basic law."

"What do they call this sport now?" Theo asked.

"Association football," Bit said. "Schoolboys shortened 'assoc' into a nickname. By the **1880s**, that nickname was — "

"**Soccer**," Theo finished, grinning. "That word's been real this whole time?"

"Since the actual 1880s," Bit confirmed. "You've just been saying it your whole life like a champion."

The grumpy room cheered as the rule got written down for good. A third coin landed in Theo's pocket, heavier than the last two, like it knew how important this one was.
chapters.shout_line: IT'S BEEN SOCCER THE WHOLE TIME!

chapters.heading: Level 4: A World Full of Firsts (1871–1904)
chapters.text:
The screen split into three glowing doors, each stamped with a date.

"Three firsts," Bit said. "Pick an order and I'll show you each one."

Theo studied the doors the way he studied a build order in Roblox Studio — biggest foundation first, details after.

"Competitions before countries," he said, "and countries before the whole world." He pointed at the doors in that order.

Door one swung open on a packed stadium with a silver cup held high. "The **FA Cup** started in **1871-72**," Bit said. "It's the oldest football competition still being played anywhere on Earth."

Door two showed a foggy field in Scotland, two teams lined up, nobody scoring. "**Scotland and England played the first official international match in 1872, in Glasgow**," Bit said. "Final score: nothing to nothing."

"That's it? A tie?" Theo said, using the word his coach always used for a game with no winner.

"A proud, scoreless, historic tie," Bit agreed.

Door three opened on a meeting room in Paris, seven flags on the table. "**FIFA**, the organization that still runs football's biggest tournaments, was **founded here in Paris in 1904**," Bit said. "Seven countries started it."

Theo looked back at his own order — competitions, then countries, then the whole world. "That's basically how I built my stadium map too. Small stuff first, then it gets huge."

"Builder's brain strikes again," Bit said, and three golden coins — one for each door — dropped into Theo's pocket at once.

"BZZZT," Bit added happily. "Overachiever."

chapters.heading: Level 5: The First World Cup (Uruguay, 1930)
chapters.text:
The next level roared to life with actual crowd noise, thousands of people packed into a brand-new stadium.

"Where's this?" Theo shouted over the noise.

"**Uruguay**, **1930**," Bit shouted back. "The very first **World Cup**. Uruguay's hosting — and so far, undefeated."

Theo watched teams in bright kits jog onto the grass. "How many teams made it?"

"Not many. Getting to South America back then meant weeks on a boat. A lot of European teams just didn't bother showing up."

Theo frowned at the half-empty list of flags. "That seems like a problem you'd fix in an update."

"They did, eventually," Bit said. "Give it decades."

A huge cheer rattled the stadium as the home team scored.

"Who's winning?" Theo asked.

Bit checked an invisible scoreboard only Bit could see. "**Uruguay beats Argentina in the final**," Bit reported. "The home crowd is not going home sad tonight."

Theo noticed a gleaming trophy on a stand near the sideline, smaller than he expected for something this important.

"That little thing is the whole prize?" Theo asked.

"That little thing," Bit said, "is the start of the **World Cup**. People will be chasing it for the next hundred years."

Theo held his hand near the trophy — not touching it, just admiring the shine — and a golden coin lifted off its base instead, floating straight to him.

"Guess it likes you," Bit said. "Five coins now. Want to see where that trophy ends up?"

"Obviously," Theo said.

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Dognapped Trophy (England, 1966)
chapters.text:
The green static cleared into a cluttered London hall, trophies locked in glass cases.

"This feels like a heist movie," Theo said.

"Close," Bit said. "In **1966**, right before England hosted the World Cup, somebody stole the actual **World Cup trophy** out of its case."

Theo's stomach dropped a little. "Before the tournament even started?"

"For about a week," Bit said. "The whole country went looking."

Theo looked around the hall — no trophy in sight, just scuffed footprints near an open window and a scrap of wrapping paper on the floor.

"Footprints lead outside," Theo said, pointing. "If I were hiding something I didn't want found, I wouldn't leave it in a building everyone's already searching."

Outside, a dog was sniffing along a hedge, tail going like a windshield wiper. Theo didn't touch him, didn't call him over — just watched where his nose pulled him, the way you'd watch a teammate who already knows where the ball is going.

The dog shoved his nose under the hedge and barked once, sharp and proud.

"That," Bit said, grinning wide, "is **Pickles**. A dog who found the missing World Cup trophy, wrapped in newspaper under a hedge, exactly one week after it vanished."

"Good dog," Theo said, staying well back and letting Pickles have his moment.

"**England hosted — and won — that World Cup**," Bit added. "Their only title so far. Not bad for a tournament that almost lost its own trophy."

A sixth coin, slightly dog-eared at the edges, landed in Theo's pocket.

"Level complete," Bit said. "And nothing got chewed."

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Three-Time Champion (Brazil)
chapters.text:
The next field was impossibly green, and one player on it made the ball look like it was on a string.

"Who is THAT?" Theo said, watching a trick that would've broken his Roblox physics engine.

"**Pele**," Bit said. "Brazilian forward. Watch."

Pele flicked the ball over one defender, then another, like they were standing still.

"He's good," Theo said, "but is he World-Cup good?"

"He's the only player ever to be on **three World Cup-winning teams** — **1958, 1962, and 1970**," Bit said. "Nobody's matched that since."

Theo did the math out loud. "That's three tournaments, years apart. He just kept being that good?"

"Kept being that good," Bit confirmed.

Theo watched Pele set up a shot and copied his own stance without thinking — plant foot, strike through the laces, the same move his coach drilled every Tuesday. It wasn't the same as doing it for real, but it felt close enough.

"I practice that shot every week," Theo said. "He basically invented it."

"He didn't invent the shot," Bit said, "but he probably perfected about nine other things while you were saying that sentence."

Pele's shot curled into the top corner. The crowd went off like a stadium-sized firework.

A seventh coin dropped into Theo's pocket, warm, like it had soaked up some of the goal's energy.

"Okay," Theo admitted, "that guy's getting a statue in my next build."

chapters.heading: Level 8: The Team They Tried to Stop (England, 1921–1991)
chapters.text:
The static cleared into a packed stadium, way more packed than Theo expected.

"This can't be a small game," Theo said. "Look at all these people."

"It's not small," Bit said. "This is the **Dick, Kerr Ladies**, one of England's most popular football teams — thanks partly to their star player, **Lily Parr**."

Theo watched Parr blast a shot past a diving goalkeeper. "She's incredible. Why have I never heard of her?"

Bit's screen flickered, a little less cheerful than usual. "Because right after this, the people running English football decided women couldn't play on their official grounds anymore. The ban started in **1921**."

Theo's face fell. "That's not fair. She was clearly amazing."

"It wasn't fair," Bit agreed. "And it lasted a long time."

"How long?"

"**Fifty years**," Bit said. "The FA didn't lift that ban until **1971**."

Theo sat with that for a second, genuinely annoyed on behalf of a player he'd met five minutes ago. Then he noticed something flickering on the stadium scoreboard — a date trying to load.

"What's that trying to show?" Theo asked, pointing.

Bit followed his finger, and the screen resolved into a different stadium, decades later, flags from all over the world.

"That's what happened once they got the chance," Bit said. "The **first official Women's World Cup was held in China in 1991** — and the **United States won it**."

Theo grinned, relieved. "So she basically kicked the door open."

"Someone had to kick first," Bit said. "You'd know."

An eighth coin, gold with a tiny stitched pattern like a jersey, dropped into Theo's hand.

"Last level's coming up," Bit said. "Ready to go home?"

chapters.heading: Level 9: Home Screen
chapters.text:
The green static cleared for the last time, and Theo's actual bedroom came back into focus — same stadium build glowing on his laptop, same messy carpet underneath him.

Eight golden coins sat scattered across his keyboard, each one humming faintly.

"Okay," Theo said, "what happens to all these?"

"Watch," Bit said.

The coins lifted off the keyboard, spun together in midair, and melted into one shape — a small golden trophy, not unlike the one from Uruguay, sitting right there on his desk.

"One trophy," Bit said, "for every level you actually solved instead of just watching. The hoop shot. The hidden ball. The rulebook. All of it."

Theo picked it up — not a real historical artifact, just a glowing souvenir that was somehow, impossibly, real on his desk — and turned it over in his hands. "So soccer's basically been one long update. Cuju, then rules, then cups, then the whole world playing."

"And it's still updating," Bit said. "New rules. New teams. New players nobody's heard of yet."

Theo thought about his own game, half-built, waiting on his screen. He thought about Lily Parr kicking a door open, and Pele making physics look optional, and a dog finding a trophy nobody else could.

"I've got ideas for my map now," Theo said.

Bit's pixel eyes went a little watery, same as always right before the screen faded. "Save your progress, Player One."

The screen dimmed to standby. The little trophy stayed exactly where it was, catching the hallway light.

Tomorrow, Theo had a stadium to finish.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, Theo had a stadium to finish.

story.title: Juno, Milo, and Theo and the Rumbly Rock
story.subtitle: A whooshing journey through how volcanoes work.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Rumbly Rock
chapters.text:
Juno lined up her dinosaurs in a neat row, matching the pillow mountain behind them. Milo snapped together a LEGO shark, perfect for guarding his pretend LEGO reef. Theo tapped his tablet, deep in a Roblox game. It was way past bedtime, but nobody felt sleepy yet.

On the shelf, a small gray rock began to glow. It gave a tiny RRRUMBLE.

'That rock is glowing!' Theo said. He leaned close. The glow pulsed, on and off, just like his game's loading screen.

Theo tapped the rock, twice, the way he always tapped to start a level.

The rock popped open like a tiny hatch. A warm, rumbly voice said, 'Hello! I'm Rumble. I'm a tiny piece of something huge — a **volcano**!'

'What's a volcano?' Juno asked, hugging her favorite dinosaur close.

'A volcano is a secret door in the ground,' said Rumble. 'Hot melty rock can push up through it, way down deep.'

'Whoa,' said Milo. 'Like a secret hatch, but for rocks!'

'Exactly like that,' said Rumble. 'Want to see one, up close?'

'YES!' all three kids shouted at once.

Rumble glowed bright and warm. 'Rumble rumble, ready to roll!'

WHOOOOSH! The bedroom spun into orange light.

When it stopped, warm ground sat under their feet. Ahead of them, a crack in the earth glowed bright orange, like a sleepy eye, slowly opening.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Magma's Secret Name
chapters.text:
The glowing crack bubbled, slow and thick, like soup on a stove.

Juno peeked over the edge, careful and curious.

'It's glowy orange goo,' she said. 'Is that lava?'

Rumble gave a rumbly little laugh. 'Close! While it's still down here, under the ground, we call it **magma**. The very same melty rock gets a brand-new name — **lava** — once it comes outside.'

'So... underground name, outside name?' Milo asked, snapping two LEGO bricks together.

'Exactly,' said Rumble.

Juno watched one bubble pop. 'That one's still down here,' she said. 'So it's still magma!'

'You got it, Juno,' said Rumble. 'You just figured out the rule, all by yourself.'

Milo swam his toy shark near the warm rock. 'Even sharks would want a snack break from this heat,' he said. Everybody giggled.

Theo grinned. 'So lava is basically magma's outside name. Like a secret identity.'

Rumble rumbled happily. 'Something like that.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Ring of Fire
chapters.text:
Rumble pulled out a small, glowing map, round like a tiny globe.

'The ground of Earth is cracked into giant puzzle pieces, called **plates**,' said Rumble. 'Most volcanoes live right where plates meet, push, or slide past each other.'

Theo studied the map. Orange dots curled all around one big ocean, in a long, bendy shape.

'That looks like a horseshoe!' Theo said. 'Or a goal net, bent clean around the whole ocean.'

'Good eye,' said Rumble. 'People call that shape the **Ring of Fire**. About seventy-five out of every hundred awake volcanoes on Earth live along it.'

Milo counted glowing dots bunched close together, near a cluster of islands.

'There's a ton right here!' Milo said, pointing.

'That's **Indonesia**,' said Rumble. 'More volcanoes live there than in any other country on Earth.'

'Called it!' Milo cheered, doing a little victory dance.

Juno spun in a circle. 'I'm an awake volcano too!' she yelled.

Everybody laughed, and even the glowing map seemed to wobble along with them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Kilauea Never Stops
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH! Rumble zoomed them to a warm, sunny island.

'Where are we?' Milo asked, sniffing salty air. 'Smells like shark country.'

'Hawaii,' said Rumble. 'This volcano isn't on the edge of a plate. It sits over a hot spot — extra-hot rock rising up from deep down below.'

A steady BUMP... BUMP... BUMP came from the ground.

Milo tilted his head, listening close. 'It keeps doing that. Does it ever stop?'

'Barely,' said Rumble. 'This one is called **Kilauea**. It has been **erupting** — spitting out hot rock — almost nonstop, for years and years.'

'That's one busy volcano,' Milo said. 'Like a shark that never stops swimming.'

Theo nodded. 'Kilauea basically has infinite respawns.'

Juno held her hand near the warm ground, not too close, and felt the BUMP BUMP. 'I can feel its heartbeat!' she said.

Everyone smiled. Even Rumble's glow gave a happy little flicker.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Shield Mountain
chapters.text:
Rumble floated them up high, above a wide, giant mountain, round and smooth like a dome.

'This one is **Mauna Loa**,' said Rumble. 'It's the biggest awake volcano on Earth. It rises over **four thousand meters** above the sea.'

Milo's eyes went huge. 'That is SO tall.'

'Some volcanoes are wide and flat, like a shield,' said Rumble. 'Others are tall and pointy, like a party hat. Mauna Loa is the wide, shield kind.'

Milo pictured two LEGO shapes in his head — one flat dome, one tall cone.

'This one has to be the flat shield shape,' he said. 'It's way too wide to be pointy!'

'Exactly right,' said Rumble.

Theo grinned. 'Mount Fuji in Japan is the pointy, party-hat kind, right?'

'You got it,' said Rumble.

Juno giggled. 'Party hat volcano! Like a birthday, but spicy!'

Everybody laughed so hard, Rumble wobbled and nearly rolled right off the mountain.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Baby Island
chapters.text:
Next, Rumble brought them to a cool, breezy island.

'This is Iceland,' said Rumble. 'It sits right where two giant plates are slowly pulling apart.'

Theo watched a thin crack in the ground, inching wider. 'Like two puzzle pieces sliding apart, in slow motion,' he said.

'Exactly,' said Rumble. 'And sometimes, when a volcano erupts under the sea nearby, something amazing happens.'

The ocean in front of them fizzed and popped. Juno leaned in, watching bubbles gather in one spot, again and again.

'Something's growing there!' Juno said, pointing. 'It's getting taller every time it bubbles!'

'You found it,' said Rumble. 'Back in **1963**, a brand-new island rose right out of the sea, just like that. They named it **Surtsey**.'

'A whole new island, just born?' Milo said. 'That's wild.'

'From nothing to an island,' Theo said. 'Better than any Roblox build.'

Juno clapped. 'I found the baby island!'

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Tallest Mountain Ever
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH! The ground turned red and dusty, crunching under their feet.

'Where are we now?' Milo asked.

'Not on Earth at all,' said Rumble. 'Say hello to Mars.'

Ahead, a mountain rose so tall, its top vanished into the pink sky.

'Give me a number, Rumble,' Theo said, the way he always asked for stats before a big match.

'This is **Olympus Mons**,' said Rumble. 'It's about **thirteen point six miles** high. Stack up nearly three Mount Everests, and you would still look up at it.'

Theo did quick math in his head, the way he counted goals in a tied match. 'Three Everests? That's not a mountain. That's a tower!'

'It's the biggest volcano anyone has ever found, anywhere,' said Rumble.

Juno looked way, way up. 'I can't even see the top-top!'

Theo pointed straight at the peak, calling it like a shot on goal. 'I vote this one. Biggest volcano champion, no contest.'

'Good call,' said Rumble. 'Nobody has found a bigger one yet.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again
chapters.text:
Back near the warm island, Rumble showed them a small, quiet machine, blinking softly in the dark.

'Scientists use a machine called a **seismograph**,' said Rumble. 'It feels teeny-tiny shakes in the ground. If the ground wiggles more than usual, a volcano might be waking up.'

Juno put her ear close to the ground, careful not to touch the warm rock. She listened hard. 'I hear a teeny tiny wiggle!' she said.

'Good listening,' said Rumble. 'That is just what the machine does, with its whole metal body.'

Milo looked at the dark, dusty ground nearby. 'Why would anybody live so close to a volcano, if it wiggles and pops?'

'Because when the ash settles down,' said Rumble, 'it turns into some of the best dirt for growing food. Farmers plant their crops right next to volcanoes, because that dirt helps plants grow big and strong.'

'Spicy dirt, super plants,' Theo said. 'Nature's weird, but kind of brilliant.'

Rumble's glow dimmed, soft and sleepy. 'Time to go home, I think.'

'Rumble rumble, ready to roll!' all three kids shouted together.

WHOOOOSH! Orange light spun around them — and then: carpet. Bedroom. Juno's dinosaurs, still lined up. Milo's LEGO shark, still on guard. Theo's tablet, screen dark and quiet.

On the rug sat one small, warm, gray rock, glowing just a little, like it was still a tiny bit awake.

'Goodnight, Rumble,' Milo whispered, tucking it next to his shark, right where it belonged.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Theo. Rumble rumble... sleep well.

A giant horseshoe shape around the ocean, called the **Ring of Fire**, holds most of the world's awake volcanoes.

story.title: Juno and the Buzzy Hive
story.subtitle: A tiny adventure inside a bee's busy home.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Buzzy Light
chapters.text:
Juno lined up her dinosaurs on the rug, stomp, stomp, stomp.

Her nightlight was shaped like a little gold bee. Tonight it buzzed — BUZZZZ! — and glowed bright.

"Hello?" Juno whispered.

The bee light opened like a tiny door. WHOOOSH! Juno shrank down, down, down, right through it.

She landed inside a hive — a bee's cozy house. Gold walls hummed all around. A big bee floated close.

"I'm the queen," she said. "I lay the eggs here."

"How many?" Juno asked.

"Up to two thousand. Every single day!"

Juno tried to count on her fingers and gave up fast. "That's SO many!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Busy, Busy Bees
chapters.text:
Bees zoomed past in every direction. Juno ducked.

"Who are they?" she asked.

"Worker bees," said the queen. "All girls. They do every job — cleaning, guarding, finding flowers. They take turns."

Juno watched one bee get stuck in a crowd near the door.

"Make a path!" Juno called out.

The bees heard her and scooted apart. The stuck bee zipped through. CLICK — right into her spot.

"Nice fix," said the queen.

Juno beamed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Five Eyes and Fast Wings
chapters.text:
A worker bee hovered close, buzzing loud.

"Why so loud?" Juno covered her ears a little.

"My wings flap two hundred times every second," the bee said. "That's the buzz!"

Juno looked closer. "You have lots of eyes!"

"Five," said the bee. "Two big ones for colors and shapes. Three tiny ones on top, just for light."

Juno counted them out loud. "One, two... five! Got it!"

She pointed to a bee near the door. "That one's going flower-hunting, I bet."

"Good guess," said the queen. "Follow her."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Waggle Dance
chapters.text:
They followed the flower-hunter to a flat wall of wax.

The bee wiggled — left, right, left, right, round in a circle.

Juno giggled. "Is she dancing?"

"She's telling everyone where the flowers are," said the queen. "It's called the waggle dance. A scientist named Karl figured out what it meant."

The wiggle pointed toward a sunny patch outside.

"She's pointing THAT way!" Juno shouted, pointing too.

The other bees buzzed off, straight toward the sun.

"You read her dance just right," said the queen.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Two Million Flowers
chapters.text:
They floated out into a sunny meadow full of flowers.

"Bees drink the sweet juice inside flowers," said the queen. "It's called nectar."

Juno watched a bee dip into one flower, then another, then another.

"How many flowers for one pound of honey?" Juno asked.

"About two million," said the queen.

Juno's mouth popped open. "TWO MILLION? That's more than all my dinosaurs!"

"And one bee only makes a tiny drop in her whole life," said the queen, "smaller than a teaspoon."

Juno patted her tummy. "I'd need a LOT of bees for breakfast toast."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Six-Sided Rooms
chapters.text:
Back in the hive, Juno looked closely at the walls.

Every little room had six straight sides, like a stop sign.

"Why six sides?" Juno asked.

"Six-sided rooms hold the most honey using the least wax," said the queen. "Bees are great builders."

Juno counted the sides slowly with her finger. "One, two, three, four, five, six!"

"Perfect hexagon," said the queen. "That's the fancy word for a six-sided shape."

Juno grinned. "Hexagon. I like that word."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Shivery and Warm
chapters.text:
Outside, wind rattled the hive. Juno shivered. "Is it getting cold?"

"Watch," said the queen.

All the bees huddled together in one big clump, shivering their wings fast and buzzy.

Juno felt the air warm up right away. "It's toasty again!"

"Bees shiver together to keep the hive warm," said the queen. "Just right, every time."

Juno copied the shiver-dance, hugging her own arms. "I'm a heater bee!"

The queen laughed, low and buzzy. "Best heater I've seen."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Bees With the Dinosaurs
chapters.text:
Juno spotted a shiny gold lump on a shelf nearby.

"What's that?" she asked, pointing without touching.

"Amber," said the queen. "Sticky tree drops that turned hard as rock. Some amber is super old — as old as the dinosaurs!"

Juno gasped. "Bees lived with DINOSAURS?"

"They sure did," said the queen. "Scientists found tiny bees stuck inside amber from about one hundred million years ago."

Juno pictured her toy triceratops and grinned. "You and my dinosaurs are old friends, then."

"Oldest friends ever," buzzed the queen.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Honey That Never Spoils
chapters.text:
"One more thing," said the queen. "Honey almost never goes bad."

"Never?" Juno asked.

"People in Egypt kept bees a very, very long time ago," said the queen. "And honey pots found from back then are still good to eat!"

Juno looked around the hive one more time — the gold walls, the busy buzzing.

"Time to go home," the queen said gently, nudging the glowing door open.

WHOOOSH! Juno tumbled back onto her bedroom rug, dinosaurs still lined up in a row.

On her shelf, the bee nightlight glowed soft and gold. Beside it sat a tiny gold sticker, shaped like a hexagon, that hadn't been there before.

Juno smiled and climbed into bed.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Buzz well, little bee.

true_facts.text: A beehive has **one queen bee** and lots of worker bees who help her.
The queen bee can lay up to **2,000 eggs** in just one day!
**Worker bees** are all girls, and they take turns doing every job in the hive.
A bee has **five eyes** — two big ones and three tiny ones on top of its head.
A bee's wings flap about **200 times every second**, and that's the buzzing sound!
Bees do a wiggly **waggle dance** to show the others where the flowers are.
Bees visit about **two million flowers** just to make one pound of honey.
One bee only makes a tiny bit of honey, smaller than a **teaspoon**, in her whole life.
Honeycomb rooms have **six sides**, called a **hexagon**, so bees can store lots of honey with just a little wax.
On cold days, bees **huddle together and shiver** to keep the hive warm.
Bees have been around since the time of the **dinosaurs** — scientists found tiny bees stuck in **amber** about 100 million years old.
Honey almost never goes bad — people even found old pots of honey in **Egypt** that were still good to eat!
People in **Egypt** were keeping bees a very, very long time ago.
