story.title: Sam and the Sticky Toes of Tiko the Gecko
story.subtitle: A true backyard adventure about how animals climb walls

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Gecko Door
chapters.text:
Sam knelt in the grass with his magnifying glass. He loved finding bugs.

A roly-poly rolled past his sneaker. Sam watched it curl into a tiny ball.

Then something glowed by the flowerpot. Green light. Blink, blink, blink.

Sam leaned close. It was his toy gecko nightlight! It never glowed outside before.

"Hello?" Sam whispered.

The little gecko blinked back. Its eyes went bright green. A swirly door opened in the air, right by the roses.

"Whoa," said Sam.

A real gecko popped through the door. He was orange and spotted and grinning.

"I'm Tiko," said the gecko. "I climb walls. Want to see how?"

"Yes! Yes! Yes!" Sam grinned.

He stepped through the swirly door, magnifying glass and all. **CLICK!** The door shut softly behind him.

They landed on a giant glass window. Tiko scurried straight up it, easy as walking on the ground.

"How are you not falling?" Sam asked.

"Look at my toes," said Tiko, and lifted one foot.

Sam pressed his magnifying glass close. He saw tiny lines, like tiny hairs, all over every toe.

"**Millions of tiny hairs**," said Tiko. "So small you'd need your magnifying glass times a hundred. Each hair grabs the glass just a little bit. Millions of little grabs make one big stick."

"Is it glue?" Sam asked.

"Nope!" Tiko peeled one toe up, then the next, then the next. "No glue, no mess. I just peel my toes off, like pulling up tape."

Sam tried pressing his own hand on the glass. He pulled. It came right off.

"My hand doesn't have the hairs," Sam said.

"Good thing," laughed Tiko. "You'd never get your hand off the window!"

Sam laughed so hard he snorted. Tiko laughed too, upside down.

"Where to next?" Sam asked.

Tiko pointed a toe toward a buzzing sound. "Follow that fly."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Buzzing Fly
chapters.text:
A buzzing sound got louder. **BZZZZ.**

A fat little fly landed right on the window, upside down.

"Watch this," said Tiko.

The fly walked in circles, upside down, easy as pie.

Sam pressed his magnifying glass close. He saw tiny shiny dots under each of the fly's feet.

"What's that goo?" Sam asked.

"That's its trick," said Tiko. "Flies and some beetles **squeeze a tiny bit of sticky goo** out of their feet. Like a drop of syrup under every toe."

"So it IS glue?" Sam asked.

"Sort of," said Tiko. "A gooey glue that never runs out, and it washes off clean."

Sam watched the fly lift one foot, then another. Tiny strings of goo stretched, then snapped.

"EWW! Cool!" Sam yelled.

He pressed his nose almost to the glass to look closer. The fly buzzed off, right past his ear.

"Whoa!" Sam ducked, giggling.

"Don't worry," said Tiko. "Flies are friendly. Mostly annoying, but friendly."

Sam laughed. "You're funny, Tiko."

"I try," said the gecko, doing a little spin on the glass.

Sam spotted a sparkly thread in the corner. "What's that?"

"Follow the web," said Tiko, "and find out."

Sam marched over, magnifying glass ready. He loved webs best of all, almost as much as geckos.

"Spiders!" Sam whispered, bouncing on his toes.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Sam's Favorite Spider
chapters.text:
A spider sat in the corner of the web, by the glass.

Sam's eyes went wide. Spiders were his very favorite bug of all.

"Look how she climbs," said Tiko.

The spider skittered straight up the smooth window, no slipping at all.

Sam put his magnifying glass right up to her little leg.

"Her legs are FUZZY," Sam said. "Just like your toes, Tiko!"

"Good eye," said Tiko. "**Spiders have thousands of tiny hairs on their feet too.** That's why so many spiders can climb glass, same trick as me."

"So you're cousins!" Sam said.

"Sort of cousins," Tiko chuckled. "Climbing cousins."

The spider lifted one leg and waved it, almost like hello.

Sam waved back with his whole arm. "Hi, spider! I pick up bugs in my yard all the time. I never squish them."

"She likes you for it," said Tiko. "Watch where she puts her feet."

Sam watched closely. The spider never touched her, just looked. She climbed on her own, up and over the window frame.

"I'm never scared of spiders," Sam said proudly. "I just watch."

"That's exactly right," said Tiko. "Watching is the best way to be friends with a bug."

Sam puffed up a little, proud of himself.

A tiny ant marched past his sneaker, heading up a twig toward the glass.

"Ooh, an ant!" Sam said. "Let's follow HIM."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Ant's Two Tricks
chapters.text:
The ant marched up the bark of an old twig, fast as fast could be.

Sam watched through his magnifying glass. Tiny claws on the ant's feet dug into little bumps.

"Look how he grips the rough bark," said Tiko.

Then the ant reached the smooth glass window. Sam leaned in close, waiting.

The ant's walk changed. It slowed down. Its feet seemed to stick a little, step by step.

"He's using a different trick now!" Sam said.

"You got it," said Tiko. "**Ants use sharp little claws for rough stuff, and sticky pads for smooth stuff.** They switch tools depending on the wall."

"Like how I use my rain boots for mud and my sneakers for sidewalks!" Sam said.

"Exactly like that," said Tiko, grinning.

More ants came marching, one after another, in a wobbly little line.

Sam giggled. "It's an ant conga line!"

He did a silly wiggle dance, right there on the glass ledge.

Tiko wiggled too, four legs going everywhere at once, and nearly fell off the window before catching himself with a sticky *SMACK*.

"Whoa, careful!" Sam laughed.

"Sticky feet save the day," Tiko said, dusting himself off.

Sam looked out past the window. Far away stood a tall, rocky mountain.

"What's way out there?" Sam asked.

"Someone with no sticky feet at all," said Tiko, "who still climbs like a champion. Let's go see."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Up the Rocky Cliff
chapters.text:
The swirly door opened again. **WHOOOOSH!**

Sam and Tiko floated gently above a steep, rocky cliff.

A shaggy mountain goat stood near the top, calm as could be.

"How does he not slide off?" Sam asked.

"Check his feet," said Tiko.

Sam peered through his magnifying glass at a picture Tiko held up.

"His feet have a hard edge, like a fingernail," Sam said, "and something squishy in the middle!"

"**Mountain goat hooves have a hard outer edge and a soft, grippy middle that molds to the rock,**" said Tiko. "That's why he never slips."

"Cool trick," Sam said. "No sticky hairs needed!"

Nearby, a squirrel scrambled straight up a tree trunk, quick as a flash.

"What about her?" Sam asked.

"Curved claws," said Tiko. "**Squirrels dig sharp little claws into tiny cracks and bumps** too small for us to see."

Sam watched the squirrel zip around the trunk, chasing nothing in particular, just for fun.

"She's just showing off now," Sam laughed.

"Climbers do that," said Tiko. "Even goats. Watch."

The goat hopped sideways along a ledge no wider than a shoe.

Sam gasped — then grinned, because the goat landed perfectly, steady as ever.

"He's okay!" Sam cheered. "He's great at this!"

"Goats always are," said Tiko. "Let's visit somewhere wetter next."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Frog Toes and Snail Trails
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH!** The door opened onto a damp, green pond.

A little tree frog sat on a wet leaf, sticking without a wobble.

Sam leaned close with his magnifying glass. "His toes look like tiny honeycombs!"

"Sharp eyes," said Tiko. "**Tree frog toe pads have a tiny honeycomb pattern, and they're covered in slippery wet goo, which helps them stick to wet leaves and glass.**"

"Even when it's wet?" Sam asked.

"Especially when it's wet," said Tiko. "That's his secret."

The frog hopped to a smooth rock and stuck there too, calm as a sleepy cat.

Next to the pond, a snail inched up a smooth wall, leaving a shiny trail behind it.

"Look!" Sam pointed. "He's leaving a shiny line, like glitter glue!"

"That's slime," said Tiko. "**Snails glide on a layer of slime, gripping and rippling with one big squishy foot.** It lets them stick to smooth walls without falling."

"Slime is awesome," Sam said. "I wish MY feet made slime."

"Your sneakers would be very slippery at breakfast," said Tiko, and Sam cracked up.

The snail finally reached the top of the wall and tucked into its shell for a rest.

"Good job, snail," Sam whispered, careful not to touch, just watching the way he always did.

A sharp tapping sound echoed from the trees. *Tap tap tap tap.*

"What's that?" Sam asked.

"Follow your ears," said Tiko, already climbing that way.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Woodpecker's Trick
chapters.text:
*Tap tap tap tap.* The sound got louder as they reached a tall tree.

A woodpecker clung sideways to the trunk, pecking away.

Sam watched closely. "He's not falling down at all!"

"Look at his tail," said Tiko.

Sam saw the bird's stiff tail feathers pressed flat against the bark.

"It's like a kickstand!" Sam said. "Like on my bike!"

"**Woodpeckers use stiff tail feathers as a prop, plus toes that grip two forward and two back,** for extra hold," said Tiko. "That kickstand tail holds him steady while he taps."

"Why does he tap so much?" Sam asked, giggling at the funny rat-a-tat sound.

"Looking for snacks," said Tiko. "Bugs hiding under the bark."

"Like my backyard bugs!" Sam said. "I never eat them, though. Just look."

"Good policy," Tiko said, nodding seriously.

The woodpecker paused, cocked his head at Sam, then went right back to tapping, unbothered.

Sam tapped his own fingers on his knee, copying the rhythm. *Tap tap tap!*

Tiko tapped along too, four tiny gecko toes drumming on the bark.

They both laughed so hard Sam nearly fell over.

"Okay," Sam said, catching his breath. "Is there a trick for people too? Can WE climb glass?"

Tiko's eyes sparkled. "Funny you should ask. One more stop."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Sticky Paddle and Home Again
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH!** The door opened into a big, bright room full of glass and gadgets.

A scientist stood holding two flat paddles, each one covered in tiny sticky bumps.

"What's he doing?" Sam asked.

"Watch," said Tiko.

The scientist pressed the paddles against a tall glass wall. Then he climbed, paddle by paddle, all the way up.

Sam's mouth fell open. "He's climbing like YOU, Tiko!"

"**In 2014, scientists built sticky paddles copied from gecko feet, and used them to help a real person climb a glass wall.**" said Tiko. "They studied my toes to make it work."

"You're famous!" Sam cheered.

"A little," Tiko said, puffing up proudly.

Sam looked at his own hands. "Could I make a paddle? With tape, maybe?"

"Try it," said Tiko. "Sticky tape is the closest thing we've got to gecko toes."

Sam grabbed a strip of tape from the scientist's table and pressed it to the glass. It stuck. He peeled it off, toe-style, just like Tiko.

"IT WORKS!" Sam shouted, delighted.

Tiko laughed. "Stick with it, Sam. That's the whole secret."

The swirly door glowed one more time.

"Time to go home," said Tiko gently.

Sam stepped through, and **CLICK** — he was back in his backyard, moonlight on the roses.

His gecko nightlight sat glowing softly by the flowerpot, calm and green.

Beside it lay a little strip of tape, folded over itself, sticky side in.

Sam smiled, tucked it into his pocket, and headed inside to bed, already thinking about tomorrow's bugs.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Sam. Climb well, little bug hunter.

true_facts.text: Geckos can run up glass and walk on ceilings because their toes have **millions of tiny hairs**.
A gecko's sticky grip isn't glue — it peels its toes off like pulling up tape, and it never gets messy.
Flies squeeze a tiny bit of **sticky goo** from their feet, like a drop of syrup under every toe.
Spiders have **thousands of tiny hairs** on their feet too, which is why many spiders can climb smooth glass.
Ants switch tools: **sharp little claws** for rough bark, **sticky pads** for smooth glass.
Mountain goats climb steep cliffs with **hooves that have a hard edge and a soft, grippy middle**.
Squirrels dig **sharp curved claws** into tiny cracks and bumps too small to see.
Tree frogs have toe pads with a **tiny honeycomb pattern** and slippery goo that helps them stick to wet leaves and glass.
Snails glide up smooth walls on a trail of **slime**, gripping with one big squishy foot.
Woodpeckers climb straight up trees using **stiff tail feathers as a prop**, like a kickstand.
In **2014**, scientists built sticky paddles copied from gecko feet that let a real person climb a glass wall.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Sam returns to his backyard with his gecko nightlight glowing softly and a folded strip of sticky tape in his pocket, proof of the glass wall he climbed with Tiko.

story.title: Finn and Nell and the Honey Bee Night
story.subtitle: A tiny trip into the hive, right before bedtime.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Honey Drop
chapters.text:
Finn sat on the kitchen floor in his pajamas. He had one last bite of toast. Golden honey dripped off the edge.

Nell sat next to him, holding a yellow flower from the garden. Yellow was her favorite color of all.

Then the honey drop started to glow. It hummed, soft and low, like a tiny song.

"Did you hear that?" Finn whispered.

The glow grew bigger. It turned into a window, bright and gold. A tiny bee buzzed out of it, wings sparkling.

"Hello!" said the bee. "I'm Buzz. I need some helpers tonight."

Nell held up her yellow flower. "Can we help with flowers?"

"You bet," said Buzz. "Hold on, and hop in!"

Finn grabbed Nell's hand. Together they stepped through the glowing window.

WHOOSH! They landed in a sunny meadow, buzzing with bees.

"This is where honey starts," said Buzz. "Watch."

A bee landed on a flower. She dipped in her long tongue, curly like a straw. She sipped up sweet juice called **nectar** — the sugary juice inside flowers.

Finn pointed. "She's drinking the flower!"

"That's right," said Buzz. "Nectar is bee food, and it's the start of honey too."

Nell giggled. "Flowers are juice boxes!"

Buzz laughed so hard he did a little loop in the air.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Dancing Scout
chapters.text:
Buzz led them to a bee standing on a leaf, wiggling side to side.

"What is she doing?" asked Finn. "Is she dancing?"

"She is!" said Buzz. "That's a **waggle dance** — a wiggly dance that tells other bees where to find yummy flowers."

Nell watched closely. The bee wiggled, then walked in a tiny circle, then wiggled again.

"I think she's pointing!" said Nell. "Like an arrow!"

"Smart bee," said Buzz. "Her wiggles tell them which way to fly, and how far."

Finn counted the wiggles. "One, two, three!"

Three other bees buzzed up, watching the dance. Then they zoomed off toward the flowers Nell had spotted.

"They followed her dance!" said Finn.

"Because of your sharp eyes, Nell, we know right where to go too," said Buzz, winking.

Nell twirled her own yellow flower, happy as could be.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Yellow Flower Patch
chapters.text:
They flew along and landed in a patch of flowers, all bright yellow.

Nell spun around. "My favorite color, everywhere!"

A bee crawled onto a flower. Little clumps of yellow dust stuck to her legs.

"What's that yellow stuff?" asked Finn.

"That's **pollen**," said Buzz, "yellow dust that flowers use to make new flowers. Bees carry it along without even trying."

Nell pointed at the bee's legs. "She's got pollen pants!"

Buzz laughed. "Good eye, Nell. Those fuzzy baskets on her legs are full of it."

"So the bee helps the flowers grow more flowers?" asked Finn.

"Exactly," said Buzz. "Bees get nectar, flowers get help growing. Everybody wins."

Nell found the flower with the most yellow dust and showed Buzz. "This one has the most!"

"Great find," said Buzz. "That means lots of nectar too. Follow me!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Tiny Tummy
chapters.text:
Back in the air, Finn noticed something. "Buzz, that bee's tummy looks round and shiny!"

Buzz nodded. "Good eyes! Bees have a special tummy just for nectar. It's not for eating. It's like a tiny backpack for juice."

"A juice backpack!" said Finn, giggling.

"She can carry lots of nectar home in there," said Buzz, "without using it up as food."

Nell asked, "Does it get heavy?"

"A little," said Buzz, "but she's a strong flier."

Finn watched the bee zoom toward a big old tree. "She's heading home! Should we follow her?"

"Great idea," said Buzz. "Let's go see the hive."

Nell squeezed Finn's hand. "Honey hunt!" she whispered, and off they flew.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Bee Kisses
chapters.text:
They landed outside a big tree stump. Buzz called it the **hive** — that's the bees' busy house.

Inside, it buzzed louder than ever. Nell peeked in. "There are so many bees!"

Finn watched one bee land and touch mouths with another bee.

"Why are they kissing?" asked Finn.

Buzz chuckled. "That's how they share the nectar. One bee passes it, mouth to mouth, to a house bee waiting inside."

Nell counted. "One, two, three bee kisses!"

"Every time it passes along," said Buzz, "it changes a little, getting closer and closer to real honey."

"Like passing a secret?" asked Finn.

"Just like that," said Buzz, "a sweet secret, passed all the way down the line."

Nell gave her own flower a little bee-kiss sniff, and sneezed from the tickle. Everybody laughed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Honeycomb Shapes
chapters.text:
Inside the hive, Buzz showed them walls full of tiny holes, each shaped the same.

"Count the sides," said Buzz.

Finn traced a shape in the air with his finger. "One, two, three, four, five, six!"

"Six sides, every single time," said Buzz. "Bees build these little rooms from **wax** — soft stuff bees make themselves, like tiny bricks."

Nell traced a shape with her eyes. "They're like little yellow rooms!"

"Perfect little rooms for nectar," said Buzz. "A house bee spreads the nectar right inside."

Finn pointed to an empty one nearby. "This one's empty! Can we watch it fill up?"

"Smart idea," said Buzz. "Let's wait and see."

They settled in to watch, Nell's flower tucked safely behind her ear.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Wing Fans
chapters.text:
Suddenly the air inside buzzed louder. Rows of bees stood by the open cells, wings a blur.

"What are they doing?" asked Nell, holding her flower close.

"They're fanning," said Buzz. "Their wings beat about two hundred times every second, faster than you can blink."

Finn felt a little breeze on his cheek. "It's like a tiny fan!"

"Exactly," said Buzz. "All that fanning dries up the watery nectar. It turns thick and sticky — into real honey."

Nell sniffed the air. "It smells sweet already!"

"Good nose," said Buzz. "A few more days of fanning, and that cell will be full of golden honey."

Finn grinned. "Just like the honey on my toast!"

"Exactly like that," said Buzz.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Sealed for Winter
chapters.text:
The honey cell Finn had watched was finally full, golden and thick.

A bee walked over and spread a thin lid of wax across the top, sealing it shut, like a tiny lid closing.

"Why seal it?" asked Nell.

"To keep it clean and safe," said Buzz. "Sealed honey stays good for a very, very long time. It almost never goes bad."

Finn's eyes went wide. "Never? Not even after a hundred years?"

"Not even then," said Buzz, "as long as it stays sealed up tight."

Nell asked, "But why make so much?"

"For winter," said Buzz. "When flowers stop blooming, there's no nectar to find. So the bees eat the honey they saved."

Finn nodded slowly. "Like packing a lunchbox for later."

"Just like that," said Buzz, smiling. "Smart bees, smart boy."

Nell patted her own yellow flower gently, not the bee, just her flower, and smiled. "I'm glad they save some for winter."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Busy Queen, and Home Again
chapters.text:
Deep in the hive, they found the biggest bee of all.

"That's the queen bee," said Buzz. "She's the busy mom of almost every bee here."

"Busy how?" asked Finn.

"She lays eggs," said Buzz, "sometimes more than a thousand in one single day."

Nell's mouth dropped open. "A thousand baby bees? In one day?"

"Yep," said Buzz. "Most of them grow up to be worker bees, busy bee sisters who do every job there is."

Finn looked around at the buzzing crowd. "How many bees live here?"

"This one hive has tens of thousands of bees," said Buzz, "all working together."

Nell squeezed Finn's hand. "That's a lot of helpers for one little bit of honey."

"Funny you say that," said Buzz. "It takes about twelve bees their whole lives just to make one teaspoon of honey."

Finn gasped. "One teaspoon? That's all my toast gets, and it took twelve whole bees?"

"Every drop matters," said Buzz, smiling. "Speaking of toast, I think it's time you two went home."

He led them back through the glowing window. WHOOSH! Finn and Nell tumbled softly onto the kitchen floor, right where they'd started.

The honey drop on Finn's plate glowed one last time, then faded back to plain honey.

Nell looked down at her yellow flower, still in her hand. "We really went to the hive."

Finn grinned and licked the very last bit of honey off his toast. "Twelve bees made this bite. I'm going to say thank you every time."

They climbed into bed, sleepy and sweet, the whole hive humming softly in their dreams.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Finn. Goodnight, Nell. Sleep sweet, like honey.

true_facts.text: A bee drinks sweet juice from flowers, called **nectar**, with a long tongue like a curly straw.
A scout bee does a **wiggly waggle dance** to tell her friends which way to fly for good flowers.
Bees carry **yellow pollen dust** on their legs, which helps flowers make more flowers.
Bees have a special **tummy just for nectar**, like a little backpack, separate from their food tummy.
Bees pass nectar **mouth to mouth** to other bees back at the hive.
Bees build little rooms with **six sides** out of wax they make themselves.
Bees **fan the nectar with their wings** until it turns thick and sticky, into real honey.
When honey is ready, bees **seal the little room with a wax lid** to keep it safe.
Bees save honey for **winter**, when there are no flowers to find.
A **queen bee** can lay more than **a thousand eggs in one day**.
One hive can hold **tens of thousands of bees**, all working together.
It takes about **twelve bees their whole lives** to make just **one teaspoon of honey**.

story.title: Omar and the Spoke That Remembered Everything
story.subtitle: A midnight ride through two hundred years of bicycles

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Wheel With No Pedals (1817)
chapters.text:
Omar crouched on his bike at the top of the driveway, long after bedtime. He popped a quick bunny hop over a crack in the pavement.

His front wheel wobbled, then one spoke lit up silver. CLICK. The light spun faster and faster until the whole wheel glowed like a tiny moon.

"Whoa," Omar said, gripping the handlebars tight.

WHOOOOSH. The driveway melted into dirt roads and wooden buildings. A man rolled by on a strange wooden machine with two wheels and no pedals at all.

"No pedals?!" Omar blurted.

The man hopped off, grinning. "I'm Karl. This is my running machine. You push it along with your feet, like walking, only faster." The spoke hummed softly: **1817** — this clunky wooden thing was the very first two-wheeler anyone ever built.

Omar tried the handlebars. They turned exactly like his own. "Steering's already perfect," he said. "Just needs pedals."

Karl laughed. "Folks call it the hobby horse. Some say draisine, after my last name — von Drais."

Omar pushed off down the street, gliding smooth as any BMX line he'd ever rolled. The glowing spoke pulled him forward, toward the bikes that got pedals first.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Pedals and Bone-Shaking (1860s)
chapters.text:
The wheel glowed and dropped Omar onto bumpy cobblestones. CLUNK-CLUNK-CLUNK went something beneath him.

He looked down — pedals bolted straight onto the front wheel.

"Whoa, bumpy!" Omar said, his teeth rattling with every stone.

A woman at a nearby cart laughed. "That's why we call it the boneshaker. Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement bolted those pedals on in the **1860s**."

"No gears, no smooth tires, nothing?" Omar asked.

"Nothing yet," the woman said. "Just you and every single bump."

Omar hopped the front wheel over a pothole, like he was clearing a skate-park ledge. "Honestly? Kind of fun," he said.

The spoke buzzed happily and spun him onward.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Giant Wheel (1870s)
chapters.text:
A wheel taller than a doorway rolled past, trailing a tiny back wheel behind it.

"That thing is HUGE," Omar said.

A rider waved from way up top. "Penny-farthing," he called down. "Named after two old coins — a big one, the penny, and a tiny one, the farthing. One turn of the pedals and you really fly."

Omar watched the giant wheel spin. "One push equals way more distance," he said slowly. "Kind of like a bigger gear."

"Exactly," the rider said. "Though stop too fast up here, and you go flying over the handlebars — we call that 'taking a header.'" He chuckled. "Don't worry, nobody's taking one tonight."

Omar laughed, relieved. "I'll stick to flat ground, thanks."

The spoke flashed, agreeing completely, and tugged him toward steadier wheels.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Safety Bike (1885)
chapters.text:
CLINK, CLINK went a chain as a man circled on a strange new bike.

Two wheels, the same size. A comfy seat. A chain looping between the pedals and the back wheel.

"John Kemp Starley," the man called. "Rover Safety Bicycle, **1885**. No more teetering way up on a giant wheel."

Omar crouched by the chain, tracing the links with one finger, just like he did on his own BMX. "The chain spins the back wheel," he said, "so the pedals can stay down low."

"Exactly why it's so much safer," Starley said, impressed.

Omar pedaled a slow circle, feet steady beneath him instead of way up high. "This," he said, "finally feels like a real bike."

The spoke pulsed happily and rolled him forward again.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Filled With Air (1888)
chapters.text:
BUMP BUMP BUMP — then suddenly, smooth, like gliding on a cloud.

Omar looked down and poked his tire. It squished. "These are filled with air!"

A man with a toolkit grinned. "John Boyd Dunlop. Built this kind of tire for my son's tricycle, back in **1888**. Air inside soaks up every bump."

Omar bounced the bike, feeling it bob like a tiny trampoline. "My BMX tires do this too," he said. "That's why landings don't hurt so much."

"Precisely," Dunlop said. "My little company even grew into Dunlop Tyres. You might've heard of it."

"My dad's car has those!" Omar said.

The spoke whirred, delighted, and spun onward — into a street packed with bikes.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Bicycles for Everyone (1890s)
chapters.text:
Bells rang everywhere. Bikes rolled past in every direction.

"The **1890s**," the spoke explained. "So many people bought bikes, folks called it the Golden Age."

Omar spotted women riding in baggy, puffy pants instead of long skirts. "Why do their pants look like that?" he asked.

A woman nearby pointed to her own outfit. "Long skirts get caught in the gears. These are bloomers — much safer for riding."

"Makes sense," Omar said. "You wouldn't ride a skate park in a skirt either."

She laughed. "A reformer named Susan B. Anthony even said bicycles helped women go wherever they wanted, all on their own — more than almost anything else ever had."

Omar watched the happy crowd roll by. The spoke tugged him toward a crooked little sign down the road.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Bike Shop That Flew (1900s)
chapters.text:
The smell of oil hung in the air. Two brothers tightened spokes on a wheel.

"I'm Wilbur. This is Orville. We fix bikes here in Dayton, Ohio."

Omar looked around — metal tubing, spoked wheels, tools everywhere. "This stuff looks like airplane parts," he said.

Orville raised an eyebrow. "Funny you say that. We're using these same lightweight tubes and wheel tricks to build something that flies."

"In **1903**," the spoke whispered, "these two build the world's first successful airplane."

Omar's jaw dropped. "BIKE GUYS INVENTED THE AIRPLANE?!"

"Bike guys know lightweight," Wilbur said, grinning. "Strong but not heavy — same thing you want in a good wheel."

Omar grinned back, suddenly proud of his own banged-up BMX. "Guess bikes are kind of a big deal," he said.

The spoke spun brighter than ever and pulled Omar all the way home.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Driveway
chapters.text:
Omar landed with a soft THUD, back on his own driveway, under the same porch light.

His bike looked the same as always — except one spoke still shimmered, slowly waking up.

"BMX bikes showed up in the **1970s**," the spoke said quietly. "Built tough for tricks, just like yours."

Omar grinned down at his own knobby tires. "So I'm basically riding history," he said.

"More than a billion bikes exist in the world today," the spoke added. "More than any other ride on Earth."

Omar patted his handlebars like an old friend. "Thanks for the tour," he whispered.

The spoke dimmed to a soft glow, saving its sparkle for another night.

Omar wheeled his bike quietly into the garage and tiptoed inside, past bedtime but full of wonder.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Omar. Ride well.

true_facts.text: The very first two-wheeler had no pedals at all — in **1817**, riders just pushed it along with their feet.
People nicknamed it the hobby horse, and it steered with handlebars just like a bike today.
In the **1860s**, inventors bolted pedals straight onto the front wheel, making a bumpy ride called the boneshaker.
In the **1870s**, the penny-farthing had a giant front wheel and a tiny back wheel, so one pedal turn went a long way.
Penny-farthing riders could sometimes fly over the handlebars in a fall called 'taking a header.'
In **1885**, John Kemp Starley built a bike with two same-size wheels and a chain — much closer to bikes today.
That safer design quickly became the normal kind of bike everywhere.
In **1888**, John Boyd Dunlop built air-filled tires that made the ride way smoother.
A reformer named Susan B. Anthony said bicycles helped women travel on their own more than almost anything else.
Long skirts could get caught in bike gears, so people switched to safer, puffier pants called bloomers.
The Wright brothers ran a bicycle shop in **Dayton, Ohio**, before they built their famous flying machine.
They used lightweight bike-building tricks, like thin metal tubing, to help design that flying machine.
BMX bikes, tough and built for tricks, became popular in the **1970s**.
Today there are more than a billion bicycles in the whole world.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Omar coasts home from his night ride through bicycle history, parking his bike in the garage while one spoke keeps a last faint shimmer.

story.title: Ada and the Magnet That Buzzed
story.subtitle: A fridge magnet, a tiny robot, and a planet-sized pull

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Magnet That Buzzed
chapters.text:
Ada sat on her bedroom floor. She lined up fridge magnets into a little robot shape. It had arms, legs, and a round magnet head.

The house was quiet. Everyone else was asleep.

Then one magnet buzzed. It glowed soft green.

"Whoa," Ada whispered.

The little robot sat up by itself. Its eyes blinked like two tiny magnets. "Hello, Ada," it said. "I'm Sprocket. I'm made of magnets, just like your robot."

Ada grinned. "Can you teach me how magnets work?"

"Every magnet has two ends," Sprocket said. "We call them **poles**. One is north. One is south. The pull is strongest right there."

Ada flipped a magnet over. SNAP! It stuck to another one.

She flipped it back. The two magnets slid apart, like they didn't want to touch.

"North and south love to stick," Sprocket said. "But north and north push away. So do south and south."

Ada tried again, just to hear it. SNAP! SNAP! SNAP!

"IT SNAPS!" she shouted, giggling.

"Want to see more?" Sprocket asked, holding out a tiny magnet hand.

Ada took it. The bedroom swirled into bright, curvy light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Tug of War
chapters.text:
They landed in a glowing room full of tiny spinning dots.

"These are **electrons**," Sprocket said. "Teeny spinning bits inside everything. In iron, they can team up."

Ada squinted. "Team up?"

"We call the teams **domains**," Sprocket said. "Picture mini soldiers. When they all point the same way, the whole piece turns into one strong magnet."

In wood or plastic, he added, the tiny spinners point every which way. That's why a wooden spoon never sticks to the fridge.

Ada spotted a scattered pile of dots, all pointing different directions. She waved a toy wand over them.

The dots snapped into one neat line.

WHOOSH! A brand new magnet glowed in her hand.

"You did that," Sprocket said. "You lined up the team."

Ada beamed. "I'm a magnet coach!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Magnet Rainbows
chapters.text:
On a little table sat a bar magnet and a shaker of black dust.

"Every magnet has an invisible push-and-pull zone around it," Sprocket said. "We call it a **magnetic field**. You can't see it... unless you sprinkle this."

He handed Ada the shaker. Tiny metal bits called **iron filings** poured out.

Ada sprinkled them near the magnet. The bits curved into loops, from one end to the other.

"It's like the magnet is hugging the air!" Ada said.

"That's the shape of the field," Sprocket said. "Curvy lines, end to end."

Ada sprinkled more on purpose, making the loops bigger and bigger.

"I made magnet rainbows!" she cheered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Rock That Wouldn't Turn
chapters.text:
They landed on a dusty old road. A cart creaked by.

A merchant held up a dark rock, swinging on a string. No matter how he turned it, the rock swung back to point the same way.

"That's a **lodestone**," Sprocket said. "A rock that's magnetic all by itself. People in China found rocks like this always point one direction. More than **2,000 years ago**, they used them to make the very first compasses."

Ada shut her eyes, spun around, and pointed where she guessed the rock pointed.

She opened her eyes. She'd guessed right!

"You've got a compass brain," Sprocket laughed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Follow the Leader
chapters.text:
Next they landed on a windy hilltop. Sprocket held a little compass needle, floating in water.

"Our whole planet is one giant magnet," Sprocket said. "Deep inside, swirly melted iron spins around. That makes Earth's own magnetic pull, way bigger than any fridge magnet."

The needle wobbled, then settled, pointing the same way every time.

"It's pointing north," Ada said. "Because it likes Earth's north pole!"

"Exactly," Sprocket said. "Compasses have helped travelers find their way for ages."

Ada spun in a circle. The needle swung right back to match her.

"It's playing follow the leader with the whole planet!" she laughed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Switch in the Junkyard
chapters.text:
They landed by a junkyard. A giant crane swung a rusty old car high in the air, held by nothing but a big round magnet.

Ada gasped. "What if it drops?!"

"It won't," Sprocket said. "That's an **electromagnet** — wire wrapped in loops, with electricity running through. Flip the switch on, it's strong. Flip it off, it lets go."

The crane operator flipped the switch. The car lowered gently onto a soft pile of tires. Safe and sound.

"Electromagnets are everywhere," Sprocket said. "Doorbells, speakers, even that crane."

Ada reached for a tiny switch of her own. Sprocket handed it over.

She flipped it. CLICK! A little magnet nearby lit right up.

"IT CLICKS!" Ada cheered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Magnet Babies
chapters.text:
Sprocket held up a bar magnet marked N on one end and S on the other.

"What happens if we cut it in half?" he asked.

Ada thought hard. "Does one half get all the north, and the other get all the south?"

"Good guess! But no." Sprocket snapped the magnet in two. CRACK!

Each little piece had its own north end and its own south end, just smaller.

"Every piece is its own whole magnet," Sprocket said. "You can never get just a north, all by itself."

Ada snapped it again and again, making a pile of tiny matching magnets.

"It's like magnet babies!" she giggled.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home on the Fridge
chapters.text:
They zoomed back through the swirly light, landing softly on Ada's bedroom carpet.

The green glow in her little magnet robot cooled down. Sprocket shrank smaller and smaller, until he was just a regular magnet shape in her palm.

"Will I see you again?" Ada asked.

"Whenever you line up your magnets just right," Sprocket said softly, his glow fading.

Ada looked at her fridge magnets, scattered on the carpet. "Even you're special," she said. "Bendy and rubbery, with tiny magnet bits mixed inside, so you can bend without losing your stick."

She carried her magnet robot into the kitchen and pressed him onto the fridge door. He held tight.

Then she climbed back into bed, yawning a big yawn.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ada. Stick together, shine bright, and dream in swirly lines.

true_facts.text: Every magnet has two ends called **poles** — one north, one south — where the pull is strongest.
**North and south** poles snap together, but two of the same kind push apart.
Inside magnetic metal like iron, tiny spinning bits team up as **domains**, all pointing the same way.
In things like wood or plastic, those tiny spinners point every which way, so they never stick to a magnet.
Every magnet has an invisible push-and-pull zone around it called its **magnetic field**.
Sprinkling tiny metal bits called **iron filings** near a magnet shows curvy lines looping from pole to pole.
More than **2,000 years ago**, people in China used a magnetic rock called a **lodestone** to make the first compasses.
Earth itself acts like one giant magnet because of swirly melted iron deep inside it.
A compass needle points north because it lines up with Earth's own magnetic pull.
An **electromagnet** is made from wire wrapped in loops with electricity running through it, and it can switch on and off.
Electromagnets are used in doorbells, speakers, and giant cranes that lift old cars.
If you cut a magnet in half, you don't get a north piece and a south piece — each new piece becomes its own small magnet with both ends.
Fridge magnets are made from bendy rubber with tiny magnet bits mixed in, so they can bend without losing their stick.

new_recurring.rule: A tiny robot built from fridge magnets who glows green and wakes up whenever Ada lines her magnets up just right, then shrinks the room into swirly light to guide her through a science adventure, always returning her safely home as a…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Ada comes home and presses her little magnet robot Sprocket onto the kitchen fridge before climbing back into bed.

story.title: Priya, Dev, and the Rainbow That Popped Out of a Water Pistol
story.subtitle: A squirt, a sparkle, and a whole lot of color

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Squirt That Glowed
chapters.text:
It was way past bedtime. Priya was still drawing swirly circles on her sketchpad. Dev was aiming his water pistol at the sunbeam sneaking through the curtains.

"Watch this," Dev said, and squeezed the trigger. **WHOOSH!** Tiny drops flew into the light.

They didn't just splash. They glowed red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple, spinning like a tiny wheel.

Then a round little droplet popped right out of the mist, grinning. "Finally! I'm Fizz."

Priya dropped her pencil. "You're a raindrop?"

"The friendliest one you'll meet," Fizz said. "Sunlight goes into each tiny drop, bends like it's on a little slide, bounces off the back, and bends again on the way out. That bending is called **refraction** — a fancy word for light changing direction."

"That's why the colors show up?" Priya asked.

"Smart kid," said Fizz. "Hop on the mist. Let's go see more."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Newton's Trick With a Triangle
chapters.text:
They landed with a soft **POP** in a cozy old room with a glass triangle on the table.

"This is where **Isaac Newton** did something wild," said Fizz. "In **1666**, he let sunlight through a glass triangle called a **prism**. Out came every color, in a neat row."

Dev squinted. "But sunlight looks white."

"That's the trick," Fizz said. "White sunlight is really every color mixed together. The prism — and raindrops too — just untangle them."

Priya grabbed her crayons and lined them up. "Red, orange, yellow, green, blue... purple?"

"Close," said Fizz. "People remember it as **Roy G. Biv** — red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet."

"Why's red first?" Dev asked.

"Red bends the least, so it lands on the outside. Violet bends the most, so it's tucked on the inside," Fizz said.

Priya swapped her purple crayon to the end. "Like a parking order for colors."

Dev laughed so hard he nearly dropped his pistol.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Which Way Do I Point This Thing?
chapters.text:
Back in the sunny backyard, Dev squirted mist in front of him. Nothing happened.

"Wrong way," Fizz said. "Turn around first."

Dev spun so the sun was behind him. A tiny rainbow popped up right over the spray.

"The sun has to be behind you, and the water in front," said Fizz. "That's the only way the light bounces back to your eyes."

"Sunshine on my neck, rainbow in my face," Dev said, grinning.

Priya tried it sideways. No rainbow showed.

"Face it right or it hides," Fizz said.

Priya copied her brother. There it was — her own little rainbow over the sprinkler.

"Found it because Dev found it first," she said, bumping his shoulder.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Whole Circle
chapters.text:
They floated up on the mist until the backyard looked like a tiny green stamp below.

"Whoa," Dev whispered. "The rainbow's a whole circle!"

"You found something most people never see," said Fizz. "Rainbows really are full circles all the time. We usually only see the top half, because the ground is in the way."

"So from up here—" Priya started.

"—no ground in the way," Fizz finished. "People in airplanes sometimes spot the whole circle."

Dev squirted a tiny stream straight down, just to say he'd squirted from the sky. It vanished before it landed, which made Priya giggle for a whole minute.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Two Kids, Two Rainbows
chapters.text:
Back on the ground, both kids looked at the same sprinkler.

"Mine's a little to the left of yours," Priya said.

"No way, it's right here," said Dev, pointing at his own spot.

"You're both right," Fizz said. "Every person sees their own personal rainbow, made from different drops, because everyone's standing in a slightly different place."

"So there's a Dev rainbow and a Priya rainbow?" Dev asked.

"And a Fizz rainbow," said Fizz. "Mine's extra sparkly, obviously."

Priya rolled her eyes, smiling anyway. "Total rainbow show-off."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Upside-Down Extra One
chapters.text:
A quick rain shower blew through, and just as fast, the sun popped back out.

"Watch the sky," Fizz said.

Two rainbows arched over the yard — one bright, one fainter, floating just above it.

"That one's backward!" Priya said, pointing at the faint one.

"Light bounces twice inside some drops instead of once," Fizz explained. "That flips the colors around for the second rainbow."

Dev counted colors on both with his finger, mumbling "red, orange... orange, red," until he got dizzy and flopped onto the grass, laughing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Rainbows Hiding Everywhere
chapters.text:
Fizz led them to a tiny waterfall bubbling in the garden pond.

"Rainbows don't need rain clouds," Fizz said. "They show up in waterfalls, misty spray, even your own hose."

Dev squirted his pistol into the splash, and a rainbow bloomed right over it.

"Does the moon make one?" Priya asked, watching the sky turn dim.

"At night, moonlight can make a **moonbow**," said Fizz. "It's usually too pale to look colorful — just silvery gray. A camera can catch the colors, though."

"All of this bending and bouncing light is called **optics**," Fizz added. "That's the science of how light plays tricks like this."

"Optics," Dev repeated slowly. "Sounds like a robot name."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Old Stories, New Rainbow
chapters.text:
As the sky turned orange, Fizz settled onto the porch railing.

"People have told rainbow stories forever," Fizz said. "In old Norse tales, a rainbow bridge called **Bifrost** connected Earth to the home of the gods."

"And in a very old story in the Bible, a rainbow showed up after a big storm, as a sign of a promise that good times were coming," Fizz said gently.

"What about the gold?" Dev bounced on his toes. "I heard there's gold at the end!"

"Irish stories tell of a leprechaun — a tricky little fellow — guarding gold at a rainbow's end," Fizz said. "That part's probably just a fun tale, since a rainbow's end moves every time you move toward it."

"So you can never actually catch one," Priya said.

"Never," said Fizz. "You can't walk up and touch a rainbow, no matter how fast you run."

Dev looked a little let down, then shrugged. "Good thing the chasing was the fun part."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
With a soft **POP**, the mist set them down on the living room carpet.

"Remember," Fizz said, already fading into a sparkle, "you need sunshine and water drops at the same time. That's the only way a rainbow shows up."

"Got it," said Priya, sketching a careful arc — red on the outside, violet tucked inside.

Dev set his water pistol gently by the window, right where morning sun would hit it.

"Night, Fizz," he whispered.

A last tiny sparkle winked from the curtain, and then the room was quiet.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Priya. Goodnight, Dev. Sweet rainbow dreams, you two.

true_facts.text: Sunlight goes into a raindrop, bends, bounces off the back, and bends again on the way out — that's how a rainbow starts.
This bending of light is called **refraction**, and it happens when light moves from air into water.
White sunlight is really every color mixed together, and raindrops untangle them into a row of colors.
The rainbow color order is remembered as **Roy G. Biv**: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
Red sits on the outside of a rainbow because it bends the least; violet sits on the inside because it bends the most.
To see a rainbow, the sun has to be behind you and the water has to be in front of you.
Rainbows are really whole circles — we usually only see the top half because the ground blocks the rest.
From way up in an airplane, with no ground in the way, people sometimes see the whole circle rainbow.
Every person actually sees their own personal rainbow, made from slightly different raindrops because of where they're standing.
Sometimes a fainter second rainbow shows up above the first one, with its colors flipped backward.
In **1666**, **Isaac Newton** used a glass **prism** to split sunlight into the same rainbow of colors.
Old Irish stories tell of a leprechaun guarding gold at a rainbow's end — a fun tale, since a rainbow's end always moves when you move toward it.
You can never actually walk up and touch a rainbow, because it depends on exactly where you're standing.
Rainbows need sunshine and water drops at the same time, which is why they often show up around rain showers.

story.title: Jack, Ellie, and the Whisper Shell
story.subtitle: A bedtime swim through four hundred million years of sharks.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Whisper Shell
chapters.text:
Jack lay on his bunk, spinning his shark-tooth necklace in the lamp light. He had found the tooth on the beach last summer, and he never took it off.

On the other bed, Ellie lined up her shell collection in a neat curling row, biggest to smallest. The biggest shell sat right by her pillow. She called it the Whisper Shell.

"Sharks beat mermaids," Jack said, for the hundredth time.

"Mermaids beat sharks," Ellie said back, just as fast. It was their favorite fight, and neither of them ever won it.

Then the Whisper Shell began to glow.

It was not the soft glow of a nightlight. It was deep blue-green, like moonlight through water, and it pulsed like something breathing.

"Jack," Ellie whispered. "Do shells do that?"

"No," Jack whispered back. "They do not."

A voice rose out of the shell, soft and bubbly, like it was talking through water. "Hello," it said. "I'm Pearl. Want to see who's really the champion of the sea?"

The shell cracked open into a round, glowing porthole, swirling with blue light.

Ellie grabbed Jack's sleeve. Jack grabbed her hand right back — not that he would ever admit it — and together they stepped through.

**WHOOOSH.**

They landed inside a huge, clear bubble, floating in the middle of the ocean. Fish flickered past the curved walls like silver confetti.

"First stop," said Pearl. "A shark close enough to see — but we stay safe inside here."

A gray shape glided by and bent itself clean around a rock, smooth as a ribbon.

"Its whole body just *bent*," Jack said. "Sharks don't have bones like us, do they?"

"Good eye," said Pearl. "A shark's skeleton is made of **cartilage** — the same bendy stuff in the top of your ear. Go ahead, give your ear a wiggle."

Both kids bent their ears. Ellie's flopped like a taco.

"Fish bend-bones," Ellie announced. "I'm telling everyone at school."

Jack grinned. "Called it. Point one, sharks."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Older Than Dinosaurs
chapters.text:
The bubble began to drift, and the water around them turned murky and thick, like swimming through cloudy green soup.

"Why's it such a weird color?" Ellie asked, wrinkling her nose.

"Because we're not just somewhere else," said Pearl. "We're some*when* else. Very, very far back."

Jack pressed his face to the glass. No dolphins. No whales. Not even a crab.

"There's nothing normal here," he said slowly. "Wait — are we before the dinosaurs?"

"Even further back than that," said Pearl. "Sharks first swam in the ocean more than **400 million years ago**. Dinosaurs didn't show up for ages after that."

Ellie gasped. "So sharks got here first and just... waited?"

"Pretty much," said Pearl. "They were swimming around long before any dinosaur ever took a single step."

"Ha!" said Jack. "Dinosaurs showed up late to the pool party."

Ellie giggled so hard she snorted, which made Jack laugh even harder, which made the whole bubble wobble.

"Careful," said Pearl, amused. "You'll scare off the neighbors."

As if on cue, a shadowy fin sliced through the green water ahead, old and patient, like it had all the time in the world. Which, Jack thought, it kind of did.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Tooth as Big as a Hand
chapters.text:
The bubble bumped gently against a rocky sea cliff, and something huge and pale stuck out of the stone.

Ellie pointed. "What is THAT?"

It was a tooth — but not a normal tooth. It was as long as her whole hand.

"That," said Pearl, "is a **fossil**. A fossil is something old, like a bone or a tooth, that turned hard as rock after being buried a very, very long time."

Jack held his own hand up next to it. His fingers barely covered half.

"Whatever had this tooth," he said, "must have been enormous."

"That was **Megalodon**," said Pearl. "One of the biggest sharks that ever lived. It's **extinct** now — that means none are left anywhere on Earth."

"Could it still be hiding somewhere?" Ellie asked, just a little nervous.

"Nowhere," said Pearl gently. "Not one, anywhere. You are completely safe."

Ellie relaxed, satisfied.

"Shark skeletons rarely turn to stone," Pearl went on. "So almost everything we know about Megalodon comes from teeth just like this one."

Jack tapped the giant tooth with one finger, careful not to budge it loose. "A whole shark," he said, "and all that's left is its teeth. Rude."

Ellie laughed so hard she nearly let go of the bubble wall.
chapters.shout_line: THAT TOOTH IS AS BIG AS MY HAND!

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
A shadow fell across the bubble, bigger than a school bus.

Ellie squeaked and grabbed Jack's arm.

Then the shadow turned, and they saw a huge, spotted shark cruising past, its mouth wide open like a cave.

"That's the **whale shark**," said Pearl. "The biggest fish in the whole ocean, over **40 feet long**."

"Is it going to eat us?" Ellie asked.

"Nope," said Pearl. "It only eats **plankton** — tiny floating bits of food, too small for us to even see properly. Like underwater dust made of yummy specks."

Jack watched the giant mouth filter the water like a strainer. "So the biggest shark in the sea eats the tiniest snacks?"

"Exactly," said Pearl. "And some whale sharks live over **100 years**. That one might be older than your great-great-grandma."

Ellie waved politely at the slow, gentle giant. "Hello, old lady shark."

The whale shark didn't seem to notice them. It just kept gliding, kept filtering, kept being enormous and calm.

"Big," Jack said, "but not scary."

"Most things are like that," said Pearl, "once you know them a little better."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Rows and Rows of Teeth
chapters.text:
**CHOMP.**

The sound echoed through the water before they saw anything.

Then a sleek gray shark rolled sideways to snatch a fish, and Jack caught a flash of its open mouth.

"Whoa — did you see all those teeth?" he said. "There were like five rows!"

"That's the **great white shark**," said Pearl. "It can grow up to **20 feet long**, with rows of pointy, saw-edged teeth."

"What happens if one falls out?" Jack asked.

"A new one moves up to take its place," said Pearl. "Sharks grow **thousands of teeth** over a lifetime. There's always a spare waiting in line."

Ellie's eyes went wide. "Thousands? The tooth fairy would be SO tired."

"She'd need a bigger pillow," Jack said, "and a bigger wallet."

They watched another row slide forward, smooth and automatic, like a conveyor belt of teeth.

Jack counted rows through the glass until he lost track. "I give up at seven," he announced. "That's more teeth than me and Ellie put together."

Ellie bared her own teeth at him, and Jack laughed so hard he fogged up the glass.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Hammer-Shaped Head
chapters.text:
A strange shadow crossed overhead — wide and flat, shaped like the end of a hammer.

Ellie tilted her head sideways, studying it. "That shark's head looks squished!"

"That's a **hammerhead shark**," said Pearl. "Its head is wide and flat on purpose, with one eye on each end."

"Why would you want your eyes so far apart?" Jack asked.

Ellie covered one eye with her hand, then the other, testing how much she could see. "Maybe... so you can see more at once?"

"Exactly right," said Pearl. "With eyes spread that wide, a hammerhead gets a wraparound view, almost the whole circle around it, which helps it spot things to eat."

"So its weird head is actually its superpower," Jack said.

"Most weird things are, if you ask them nicely," said Pearl.

The hammerhead swung its strange head slowly side to side, like a lighthouse beam, before gliding off into the blue.

Ellie kept covering one eye, then the other, until it disappeared. "I still can't see behind me," she said, disappointed.

"That's because you're not a hammerhead," Jack said.

"Yet," said Ellie, and Jack decided not to argue with that.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Shark That Walks
chapters.text:
The bubble settled near a shallow tide pool, rocks poking up like little islands.

"Wait," Jack said, squinting. "Is that shark... walking?"

Sure enough, a small spotted shark was flip-flopping across the rocks on its fins, more like a puppy crossing a kitchen floor than a fish in the sea.

"That's an **epaulette shark**," said Pearl. "It uses its paddle-shaped fins like little feet to cross reefs and tide pools."

"It needs shoes," Ellie said solemnly.

"It also barely needs to breathe while it's doing it," Pearl added. "It can go for hours on very little **oxygen** — the part of air our bodies need to work."

Jack watched it flop-flop-flop over a rock and plop back into a puddle. "That is the weirdest, best thing I've seen all night."

"Better than the hammerhead?" Ellie asked.

"Different kind of best," Jack said diplomatically, already learning how to survive sibling arguments.

The little shark paused, looked almost right at the bubble, then kept walking, business as usual.

"Some sharks swim," said Pearl. "Some sharks walk. The ocean's full of surprises."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Ellie's Discovery
chapters.text:
Something small and dark drifted past the bubble, leathery and shaped like a tiny pouch with curly strings at each corner.

Ellie's whole face lit up. "I know what that is! Grandma showed me one on the beach once. It's a **mermaid's purse**!"

"You got there before I even asked," said Pearl, sounding impressed. "That's exactly right. Some sharks lay eggs inside cases just like that one, while other sharks give birth to live pups instead."

"So a baby shark could be curled up inside, right now?" Ellie asked, pressing close to the glass, careful not to touch it.

"Maybe," said Pearl. "Growing quietly, safe inside, until it's ready."

Jack had been quiet, thinking. "Pearl... are sharks dangerous? Like, to us?"

"Barely ever," said Pearl. "Shark attacks on people are **extremely rare**. Honestly, people cause sharks far more trouble than sharks cause us, but more people are working hard now to keep sharks safe."

"Good," Jack said. "I'd like to keep all my rows of teeth free."

Ellie rolled her eyes, but she was still smiling at the little purse drifting into the blue, carrying its secret.

"Told you mermaids and sharks go together," she said.

"They do not," Jack said automatically, then paused. "Okay, maybe a little."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Shark Lady, and Home Again
chapters.text:
A diver in an old-fashioned wetsuit swam calmly past the bubble, completely at ease among the sharks around her, never touching a single one.

"Who's that?" Jack asked.

"That's **Eugenie Clark**," said Pearl. "People called her the Shark Lady. She studied sharks for most of her life and showed everyone something important."

"What's that?" Ellie asked.

"That sharks are curious," said Pearl, "and that they can even learn tricks, just like a dog can."

The diver raised one hand, and a nurse shark swam toward a target she was holding, then turned gently away, never bumping her.

"It followed her signal," Jack said, amazed. "Like it was listening."

"She proved sharks were smarter than people gave them credit for," said Pearl. "That changed how scientists everywhere studied them."

Jack watched the Shark Lady glide off, utterly unafraid. "I want to do that when I grow up," he said. "Dive with sharks. Study them. Show everyone they're not scary."

"I'll believe you," said Ellie, "if you let me study mermaids at the same time."

"Deal," said Jack.

Pearl's glow brightened. "Time to swim home, you two."

**WHOOOSH.**

The bubble, the water, and the glowing diver melted away, and the Whisper Shell's porthole closed behind them with a soft click.

Jack and Ellie landed back on their own beds, blankets rumpled, shark tooth and shell both glowing one last, gentle time.

Tucked beside Ellie's pillow, right next to the Whisper Shell, sat one small, leathery mermaid's purse — empty, dry, and completely real.

Ellie picked it up and grinned at her brother. "Sharks AND mermaids," she said. "Both champions."

Jack, for once, didn't argue.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Jack. Goodnight, Ellie. Swim gently, and dream deep.

true_facts.text: A shark's skeleton is made of **cartilage** — bendy stuff like the top of your ear, not hard bone.
Sharks first swam in the ocean more than **400 million years ago**, long before dinosaurs showed up.
**Megalodon** was a giant shark that lived long ago and is **extinct** now — none are left anywhere.
Because shark skeletons rarely turn to stone, almost everything we know about Megalodon comes from its huge **fossil** teeth.
The **whale shark** is the biggest fish in the sea, over **40 feet long**, but it only eats tiny **plankton**.
Some **whale sharks** live over **100 years** — maybe as old as a great-great-grandma!
The **great white shark** can grow up to **20 feet long** and has rows of sharp, saw-edged teeth.
Sharks grow **thousands of teeth** over a lifetime — when one falls out, a new one moves up to replace it.
A **hammerhead shark**'s wide, flat head spreads its eyes apart, giving it a wraparound view all around itself.
The **epaulette shark** can 'walk' across rocks and tide pools using its fins like little feet.
Some sharks lay eggs inside leathery cases nicknamed **mermaid's purses**, while others give birth to live pups.
Shark attacks on people are **extremely rare** — people cause sharks far more trouble than sharks cause us.
Scientist **Eugenie Clark**, the 'Shark Lady,' showed that sharks are curious and can even learn tricks.

story.title: Nora and the Glowing Tile of Pompeii
story.subtitle: A bedtime journey into the town that time forgot

chapters.heading: Chapter One: The Tile That Glowed
chapters.text:
Nora was lying on her bedroom floor, way past bedtime, sorting tiny colored tiles for her mosaic. Click. Click. Click. She loved snapping each piece into place until a picture appeared.

One tile did not match the others. It was dusty gold, chipped at the edge, and it was warm. Then it began to glow, soft blue-green, like a nightlight underwater.

"Don't drop me," said a small voice. The tile had a tiny painted face. "I'm **Tessera**. I come from a very old floor. Want to see where I used to live?"

Before Nora could answer, the glow swallowed the room. **WHOOOOSH**. Her carpet turned to warm stone under her bare feet, and sunlight poured down on a street full of raised stone blocks with gaps between them.

"Why does the street look like stairs lying down?" Nora asked.

"Guess," said Tessera. "You're the one who loves patterns."

Nora crouched and looked at the gaps. "So carts can roll through the spaces — but people still get to hop across without stepping in puddles!"

"Exactly right," said Tessera, glowing brighter. "This is **Pompeii**, a busy Roman town that once had about **11,000 to 15,000 people** — shops, bathhouses, theaters, all of it."

Nora grinned and hopped from stone to stone like the Romans once did, careful never to touch the gap. "I'm getting good at this already," she said.

chapters.heading: Chapter Two: Bread in the Oven
chapters.text:
A smell drifted down the street — warm, a little smoky, like toast that had waited two thousand years. Nora followed it to a stone counter with round holes on top.

"This was a bakery," said Tessera. "Look inside the oven, carefully."

Nora bent down and peeked in. Sitting on the ash was a round loaf of bread, its top cut into neat wedges like a pizza, frozen in place.

"It's still shaped like bread!" Nora said. "How?"

"The ash came down so fast and so thick, it covered everything before it could rot away," said Tessera. "Scientists really did find a **loaf of bread** here, marks and all."

Nora leaned closer and spotted a little stamped pattern pressed into the crust. "Wait — is that the baker's mark? Like how I sign my mosaics in the corner?"

"You've got sharp eyes," said Tessera. "Bakers really did stamp their bread, so everyone knew whose oven it came from."

"Smart," said Nora. "Although if I made bread, I'd probably just eat the evidence."

Tessera's painted face wobbled, which Nora decided was a laugh. "Come on," said Tessera. "There's a whole town of clues left to find, and you're the one piecing them together."

chapters.heading: Chapter Three: Water That Never Stopped
chapters.text:
A trickling sound led them to a stone fountain at a crossroads, water pouring steadily from a carved spout.

"It's still running?" Nora asked, surprised.

"Back then, yes," said Tessera. "Pompeii had **pipes** running under the streets, carrying water to fountains all over town, so anyone could fill a jug."

Nora crouched and traced the pipe's path with her finger along the stone. It ran straight, then turned, then split into two — almost like the grid lines she used to plan her mosaics before placing a single tile.

"It's laid out like a pattern," she said. "If I follow the turns, I bet I can guess where it goes next."

"Try it," said Tessera.

Nora followed the pipe's turn to the left, past a wall, and it led straight to a steamy building with a line of stone benches inside.

"A bathhouse!" said Tessera. "Good guessing. The water system was clever enough to fill fountains and baths all through town."

"I just followed the grid," said Nora, pleased. "Mosaics taught me that."

"Everything's a pattern if you look close enough," said Tessera, glowing a little warmer.
chapters.shout_line: EVERY TINY PIECE TELLS A STORY!

chapters.heading: Chapter Four: Walls That Talk
chapters.text:
Painted words covered the next wall, red letters on white plaster, some faded and some sharp.

"What's that say?" Nora asked, tilting her head.

"Some of it's an advertisement," said Tessera. "People painted signs and slogans right onto their walls — a very old way of getting a message out."

Nora squinted at the shapes and colors. "It's kind of like a poster. Except it never comes down."

Farther along, a doorway opened into a room full of color — deep red walls covered in painted figures, tall and strange, caught mid-ceremony.

"These are **frescoes** — paintings made right on wet plaster so the color sinks in and lasts," said Tessera. "This room is called the Villa of the Mysteries. Nobody is completely sure what the painted scene means — it might be an exaggeration of what really happened here, but it still tells us people loved color and story."

Nora studied the shapes, the way the painter had blocked in color before adding detail. "It's like a mosaic," she said, "except with paint instead of tiles. Same idea — little pieces making one big picture."

"You'd have fit right in with the Roman painters," said Tessera.

Nora beamed. "I knew my hobby was secretly ancient."

chapters.heading: Chapter Five: Circles Within Circles
chapters.text:
Nora heard her own footsteps echo before she even saw the building. She turned a corner, and the sound bounced back twice as loud.

"Whoa," she said, stopping short. A huge oval space opened up ahead, with rows of stone benches curving all the way around a wide, sandy floor.

"What is this place?" she asked, spinning in a slow circle to take it all in.

"An **amphitheater**," said Tessera. "A giant oval stadium. People built this one around **70 BC**, which makes it one of the oldest ever found. Crowds came here to watch **gladiators** — fighters who put on shows for the whole town to cheer at."

Nora studied the curved rows, each one hugging the next like rings inside a target. "It's circles within circles," she said. "Just like how I build a mosaic sun — you start in the middle, then work your way out, ring by ring."

"Keep looking," said Tessera. "A mosaic-maker might spot something nobody else would."

Nora walked down toward the sandy middle and crouched by a single flat stone, smoother than all the ones around it. "This is the exact center," she said. "I bet everyone measured everything else starting from right here. That's how I keep my circles even too — find the middle first, and the rest lines up."

Tessera's glow flickered, pleased. "That is exactly how the builders worked."

Nora stood and spread her arms wide, testing the echo with a long, silly "HELLOOOO." The sound rolled around the stone oval and came rushing right back to her, twice as loud.

"I bet even a sneeze echoes in here," she said, and sneezed on purpose to check.

Tessera's painted face wobbled, which Nora had learned meant laughing. "Very scientific," said Tessera.

"Very silly," Nora agreed happily, and they both laughed until the sound bounced back at them too.

chapters.heading: Chapter Six: The Sleeping Mountain
chapters.text:
A shadow slid over the street, and Nora looked up to find its source: a wide mountain rising behind the rooftops, quiet and green.

"That's **Mount Vesuvius**," said Tessera. "It's a volcano — a mountain that can spit out hot rock and ash. It's still here today, and scientists watch it closely, because so many people live near it now."

Nora felt a small flutter of worry. "Is it going to do anything right now?"

"Not today," said Tessera gently. "It's sleeping. But a long time ago, on **August 24th, in the year 79**, it wasn't sleeping at all. It sent ash and rock down over the whole town, covering everything under more than **thirteen feet** of it. That's part of why so much got saved so well — the ash came down fast, like a blanket, before anything could crumble away."

Nora let out a slow breath. "So everything got tucked in."

"Sort of," said Tessera. "A young writer named **Pliny the Younger** watched from far across the bay and wrote it all down in two letters. He described it so carefully that scientists still use his name for this kind of eruption today — they call it **'Plinian.'**"

"There's another town too," said Tessera. "A smaller one by the sea, called **Herculaneum**. The same mountain buried it too, but with a different, thicker kind of hot material. It kept even wooden furniture and old scrolls safe — things that usually rot away completely."

Nora blinked. "Wooden chairs survived longer than any chair I've ever had?"

"Chairs, doors, even shelves," said Tessera. "Different towns, different kinds of time capsules."

"And everyone was okay?" Nora asked.

"His uncle, **Pliny the Elder**, was a brave commander," said Tessera. "He sailed his ships straight toward the mountain to help people get to safety, instead of sailing away."

Nora nodded slowly. "That's the bravest kind of hero. Sailing toward the scary part."

Down the road, past a low wall, sunlight lit up a patch of earth still humped and untouched. "Is there more town hiding under there?" Nora asked, pointing.

"There is," said Tessera, glow brightening. "Want to see who found it?"

Nora was already walking.

chapters.heading: Chapter Seven: The Diggers of 1748
chapters.text:
Tessera led Nora toward the humped, grassy patch of earth. Up close, it looked like a hill wearing a very old blanket.

"For a long, long time, nobody remembered this town was even here," said Tessera. "Pompeii slept under the ground for almost **1,700 years**, until **1748**, when workers digging in the dirt hit old walls and found objects buried below."

"That's like finding a mosaic buried under a rug," Nora said. "You'd have no idea it was there until you started pulling threads."

"Exactly like that," said Tessera. "And people are still pulling threads. Only about **two-thirds of the town** has been dug up and uncovered so far. The rest is still waiting under the ground, right where we're standing."

Nora's eyes went wide. "So there could be something nobody has ever seen, right under our feet?"

"There could," said Tessera.

Nora knelt and brushed at the dirt with careful fingers, the same slow, patient way she brushed grout dust off a finished mosaic. "You have to go slow," she said, "or you might scratch something underneath."

"That's exactly how real diggers work," said Tessera. "Slow and careful, a little at a time."

As Nora brushed, a patch of color peeked through the dirt — red, then gold, then the curve of a painted arm. A brand new painting, hiding for centuries, blinking up at the sunlight for the first time.

"I found one!" Nora whispered. "A real one!"

Not far from the painting, something else poked through the dirt — tiny colored squares, packed edge to edge into a floor. A mosaic, half-uncovered, each little piece no bigger than her fingernail.

"That looks like home," she whispered, thinking of her own tray of tiles back in her bedroom.

"People are still finding things like this," said Tessera. "Pompeii keeps surprising everyone, even today. Millions of people visit every single year, just to see what you're seeing right now."

Nora sat back on her heels, dirt on her fingers, grinning at the painting she had just helped the sunlight find.

chapters.heading: Chapter Eight: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
Tessera's glow dimmed to a soft gold, the same color Nora had seen on the very first night. "Time to go home," said Tessera. "I think you found everything you came looking for tonight."

Nora looked back once more — at the stepping-stone streets, the quiet green mountain, and the painting still blinking in its first sunlight in centuries. "I found a whole town," she said. "And I didn't even know I was looking for it."

**WHOOOOSH**. The glow swept up around her, and when it faded, Nora was back on her bedroom carpet. Her mosaic tiles were scattered exactly where she'd left them, and the rug pressed warm against her knees.

Tessera sat glowing softly in her palm. "Thank you for the tour," Nora whispered. "I think my mosaic needs one more piece."

She looked down at the little gold tile, chipped at one edge, and set it carefully into the empty space right at the center of her half-finished picture. It fit perfectly, as if it had always belonged there, waiting its whole life for exactly that spot.

"Every tiny piece tells a story," Nora murmured, echoing what Tessera had told her that very night.

The tile gave one last soft glow, then went quiet and still — just an ordinary little piece of an extraordinary mosaic.

Nora climbed into bed and pulled her blanket up to her chin, thinking of warm bread in an oven, water running through old pipes, and a painting that had waited two thousand years just to be found by the right pair of hands.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Nora. Every tiny piece tells a story.
