story.title: Maya and the Race to Space
story.subtitle: A glowing water cup, a seal named Barnacle, and one giant leap.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beep in the Water Cup (1957)
chapters.text:
Maya lay on her bedroom floor with her sketchbook open, drawing a sailboat with big white sails billowing in a wind only she could see. The house was quiet. Everyone else was asleep.

It had been one whole week since the magic water in her blue cup had gone fizzy and bright — back when the bridge finished humming its very last hum, and Barnacle waved a flipper from the water as the last rivet went in.

Tonight the cup just looked like plain water, until Maya dipped her paintbrush in to rinse off some blue paint.

The water started to glow, soft and silver, like a puddle full of tiny stars.

SPLOOSH! A round whiskery face popped up out of the cup, blinking water from his eyes.

"All aboard, Maya!" said Barnacle the harbour seal.

"Barnacle! Where are we going tonight?" Maya asked, scrambling up off the carpet.

"Up," said Barnacle, "and also a long, long time ago. Listen."

A tiny beep, beep, beep came rising out of the glowing water, steady as a heartbeat.

"That's Sputnik," Barnacle said. "The very first satellite — that's a machine that circles way up around Earth — that anybody ever built."

Maya tapped the beat on the rim of her cup with one finger, matching it exactly. The glow sharpened into a picture: a shiny silver ball with four long thin legs trailing behind it, sailing past the dark.

"It's tiny! About the size of a beach ball," Maya said.

"Fifty-eight centimeters wide, to be exact," said Barnacle. "Little, but loud. The Soviet Union launched it on October 4, 1957, and people everywhere could hear its beep on their very own radios at home, just by listening."

Maya kept tapping, and the glowing ball spun happily in time with her rhythm, like it was dancing to her own private drum.

"I'm keeping the beat!" she laughed.

Barnacle echoed the beeps and bowed with a flipper — which made him wobble sideways and flop right over into the glow. Maya giggled so hard she nearly dropped her paintbrush into the cup.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Belt Around the World (1957–1958)
chapters.text:
A soft woof echoed through the glow. Maya turned around fast.

"That's Laika," said Barnacle gently. "A brave little dog. On November 3, 1957, she rode on Sputnik 2 and became the first living creature ever to orbit Earth — that means circle all the way around it."

Maya pressed her hand flat against the glowing window and watched the little round capsule sail by. "She's famous," Maya whispered. "The whole world still knows her name."

The glow shifted, and small lights flashed like a countdown clock.

"People in America got a big shock when Sputnik went up," said Barnacle. "So on October 1, 1958, they started a brand new space team called NASA, to catch up and keep exploring."

"What did NASA build first?" Maya asked. She always wanted to know why things happened, and when, and how.

"Explorer 1," said Barnacle. "Launched January 31, 1958. Want to see what it found up there?"

As they drifted closer to Earth, Maya spotted something strange: a faint, glowing ring circling the whole planet, like a hula hoop made of light.

"Barnacle, look! There's a belt around the world!" she shouted, pointing with her whole arm.

Barnacle's whiskers twitched with delight. "Good eye! That's the Van Allen radiation belt — a ring of invisible space energy wrapped around Earth. Explorer 1 found it first, and nobody even knew it was there before that."

Because Maya spotted it first, Barnacle steered their glowing, boat-shaped bubble gently around the edge instead of straight through the middle, and the ring sparkled like sequins as they slid past.

"I found Earth's belt," Maya said proudly, "and I didn't even need to get dressed up for it."

Barnacle snorted a laugh so hard that a little spout of water shot out of his nose. "Good one, Maya. Very good one."
chapters.shout_line: THERE'S A BELT AROUND THE WORLD!

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Two Rockets, One Winner (1961)
chapters.text:
The glow spun fast, like a pinwheel caught in the wind. WHOOSH! Two rocket shapes zoomed up, side by side.

"Two rockets?" Maya asked. "Which one wins?"

"Good question," said Barnacle. "One flies way up and circles all the way around Earth. The other just pops up and comes right back down. Can you tell which is the real space trip?"

Maya grabbed her sketchbook and drew two lines fast. One looped in a big round circle. The other went straight up and straight back down, like a jump on a trampoline.

"This one," she said, tapping the circle, "goes all the way around. That's the real trip."

"Exactly right," said Barnacle. "On April 12, 1961, a Soviet pilot named Yuri Gagarin rode a ship called Vostok 1 all the way around Earth. Once around, in about 108 minutes. He was the very first human ever in space."

Maya counted on her fingers, slow and careful. "That's almost two hours," she said. "One whole loop around the whole entire planet."

The glowing ship sailed past, and through its tiny window a smiling face waved.

"He smiled the whole way," Barnacle said. "People everywhere loved him for it."

The second rocket shape rose fast, hovered a moment, then dropped back down toward the glowing blue marble below.

"That's Alan Shepard," said Barnacle. "He went up on May 5, 1961, inside a ship named Freedom 7. First American ever in space. But his ride was short. Straight up, straight down. No circling Earth at all."

Maya looked at her two drawings side by side. "So Gagarin's trip is the big loop," she said, "and Shepard's trip is just one big jump."

"You explained that better than most grown-ups," Barnacle said, and a little bubble popped right out of his nose from laughing too hard.

Maya grinned and tucked her pencil behind one ear, like a real explorer saving a tool for later.

"Both of them were brave," she said. "Even the short jump took guts."

"Every single person who ever climbed into one of those ships was brave," Barnacle agreed. "Loop or jump, it still took courage to go first."

The two glowing ships sailed on side by side into the dark, and Maya waved after them with her whole arm, the way she waved at boats leaving the harbor.
chapters.shout_line: A WHOLE LOOP AROUND THE WHOLE PLANET!

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: A Dare and a Factory Worker (1961–1963)
chapters.text:
A booming voice rolled through the glow, deep as thunder but not scary at all.

"Before this decade is out," the voice said, "we choose to go to the Moon."

Maya sat up straight. "Who said that?"

"President John F. Kennedy," said Barnacle. "On May 25, 1961, he dared his whole country to land a person on the Moon, and bring them safely home, before the 1960s ended."

"That's a really big promise," Maya said.

"The biggest," Barnacle agreed. "Nobody even knew yet exactly how to do it."

The glow swirled, and a new shape appeared: a young woman in a round helmet, grinning inside the tiny window of her ship.

"Who's that?" Maya asked.

"Guess," said Barnacle.

Maya studied the picture. The woman looked proud, like she had worked hard to get there.

"Is she... the first girl in space?" Maya asked.

"Exactly," said Barnacle, clapping two flippers together with a soft splash. "Valentina Tereshkova. She used to work in a factory. Then on June 16, 1963, she rocketed up inside Vostok 6 and became the first woman ever to fly in space."

Maya's eyes went wide. "A factory worker went to space?"

"Anybody brave enough, and trained hard enough, could go," said Barnacle. "That's the whole point of the story."

Maya flipped to a fresh page and started drawing fast — a round helmet, a big smile, little sparkly stars all around.

"I'm keeping her," Maya said. "Right here in my book. So I don't forget her."

"Smart," said Barnacle. "Drawing things down is one good way to remember them forever."

Maya finished the sketch with a tiny rocket underneath Tereshkova's boots, flames curling out the bottom.

"There," she said, holding it up proudly. "Now she's ready to fly again, anytime I want."

Barnacle leaned close to admire it, dripping a little puddle onto the page, which only made the drawing glow brighter.

"She'd like that," Barnacle said. "I bet she would."
chapters.shout_line: A FACTORY WORKER WENT TO SPACE!

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Ten Minutes Floating Free (1965)
chapters.text:
A shadow drifted outside a tiny window, slow and silent.

"Is someone... outside the ship?" Maya asked, leaning closer.

"Yes," said Barnacle. "That's Alexei Leonov. On March 18, 1965, he opened a hatch and floated right outside his spaceship, with nothing but empty space all around him."

Maya spotted something thin trailing behind the floating figure, like a loose shoelace.

"There's a rope!" she said. "A long rope, holding him on!"

"Good eye," said Barnacle. "That rope kept him attached to his ship, Voskhod 2, the whole time. He floated free for about ten minutes before climbing safely back inside."

Maya traced the rope's path with her finger, following it all the way back to the door, checking it stayed tied tight the whole way.

"It's like a boat's anchor line," she said. "You never let go of the rope, or you drift away."

"Just like sailing," Barnacle agreed. "Leonov never let go, and he made it back inside just fine."

The glow shifted again, showing two shadowy figures hunched over rocket blueprints at drafting tables.

"Who are they?" Maya asked.

"One is Sergei Korolev," said Barnacle. "He secretly designed the Soviet Union's rockets. So secretly that almost nobody knew his name until after he died, in 1966."

"That's a really good secret," Maya said.

"The other is Wernher von Braun," Barnacle continued. "He had built rockets years before, and later led the American team that built the giant Saturn V rocket for NASA."

Maya looked between the two drawings. "So there were two rocket builders," she said, "racing each other, and only one of them got to keep his name secret the whole time."

"That's exactly it," said Barnacle. "Two brilliant minds, racing from opposite sides of the world."

Maya closed her sketchbook gently over both men's faces, like tucking them in for the night.

"Goodnight, secret rocket builders," she whispered, and the glow dimmed softly in reply.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Tallest Rocket and a Rising Earth (1968)
chapters.text:
A tower of glowing light stretched up and up, so tall Maya had to lean back to see the top.

"Whoa," she said. "How tall is that thing?"

"That's the Saturn V rocket," said Barnacle. "Three hundred sixty-three feet tall. Taller than the Statue of Liberty."

Maya grabbed her sketchbook and drew a tiny Statue of Liberty next to the glowing tower, then drew the rocket stretching way past the top of the statue's torch.

"It's so much taller," she said, holding up her drawing. "Like, way taller."

"That rocket carried astronauts all the way to the Moon," Barnacle said.

The glow swept forward in time, and Maya found herself looking out a tiny window at gray, dusty ground far below.

"In December 1968," said Barnacle, "three astronauts flew all the way around the Moon aboard Apollo 8. First humans ever to do it."

Maya pressed close to the window, watching the gray ground slide by below.

Then something caught her eye at the very edge of the window: a small blue curve, rising slowly up over the gray horizon.

"Barnacle, look!" Maya shouted, pointing hard. "Earth is coming up over the edge!"

Barnacle's whiskers twitched with excitement. "You found it. One astronaut named William Anders snapped a photo of exactly that moment. People call it Earthrise, and it's one of the most famous photographs ever taken."

Maya stared at the little blue marble rising over the gray ground, tiny and bright against all that dark.

"It looks so small," she whispered. "Like it could fit in my hand."

"That's the whole world," said Barnacle softly. "Every single person you know, all on that one little ball."

Maya reached out and gently touched the glowing Earth with one fingertip. It rippled like water, then settled calm again.

"I found Earthrise," she said proudly. "Before anyone else in this cup."

Barnacle chuckled, a sound like bubbles popping. "You certainly did."
chapters.shout_line: EARTH IS COMING UP OVER THE EDGE!

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: One Giant Leap (1969)
chapters.text:
A soft beep, slow and steady, filled the glow. Maya recognized the rhythm right away.

"That's like Sputnik's beep," she said, "but slower."

"Close listening," said Barnacle. "This is a different ship, landing somewhere brand new."

The glow sharpened into dusty gray ground and a spindly-legged ship settling down gently, kicking up little clouds of dust.

"On July 20, 1969," said Barnacle, "astronaut Neil Armstrong became the very first person ever to step onto the Moon."

A figure in a bulky white suit climbed slowly down a ladder, one careful step at a time.

Maya held her breath, then matched her own voice to the moment, whispering along as Armstrong's famous words crackled through: "...one giant leap for mankind."

"I said it with him!" Maya whispered, grinning.

"You matched it perfectly," said Barnacle. "Just like you matched Sputnik's beep on your very first night."

Another figure climbed down after the first. "That's Buzz Aldrin," Barnacle said. "He joined Armstrong down on the surface."

Maya counted the footprints forming in the gray dust, then noticed something.

"Wait," she said. "There were three astronauts, right? Where's the third one?"

"Good catch," said Barnacle. "Michael Collins stayed up above the whole time, flying the ship that circled the Moon alone, waiting for his two friends to come back up."

Maya frowned thoughtfully. "He didn't get to walk on the Moon at all?"

"Not that trip," said Barnacle. "But without him flying steady circles up above, the other two couldn't have gotten home."

Maya flipped to a fresh page and drew all three astronauts together, side by side, none of them bigger than the others.

"There," she said. "Now all three of them get to be heroes. Even the one who stayed in the ship."

Barnacle nudged the drawing with his nose, leaving a small wet circle beside it like a stamp of approval.

"That's exactly fair," he said. "Collins would like that a lot."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Twelve Footprints and a Handshake (1970–1975)
chapters.text:
A soft alarm beeped once, then stopped. Maya looked up, a little worried.

"Is everything okay?" she asked.

"Let me tell you how it turned out first," said Barnacle gently. "In 1970, on a trip called Apollo 13, something broke on the way to the Moon. An air tank, the part that held the astronauts' air, had a problem. But the crew and their helpers on the ground thought fast, fixed what they could, and flew the ship safely all the way back home to Earth."

Maya let out a breath she didn't know she was holding. "They made it home okay?"

"Every single one of them," said Barnacle. "Safe and sound."

The glow shifted, showing footprint after footprint pressed into gray Moon dust, more than Maya could count on both hands.

"How many astronauts walked up there?" Maya asked.

"Between 1969 and 1972," said Barnacle, "twelve different astronauts walked on the Moon, across six separate trips that landed safely."

Maya started counting the footprint trails, tapping each one with her finger the way she'd tapped Sputnik's beep. "One, two, three..." She kept going, all the way to twelve, grinning the whole time.

"Twelve!" she announced. "I counted every single one."

The glow softened, turning warm and gold instead of silver. Two ships floated toward each other, slow and careful, until they gently touched.

"On July 17, 1975," said Barnacle, "an American ship and a Soviet ship linked together, right up in space. The astronauts inside opened a hatch and shook hands."

"After racing each other for so long?" Maya asked.

"That's how the whole race ended," said Barnacle. "Not with a winner and a loser. With a handshake."

Maya smiled, picturing it: two ships, once on opposite sides, finally shaking hands among the stars.

The glow began to dim, gentle as a tide going out. Maya felt the carpet under her knees again, and her sketchbook, and her blue cup, water calm and clear.

SPLOOSH! Barnacle's whiskery face popped up one last time.

"That's the whole trip, Maya," he said. "You found the belt, the Earthrise, and twelve footprints, all in one night."

Maya looked down at her sketchbook, now full of rockets, helmets, and a smiling woman in a round helmet, all drawn in her own careful hand.

"I'm keeping all of them," she said softly, "right here, forever."

Barnacle winked one whiskery eye, then slipped back beneath the glowing water with a last, happy SPLOOSH.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. SPLOOSH, and sweet dreams of giant leaps.

story.title: Zara and the Humming Rock
story.subtitle: A journey through Earth's fiery openings, one glowing stone at a time

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Rock That Hummed
chapters.text:
Zara sat on her bedroom floor with her whole rock collection spread out like tiny stars. She picked up a lumpy grey rock from the very back of the shelf, one she had almost forgotten she owned. It was the plainest one in the whole pile.

It felt warm. Warmer than a rock should ever feel. Then it started to hum, low and rumbly, like a sleepy bee caught in a jar.

"Whoa," Zara whispered, holding it closer to her nose.

The rock cracked open like a tiny geode, and warm golden light spilled onto the carpet. A small, crackly voice came out of the glow. "Hello, Zara. I'm Quartz." A tiny crystal face blinked up at her from inside the light.

"Are you a rock?" Zara asked, leaning in.

"I'm what's left after a rock gets very, very hot," said Quartz. "Want to see where rocks like the ones on your shelf really come from?"

Zara didn't need to think twice. She nodded, and the golden light wrapped around her like a warm, swirling tunnel.

"Before we go," said Quartz, "tell me something. What do you call hot melted rock while it's still hiding underground?"

Zara thought of the red crayon she always grabbed first. "Lava?"

"Close! While it's still hiding underground, it's called **magma**," Quartz said. "The second it bursts out into the open air, it gets a brand new name — **lava**."

"That's like me," Zara said. "I have a different voice for inside my head and outside my mouth."

Quartz laughed, a sound like tiny bells clinking together. "A volcano is simply an opening in the ground where magma, ash, and gas find a way out," he said. "Ready to see one for real?"

"CLICK!" The golden light snapped shut around them like a bubble, and the carpet disappeared beneath Zara's feet.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Gentle Giant of Hawaii
chapters.text:
They landed somewhere warm, the air smelling like rotten eggs and sunshine all at once. The ground under Zara's shoes seemed to breathe, rising and falling in slow, soft bubbles.

"Where are we?" Zara asked, crouching to peek at glowing orange cracks nearby.

"Hawaii," said Quartz. "Home of **Kilauea**, one of the most active volcanoes on Earth. It's been erupting, off and on, for decades."

Zara studied the mountain in front of them. It wasn't pointy like the volcano in her coloring book at all. It was wide, flat, and gently sloped, spreading out in every direction. "It's shaped like a shield somebody dropped," she said.

Quartz's light flickered happily. "Exactly right. That's called a **shield volcano** — wide, with gentle slopes, because the lava here is thin and runny. It spreads out flat, like pancake batter, instead of piling up steep."

"Why does it erupt here and not somewhere flatter?" Zara asked.

"This spot sits over a **hotspot**," Quartz explained, "a place deep inside the Earth where hot rock keeps rising, like a pot that never stops bubbling. Most volcanoes grow at the edges of giant puzzle pieces called plates that make up the ground. Hawaii's hotspot sits right in the middle of one instead."

Zara pressed her ear carefully to a cool patch of rock and listened. A soft rumble answered back, steady as a heartbeat. "It's always awake," she whispered.

"Almost always," Quartz agreed. "This volcano has been glowing and bubbling for longer than your grown-ups have been alive."

Zara waved politely at the warm ground, careful to keep her hand well back from the glowing cracks. "Hi, Kilauea," she said. "Nice shield."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Ring Around the Ocean
chapters.text:
Quartz lifted them up, up, up, until Hawaii shrank to a tiny dot and the whole blue Pacific Ocean spread out below like one giant puddle on a map.

"Look down," Quartz said. "What do you notice around the edges?"

Zara squinted. Little orange dots glowed all around the ocean's rim, curling into one long, bending line, like a necklace someone had dropped in a hurry. "It's shaped like a horseshoe!" she said.

"That horseshoe has a name," said Quartz. "It's called the **Ring of Fire**, and it holds about **75% of all the active volcanoes on Earth**, all curled into one giant loop."

"Why do they all line up like that?" Zara asked.

"Most volcanoes grow where Earth's plates meet," Quartz said, "pushing together, pulling apart, or sliding past one another. The Ring of Fire follows the edges where the Pacific plate bumps into its neighbors."

Zara traced the glowing line with one finger, counting the little dots as they drifted by. One cluster burned brighter and thicker than all the rest, clumped together like sprinkles on a cupcake. "That part has SO many," she said, pointing.

"Good eye," said Quartz. "That's **Indonesia** — it has more active volcanoes than any other country on Earth."

"More than anywhere?" Zara's eyes went wide.

"More than anywhere," Quartz confirmed. "Want to see a famous volcano that isn't even on this ring?"

Zara nodded so fast her ponytail bounced, and the warm light scooped them up and carried them somewhere much, much older.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Mountain Pliny Watched
chapters.text:
They landed on a warm hillside under a very old, very blue sky. Below them sat a town built from pale stone, and far across a wide bay, a mountain breathed out a thin grey thread of smoke.

"Where's the fire part?" Zara asked, confused.

"Watch," said Quartz.

The grey thread grew thicker and darker, climbing higher and higher into the sky. Down below, Zara spotted a man standing calmly on a rooftop, scribbling fast in a book instead of running.

"Why isn't he scared?" Zara asked.

"That's **Pliny the Younger**," said Quartz. "He's watching this mountain, **Vesuvius**, from across the bay, and writing down everything he sees so people long after him will know exactly what happened."

"What IS happening?" Zara whispered.

"In the year **79**, Vesuvius erupted and covered two whole towns, **Pompeii** and **Herculaneum**, in thick ash," Quartz said gently. "It's a sad old story, but a true one, and it taught scientists an enormous amount about how volcanoes behave."

Zara watched the man keep writing, steady and careful, even as the sky grew dark above him. "You should name the eruption after him," she said, "since he's the one who wrote it all down."

Quartz's light sparkled like it was laughing. "Funny you should say that. Scientists really did. Any eruption that explodes tall and fast, full of ash like this one, is now called a **Plinian eruption** — named after Pliny."

"I named a kind of volcano!" Zara said, bouncing on her toes.

"You sure did," said Quartz, and the warm light scooped them away before the sky could grow any darker.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Boom Heard Across the Sea
chapters.text:
The light set them down on a calm, dark sea, waves rocking gently under a sky crowded with stars. Everything was quiet. Too quiet, even for Quartz.

"Quartz," Zara whispered, "why are we whispering?"

"Hold on," said Quartz. "This part is loud."

A heartbeat later: **BOOM.** The sound rolled across the water so hard that Zara felt it rattle in her chest. She clapped both hands over her ears.

"It's alright," Quartz said quickly. "That's just an echo from long ago. Nobody here is in any danger. We're listening to history, not living inside it."

Zara lowered her hands slowly. "What WAS that?"

"**Krakatoa**, erupting in **1883**," said Quartz. "It made a sound so loud that people on an island almost **3,000 miles away** heard it, like someone standing in your town hearing a bang from clear across the ocean."

Zara tried to picture it. Farther than Grandma's house. Farther than the beach they drove to every summer. Farther than anywhere she had ever been in her whole life. "That's SO far," she breathed.

"The loudest sound ever recorded," Quartz agreed. "Want to guess how many oceans that sound had to cross to get heard?"

Zara held up three fingers, even though she had no idea what the real answer was. It just felt like the right number to hold up.

Quartz chimed with laughter, bright and bubbly, bouncing off the quiet water. "Close enough, rock collector. Close enough."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Summer That Forgot to Come
chapters.text:
The next stop was cold enough to make Zara shiver, even with warm golden light still wrapped around her shoulders like a scarf. Grey snow drifted down from a sky with no sun in it anywhere.

"Why is it snowing?" Zara asked. "And why can't I find the sun?"

Quartz pointed up at the thick, hazy clouds. "In **1815**, a volcano called **Tambora**, in Indonesia, had the biggest eruption ever recorded. It threw so much ash into the sky that it blocked out sunlight, not just here, but all over the whole world."

Zara studied a strange grey fleck settling on her sleeve. "Is that ash?"

"Some of it, drifted all the way from Tambora," Quartz said. "Because of it, the very next year, **1816**, got a nickname: the **Year Without a Summer**. Crops failed, snow fell in June, and nobody could figure out why, not until much later."

Zara caught a flake on her glove and squinted at it the way she studied a brand new crystal. "The sun was still there," she said slowly. "It was just hiding behind the ash, like a blanket."

"Exactly like a blanket," Quartz said warmly. "One volcano, all the way over here, changed the weather for people on the other side of the whole world."

Zara tucked that thought away carefully, the way she tucked away a really good rock for her collection. "I'm telling EVERYONE this tomorrow," she announced, and the golden light swept the cold away in one warm breath.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Mountain's Warning
chapters.text:
This time they landed behind a rope line, far back from a green mountain with a strange bulge swelling on one side, like it had swallowed something too big to hold.

A tent nearby was crowded with blinking machines. Zara crept closer, careful to stay behind the rope. "What are those for?" she asked, pointing at a machine scratching wiggly lines across a slow-moving roll of paper.

"That's a **seismograph**," Quartz said. "It feels the ground shake, even tiny wobbles that people can't feel with their own feet. Scientists also use satellites to check if the ground is swelling up, like a balloon slowly filling with air. Both are warning signs that a volcano might wake up soon."

Zara leaned in and listened to the little clicks. At first they came slow — click... click... click. Then faster. Click-click-click-click.

"It's speeding up!" Zara said, eyes wide. "Something's about to happen!"

"Good ears," said Quartz. "On **May 18, 1980**, that's exactly what scientists here noticed, right before **Mount St. Helens** erupted, right after the **biggest landslide ever recorded** slid off its side. The whole top of the mountain, about **1,300 feet** of it, blew clean off."

A dedicated scientist named **David Johnston** had been studying this very volcano up close, trying to help everyone else stay safe. "He listened to this mountain the exact same way you just did," Quartz said.

Zara stepped back behind the rope on her own, without anybody asking her to, eyes still fixed on the bulging mountain. "Then we should listen too," she said, "and stay back here where it's safe."

"Smart rock collector," said Quartz, and together they watched from far, far away, safe and warm and sound.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Island That Grew From the Sea
chapters.text:
The light dropped them onto a little boat bobbing in icy water, somewhere near **Iceland**. Steam hissed up from the waves ahead, and the sea itself seemed to be boiling in one single spot.

"Why is the ocean smoking?" Zara asked, gripping the rail with both hands.

"Watch closely," said Quartz.

Under the water, orange light flickered, and chunks of brand new black rock kept piling higher and higher, pushing up through the waves. Bit by bit, a small dark hill broke through the surface, steaming and hissing like a kettle left too long on the stove.

"It's... making land?" Zara gasped. "Brand new land?"

"Exactly right," said Quartz. "In **1963**, an underwater volcano here kept erupting until a whole new island pushed up out of the sea. People named it **Surtsey**."

"How come Iceland gets so many volcanoes?" Zara asked, watching the little island grow another few inches right in front of her.

"Iceland sits right on top of the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge**," Quartz explained, "a long crack where two giant plates are slowly pulling apart from each other. Wherever plates pull apart, melted rock finds a way to sneak up through the gap."

Zara watched the little island steam quietly in the cold water, already imagining the rocks she might find there someday — shiny, black, and fresh from under the sea. "I want a piece of THAT rock," she said.

"Maybe someday," said Quartz gently. "For now, we just watch. New islands need time to cool down before anyone goes to visit."

Zara nodded, happy enough just to witness something so brand new being born right in front of her eyes.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Home Again
chapters.text:
Golden light swirled once more, soft and slow, and the ground beneath Zara's feet turned to carpet. Her own carpet, in her own room.

She was back in her bedroom, rock collection still spread out exactly where she'd left it. The humming grey rock sat open in her palm, glowing gently, with Quartz's tiny light still blinking inside like a firefly tucked into a jar.

"Before I go," said Quartz, "one more thing. Not every volcano is loud and busy like the ones we saw tonight. **Yellowstone** sits on top of an enormous sleeping volcano. Its last huge eruption happened about **640,000 years ago**, and scientists watching it closely see no sign that it's waking up anytime soon."

"So it's just... napping?" Zara asked through a yawn of her own.

"A very, very long nap," Quartz agreed, his light dimming softly. "Rocks and volcanoes both take their time."

Zara looked down at her collection: the shiny crystals, the dull grey stones, and the one glowing rock that had started this whole adventure. She picked a small, smooth black pebble from the pile and set it carefully beside the open geode, like a new little friend joining the family.

"Will you come back?" she asked.

"Whenever a rock on your shelf starts humming," said Quartz, "I'll be right here." The light folded gently back into the grey stone, which cooled in her hand and went quiet, waiting patiently for next time.

Zara climbed into bed, her rock collection glittering faintly in the dark, and pulled the blanket up to her chin, already dreaming of shields and rings and islands still too new to visit.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Zara. Dream in rock and light.

story.title: Ben and the Pixel Trip Through Time
story.subtitle: One night, one glowing screen, and the whole history of video games.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Green Dot That Wouldn't Sleep (1958)
chapters.text:
Ben was supposed to be asleep an hour ago.

Instead he lay on his bedroom floor, tablet propped on his pillow, drawing a pixel sword one careful square at a time. Red square. Red square. Silver tip.

Then his screen hiccupped. The colors flipped to black and green, like something from a museum. A tiny shape made of glowing green dots popped up and waved both tiny arms.

"Finally," the shape said. "Someone who still knows how to build things one square at a time."

Ben sat up fast. "Who are you?"

"Name's Pix," said the dot-shaped guy. "And you just woke me up — which means it's time for a trip."

The screen flickered to show a bouncing green line on a round glowing scope, a tiny screen scientists once used to watch wiggly shapes.

"What is that, tennis?" Ben asked.

"Good eye," said Pix. "In **1958**, a scientist named **William Higinbotham** built this at a lab called **Brookhaven**. He called it **Tennis for Two** — one of the very first video games ever made."

Ben squinted at the bouncing dot. It arced just like a ball thrown high. "The ball needs more curve on the serve," he said, and tapped the screen right where the line peaked.

The dot obeyed him. It arced higher, bounced once, and the whole screen lit up neon green.

"WHOOOOSH!" Pix shouted, spinning in a circle. "You just called the shot on the first video game in history. Not bad for a kid who should be asleep."

The green light swallowed the bedroom, and Ben's stomach did a happy little flip.

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Computer That Filled a Whole Room (1962)
chapters.text:
They landed in a room stuffed with blinking boxes taller than Ben.

"Where are we?" Ben asked, stepping around a cable thick as a snake.

"MIT," said Pix. "A college. This whole room is one computer."

Ben's jaw dropped. "That's one computer? My tablet is smaller than my shoe!"

"In **1962**, computers filled whole rooms," Pix said. "A student named **Steve Russell** and his friends used this giant machine, called the **PDP-1**, to make a game called **Spacewar!** — two tiny spaceships shooting near a star."

A screen blinked on, showing two wobbly triangle ships. Ben noticed one was drifting toward the star, getting pulled in closer and closer.

"That one's about to crash into the star," Ben said, pointing. "He needs to turn now."

"Tell him yourself," Pix said, grinning.

Ben grabbed the clunky switch in front of him and flicked it. The little triangle swerved just in time, slingshotting around the star instead of smashing into it.

**CLICK!** The giant machine filled the room with cheerful beeps.

"You just flew the first spaceship fight in video game history," said Pix. "Try explaining that one to your teacher."

Ben laughed so hard he nearly tripped over a cable.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Box Full of Games (1967–1972)
chapters.text:
Next they landed in a workshop that smelled like solder and sawdust.

An engineer was hunched over a plain brown box, wires spilling out like spaghetti.

"That's **Ralph Baer**," Pix whispered. "People call him the father of video games, because he had a wild idea — what if you could play a game right on your own TV at home?"

Ben peered at the tangle of wires. "Does it even work?"

Pix nudged him toward two dials. "Try it."

Ben turned one dial, and a white square — meant to be a ball — hopped across the TV screen. He turned the other dial, and a line on his side zipped up to meet it. **BOOP.** The ball bounced back.

"That's it," Pix said. "Baer called it the **Brown Box**. By **1972**, it became a real toy you could buy, called the **Magnavox Odyssey** — the very first home game console."

Ben kept bouncing the little square back and forth, grinning wider each time. "It's like Pong, but ancient."

"It's not ancient," Pix said. "It's the great-great-grandpa of every console you own."

Ben missed the ball on purpose, just to hear it go BOOP one more time, and Pix pretended to be scandalized.

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Arcade That Got Too Popular (1972)
chapters.text:
The workshop melted away into the buzzing lights of an arcade.

Coins clinked. A crowd three-deep stood watching a white dot bounce between two paddles.

"This is **Pong**," said Pix. "Made in **1972** by **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney**, who started a company called **Atari**."

Ben pushed closer and read a handwritten sign taped to one machine: OUT OF ORDER.

"What happened to it?" Ben asked.

"Fun story," Pix said. "People say one of the very first Pong machines got so stuffed with quarters that it actually jammed shut. Nobody's totally sure that part is true, but it shows how fast everyone fell in love with this game."

Ben crouched down and spotted the coin slot bent sideways, with a few coins peeking out underneath. "Look — it really is stuffed," he said.

Pix laughed. "Nice detective work. Somebody call a repair guy."

Right on cue, a man in overalls appeared, shaking his head and grinning as he popped the machine open. A waterfall of quarters clattered onto the floor, and the whole arcade cheered.

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Box You Could Swap (1977)
chapters.text:
Their next stop was a cozy living room with a boxy TV and a pile of flat plastic cases on the carpet.

"This is an **Atari 2600**," Pix said. "It came out in **1977**. Before this, game machines could only play the one game built inside them."

Ben picked up a plastic case shaped like a cartridge. "You mean you had to buy a whole new machine for every single new game?"

"Exactly," said Pix. "This little cartridge changed that. Slide a new one in, and the console plays a brand new game."

Ben turned the cartridge over, studying it like a puzzle piece. "It's kind of like swapping a different world file in Minecraft," he said.

"Huh," said Pix. "Never thought of it that way, but — yeah, actually."

Ben slid the cartridge into the slot. **CLICK.** The TV flashed to life with a blocky racing game.

"Try another one," Pix said.

Ben swapped cartridges three more times in under a minute, grinning wider each time a new game popped up. "This is basically the best toy box ever made," he said.

chapters.heading: Level 6: Invaders and a Pizza With a Slice Missing (1978–1980)
chapters.text:
The living room buzzed into a noisy arcade again, this time full of beeping aliens marching down a screen.

"Welcome to **1978**," Pix said. "A designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado** made this game for a company called Taito. It's called **Space Invaders**, and it started a giant arcade craze all over the world."

Ben grabbed the little joystick and blasted a row of pixel aliens as they marched closer. **PEW PEW PEW.** The aliens popped like bubbles.

"Nice shooting," said Pix, as the last alien vanished. "Now check this one out."

The screen changed to show a round yellow shape gobbling dots in a maze.

"This is **Pac-Man**, made in **1980** by a designer named **Toru Iwatani**," Pix said. "Some people say he got the idea from looking at a pizza with one slice missing."

Ben studied the yellow shape's open mouth. "That actually does look like a pizza with a bite out of it," he said.

"Might just be a fun story," Pix admitted, "but it's a tasty one."

Ben steered Pac-Man around a corner, just missing a ghost, and pumped his fist. "Got away clean!"

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Big Game Pile-Up (1983)
chapters.text:
The arcade dimmed, and they landed in a huge, dusty warehouse stacked with cardboard boxes.

"What happened here?" Ben asked, poking a box labeled with a game he'd never heard of.

"In **1983**, too many rushed, not-very-good games flooded the stores," Pix explained. "People stopped buying them, and the whole video game business in North America got a lot smaller for a while. Folks call it the **video game crash**."

Ben opened a box and found it stuffed with cartridges nobody had wanted. "What did they do with all these?"

"Funny you ask," said Pix. "A famous story says a truckload of unsold cartridges — including one based on the movie E.T. — got buried out in the desert in New Mexico. People wondered for years if it was even true."

"Was it?" Ben asked.

"In **2014**, some diggers actually found the cartridges buried right there," Pix said. "So that one turned out to be real."

Ben pulled a dusty cartridge from the pile and blew the dust off it. "This feels like digging up buried treasure," he said, grinning.

"Good thing you already know how to dig," said Pix. "You've buried plenty of stuff in Minecraft."

chapters.heading: Level 8: The Plumber Who Saved Everything (1984–1985)
chapters.text:
They popped out of the warehouse into a brighter, cheerier room full of colorful game cartridges shaped like little red mushrooms.

"This is where things turned around," Pix said. "In **1985**, a company called Nintendo brought out a new console called the **NES**, and it came packed with a brand new game."

A screen flickered on, showing a mustached plumber jumping over a gap.

"That's **Mario**," said Pix. "A designer named **Shigeru Miyamoto** made him in **1985**, and he became the most famous character in video games."

Ben grabbed the controller and lined Mario up for a jump over a pit. He timed it perfectly, landing right on a floating block. "Got it!"

Before Pix could even cheer, the screen shifted to show colored blocks falling and stacking in neat rows.

"Different game," Pix said. "This is **Tetris**, made in **1984** by a scientist in Moscow named **Alexey Pajitnov**. You fit the falling shapes together so they don't pile up too high."

Ben studied the shapes the way he studied his pixel art — square by square — then rotated a block and slid it into a gap, clearing a whole row. **CLEAR!**

"LEVEL UP!" Pix cheered, as the room filled with confetti shaped like tiny pixels.

chapters.heading: Level 9: Blue Blur, Shiny Discs, and Swinging Arms (1991–2006)
chapters.text:
A blue blur zipped past so fast Ben nearly fell over.

"Meet **Sonic the Hedgehog**," Pix said, "made by Sega in **1991** to race against Mario and show off how fast games could go."

Ben tried to keep up on the controller, but the blue hedgehog was already looping through a curve. "He's basically faster than me in Minecraft on a minecart," Ben laughed.

The scene shifted to a sleek silver disc spinning inside a machine.

"This is a **PlayStation**," Pix said, "made by Sony in **1994**. It used shiny discs instead of cartridges, which let games look and sound way fuller."

Ben picked up the disc and turned it in the light, watching rainbow colors ripple across it. "It's like a tiny CD," he said.

"Exactly like one," Pix said. "Now — this next part, you'll want to stand up for."

The room cleared some space, and a little white remote appeared in Ben's hand.

"The **Wii**, from **2006**," Pix said. "Nintendo made a controller you actually swing, like a tennis racket or a sword, so even people who had never played a game before wanted to try."

Ben swung the remote like a bat, and on-screen a tiny pixel batter smacked a home run. "This is the first game where I actually have to move," he said, catching his breath and laughing.

chapters.heading: Level 10: The Block World and the Trip Home (2011–Today)
chapters.text:
The last room looked almost exactly like Ben's own bedroom — blocky, green, and strangely familiar.

"Wait," Ben said. "Is this—"

"**Minecraft**," Pix said. "Made by a Swedish game maker named **Markus Persson** — people call him 'Notch' — and released in **2011**. It became the best-selling video game ever made."

Ben looked around at the cube-shaped trees and square clouds. "I build in here every single day."

"That's the whole point," Pix said. "This game is basically one giant, endless pixel-art canvas, and you already know exactly how to use it."

One wall of the room showed rows of old game cartridges and consoles sitting behind glass, like a museum.

"This is the **World Video Game Hall of Fame**," Pix said. "It opened in **2015**, at a museum in Rochester, New York, and it keeps famous old games safe forever, so nobody forgets where it all started."

Ben spotted an empty pedestal at the end of the row, with a tiny plaque that just said: NEXT UP. "Is that for a game that doesn't exist yet?" he asked.

"Could be," Pix said. "Could be yours, someday."

The green light swallowed them both, and when it faded, Ben was back on his bedroom floor, tablet glowing softly beside him. His half-finished pixel sword still sat on the screen — but now a tiny green pixel dot blinked in the corner, right where Pix had waved goodbye.

Ben smiled and pulled his blanket up to his chin.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ben. Game well.

true_facts.text: The very first video game, called **Tennis for Two**, was built in **1958** by a scientist named **William Higinbotham**.
In **1962**, a student named **Steve Russell** used a giant room-sized computer to make **Spacewar!**, a game about two tiny spaceships.
**Ralph Baer** built a homemade TV game called the **Brown Box**, and people call him the father of video games.
Baer's box became the **Magnavox Odyssey** in **1972**, the first game console you could play on your own TV.
Also in **1972**, **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started **Atari** and made the arcade game **Pong**.
The **Atari 2600**, from **1977**, let you swap in different plastic cartridges instead of being stuck with one game.
**Space Invaders**, made in **1978** by **Tomohiro Nishikado**, started a huge arcade craze with marching alien rows.
**Pac-Man**, made in **1980** by **Toru Iwatani**, is said to have been inspired by a pizza missing a slice.
In **1983**, too many rushed, low-quality games flooded stores, and the video game business in North America shrank for a while.
In **1985**, Nintendo's **NES** console helped bring video games back, bundled with a brand new game.
**Shigeru Miyamoto** created **Mario** the plumber in **1985**, and he became gaming's most famous character.
**Tetris**, the falling-block puzzle game, was invented in **1984** by a scientist named **Alexey Pajitnov** in Moscow.
**Sonic the Hedgehog** was made by Sega in **1991** to race against Mario and show off super speed.
**Minecraft** was released in **2011** by game maker **Markus Persson** and became the best-selling video game ever made.

story.title: Lena and the Ball Called Patch
story.subtitle: A keeper's tour through the history of soccer

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Patch Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Lena was supposed to be asleep.

Instead she was in the backyard, drilling saves against the brick wall for maybe the fortieth time that night. Her left-side dive was getting lazy and she knew it. So, apparently, did the ball — because when it bounced back off the wall, it didn't roll. It glowed.

Gold light leaked out of the seams of her beat-up old practice ball, the one her coach called "ancient." A low hum came from inside it, like a radio finding a station.

"Finally," said the ball. "Do you know how long I've been waiting for a keeper who actually dives *left*?"

Lena dropped it. It bounced once and hovered at knee height.

"I'm Patch," it said. "And you're about to find out where this entire sport came from. Try to keep up — I don't do replays."

The yard folded shut like a map. When it opened again, Lena stood on packed dirt in **China**, more than **2,000 years ago**, watching young men kick a stuffed leather ball between two poles, using only feet, knees, and chests. Never hands.

"This is **Cuju**," Patch said. "One of soccer's oldest known ancestors — people playing keep-it-off-the-ground centuries before anyone called it soccer."

Lena watched a player juggle the ball off his knee without it ever touching dirt. She tried it herself — knee, foot, chest. The players stared, then grinned and waved her into the circle.

"Not bad," Patch admitted, "for someone two thousand years early."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Game the King Banned
chapters.text:
The next field was chaos.

A crowd the size of a small army was shoving down a muddy English street, kicking — and occasionally carrying, tackling, and shouting — one poor leather ball toward a church on one end of town and a mill on the other.

"Welcome to **mob football**," Patch said. "Medieval England — basically knight times — whole villages played against each other. No ref, barely any rules, and the 'field' was the entire town."

The ball squirted loose and rocketed straight at a shopkeeper's window. Lena didn't think. She dove, got a fingertip to it, and knocked it wide into a hay cart instead.

"Nice stop," Patch said, "though technically you don't exist yet, so that's between us."

"This is insane," Lena said, catching her breath. "Somebody needs actual rules before this town falls apart."

"Funny you say that," said Patch. "Because **King Edward II** agreed. In **1314**, he got so sick of the chaos he banned the whole sport in London."

Lena looked at the dented window, the toppled cart, and the hay-covered crowd still cheering like nothing happened.

"Can't say he was wrong," she admitted.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: One Rulebook to Rule Them All
chapters.text:
Centuries later, the chaos had moved indoors — into an argument.

A cluster of university students at **Cambridge** stood on a muddy field, yelling over each other. One side wanted to carry the ball. The other wanted feet only. Nobody could agree on anything, and the game kept stopping.

"This is why nothing works," Lena said. "You can't have five different games happening at once. Pick *one* way. Write it down. Everybody follows it."

A student actually stopped mid-argument and looked at her.

"She's right," he said slowly.

In **1848**, that's exactly what the Cambridge students did — writing down the **Cambridge Rules**, an early attempt at one shared rulebook everyone could use.

"And here's a bonus," Patch said, as the scene shifted to a schoolyard decades later. "The sport those rules led to got nicknamed 'assoc' — short for association football. British schoolboys in the **1880s** shortened it further."

"Let me guess," Lena said.

"Soccer," Patch said. "You're welcome."
chapters.shout_line: PICK ONE WAY AND WRITE IT DOWN!

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Man Who Wrote the Laws
chapters.text:
A man sat hunched over a desk in London, candle burning low, pen scratching fast.

"That's **Ebenezer Cobb Morley**," Patch said. "Founder of the **Football Association**, started on **October 26, 1863**. He's writing the first official rulebook — they call it the Laws of the Game."

Lena leaned over his shoulder and read: *no player may carry the ball with his hands.*

"Wait," she said. "What about the goalkeeper?"

Morley actually paused his pen.

"A fair question," he muttered, and scribbled a note in the margin.

"You just interrupted the guy writing soccer's first rulebook," Patch said, "to ask about goalkeepers. I like you."

Lena grinned. Keepers, it turned out, would get their own special hand-rules eventually — but it started with someone in the room asking the obvious question nobody else thought to.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Shutout Nobody Expected
chapters.text:
The crowd in **Glasgow** was getting restless.

"Ninety minutes," Patch said, "and not one goal. First official international match ever — **Scotland versus England**, **1872**. Ends 0-0."

A man near Lena groaned. "Rubbish match. Nothing happened."

"Nothing happened?" Lena said, turning around. "Two keepers just stopped *every single shot* for an hour and a half. That's not boring — that's both goalkeepers playing the game of their lives."

The man blinked, then actually started clapping.

"She's not wrong," Patch said. "And this same era kicked off the **FA Cup**, first played in **1871-72** — still running today. Makes it the oldest football competition in the world."

Lena watched the scoreless match end in handshakes, not boos.

"Shutouts," she said, "are underrated."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Kick They Tried to Ban
chapters.text:
The crowd here was enormous — and most of them were cheering for women.

"**Lily Parr**," Patch said, nodding at a tall player blasting a shot that nearly tore through the net. "One of the stars of the Dick, Kerr Ladies. For a while, they were one of the most popular teams in England."

Then the scene darkened. A notice went up on a wall. Women, it announced, were banned from playing on official football grounds.

"That's unfair," Lena said flatly. "She's clearly better than half the men out there."

"You're not wrong," Patch said. "But it happened anyway — and it lasted **fifty years**."

Lena walked to the wall, lined up a shot of her own, and smashed it into the fence hard enough to rattle it. "That's for Lily."

The scene jumped forward. The banned notice came down — **1971**. Then jumped again: a packed stadium in **China**, **1991**, the United States lifting the very first official Women's World Cup trophy.

"Took a while," Patch said, "but it got there."

"FINALLY!" Lena shouted, loud enough that half the stadium turned to look.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Trophy That Nearly Fell
chapters.text:
Uruguay, **1930**. The air smelled like celebration and cut grass.

"First ever **World Cup**," Patch said. "Host nation, Uruguay, just beat Argentina in the final."

An official carried a small gold statue toward the winning captain — hands shaking, feet moving too fast on the slick grass. He stumbled. The trophy tipped sideways, right off his palms.

Lena, closest to the action, lunged and caught it an inch off the ground, like it was a shot curling into the top corner.

"Nice save," Patch said. "That trophy was pushed hard by **Jules Rimet**, the man who got the whole World Cup idea off the ground — which is why they later named it after him."

Lena handed it back, polished where her hands had smudged it.

"Try not to drop history next time," she told the official.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Case of the Missing Cup
chapters.text:
London, **1966**. Something was very wrong.

"The World Cup trophy's been stolen," Patch said. "Right before the tournament even starts."

Searchers combed the streets for a week, no luck. Lena, walking near a quiet hedge, noticed the leaves rustling in a spot with no wind.

"Over there," she called, pointing without stepping closer.

A small dog came bounding out from under the hedge — nose first, tail wagging, trophy wrapped in newspaper right beside him.

"That's **Pickles**," Patch said. "Found it safe, exactly one week after it vanished."

The crowd cheered. Weeks later, **England** hosted — and won — the **1966 World Cup**, their only title so far.

"Good dog," Lena said, keeping a respectful distance. "Great eye for hedges, though. I'll take some credit."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Grass
chapters.text:
The yard folded open again, porch light humming, grass cold under Lena's socks.

Patch sat still in her hands, the glow fading to its normal scuffed brown.

"So," Lena said. "Cuju, mobs, rulebooks, Lily Parr, two World Cups, and a dog named Pickles."

"Give or take a few centuries," Patch said. "Not bad for one night."

She set the ball down by the wall, right where the first glow had started. In the dirt beside it sat something new — a small scuffed patch of leather, stitched like the oldest ball she'd ever seen, like a tiny souvenir from somewhere very far back.

She picked it up, turned it over once, and tucked it in her pocket.

Upstairs, her cleats were still by the door, muddy from practice, waiting for Saturday's match.

"Dive left more," Patch said quietly, as the glow finally went out.

Saturday couldn't come soon enough.

story.ending_line: Saturday couldn't come soon enough.

story.title: Arjun and the REM Express
story.subtitle: A night tour through comics, cricket, and the science of sleep.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Owl on the Shelf
chapters.text:
Arjun was under the blanket with a flashlight, reading the newest issue of *Captain Thunderbolt*, when his mom called that it was lights-out.

"Five more minutes," Arjun said, the way he always did.

He clicked off the flashlight and lay there replaying the comic's best panel: Captain Thunderbolt catching a cricket ball mid-air to save the city. That's when the cricket-ball night-light on his shelf started to hum. It wasn't supposed to hum. It glowed green, then brighter, and with a soft **WHOOOOSH** a small, round-eyed owl popped out and landed on his pillow.

"Name's REM," the owl said, blinking twice. "Bit on the nose, I know. You'll get why."

Before Arjun could ask anything sensible, the room stretched sideways like a comic panel unfolding, and they landed in a cold, humming lab with a sleeping boy on a cot.

"**University of Chicago, 1953**," REM said. "Watch his eyes."

Under the boy's closed eyelids, something flicked back and forth, fast, like he was watching a tennis match in his sleep. "His eyes are moving," Arjun whispered. "But he's totally asleep."

"That's exactly what a scientist named **Eugene Aserinsky** noticed," REM said, "watching a sleeping boy's eyes. He and another scientist, **Nathaniel Kleitman**, who spent basically his whole career studying sleep, figured out this flickery stage meant the sleeper was deep in a dream. They named it **REM sleep** — rapid eye movement. Yes. That's where I got the name."

"EYES ARE MOVING!" Arjun said, pointing, and the boy on the cot slept right through it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ninety-Minute Over
chapters.text:
Next stop was a room with a machine drawing wavy green lines across a scroll of paper, like a heartbeat monitor having an opinion.

"This is one whole night of sleep," REM said. "Watch the pattern."

The lines dipped low and slow, then suddenly went spiky and fast, then dipped low again. "It repeats," Arjun said. "Like overs in cricket. Six balls, then a new over, over and over."

"Close enough," REM said. "Sleep runs in cycles about **ninety minutes long**. Quiet sleep, then **REM sleep** — the dreamy, spiky kind — then quiet again, all night."

"So during the spiky bit, people are dreaming?"

"Dreaming hard," REM said. "Brain's almost as busy as if you were awake. But your muscles go floppy as a wet towel, so you can't jump up and start bowling in your dream."

Arjun counted the spikes on the scroll — one, two, three, four — and pointed at the fifth exactly as it appeared. "There's another one," he said, a beat before the line jumped.

"Lucky guess," REM said, grinning. "Or you're paying attention. I'll allow both."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Growing Stage
chapters.text:
The next room had a glass tank bubbling with something that glowed gold, like a trophy filled with lemonade.

"That," REM said, "is a model of **growth hormone** — the stuff your body makes to help you grow taller and stronger."

"When does it come out?" Arjun asked.

"Good question. Look at the graph." REM pointed at a chart with a deep dip and a tall gold spike right where the line sank lowest.

Arjun traced the lowest point with his finger. "Right here. The deepest part of sleep — the really quiet kind, no dreaming."

"Exactly there," REM said. "The deepest stage of quiet sleep pours out the most growth hormone. One big reason kids who are still growing need extra sleep."

Arjun thought about his cricket coach, who always said skip nothing in training. "So skipping sleep is like skipping training," he said slowly.

"Now you're getting it," REM said. "Growing's a training session your body runs while you're unconscious. Free of charge."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Clock Behind Your Eyes
chapters.text:
They landed inside something that looked like a tiny control room, no bigger than a shoebox, with one glowing dial on the wall.

"We're inside a brain now," REM said. "Specifically, right behind your eyes, where the two eye nerves cross."

"There's a *clock* in my brain?" Arjun said.

"A tiny one," REM said. "Scientists call it the **suprachiasmatic nucleus** — just remember it sits right where the eye nerves cross, and it works as the body's master clock for sleeping and waking."

The dial was stuck between two numbers, ticking unevenly. Arjun nudged it until it settled near twenty-four. "There," he said. "Fixed it."

"Nicely done," REM said. "That clock runs on a roughly **twenty-four-hour** rhythm scientists call **circadian** — from old Latin words that just mean 'about a day.' It's why you get sleepy at night and wake up around the same time, even on vacation. Even when you beg for five more minutes."

"That's oddly specific," Arjun said.

"I know you," REM said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Lights-Out Juice
chapters.text:
The next stop smelled faintly like a science lab, all glass bottles and handwritten labels.

"**1958**," REM said. "A scientist named **Aaron Lerner** and his team were hunting for a hormone that helps the body feel sleepy. They pulled it from a tiny gland — a little clump of cells — deep inside the brain."

On the shelf, one bottle glowed soft silver, dimmer than all the others. Arjun picked up the tag beside it: no name, just a drawing of a crescent moon.

"That one," Arjun said, pointing. "The dim, moon one. That's the sleepy stuff, right?"

"Right first time," REM said. "They named it **melatonin** — your body's own lights-out juice. Your brain makes more of it when it gets dark, which is one reason bright phone screens at bedtime are a rotten idea."

Arjun glanced guiltily at the flashlight he'd left glowing under his blanket, several time zones away.

"Don't worry," REM said. "I'm an owl, not a snitch."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Three Scientists and a Trophy
chapters.text:
A stage appeared with three empty podiums and a glowing gold medal spinning above each one.

"**2017**," REM said. "Three scientists — **Jeffrey Hall**, **Michael Rosbash**, and **Michael Young** — won the **Nobel Prize**, basically science's biggest trophy, for figuring out the genes that keep your circadian clock ticking, gear by gear."

In front of the podiums sat three scrambled puzzle pieces, each labeled with half a gene name. Arjun turned them over, matched the jagged edges, and clicked them into one strip.

"They fit in order," he said. "Like overs fit into an innings."

"They do," REM said. "Those genes switch on and off on a schedule, telling your cells when it's day and when it's night, even with your eyes shut. Three careers spent on a clock nobody can even see. I respect that kind of patience."

Arjun set the last puzzle piece down. "I can't even wait five minutes for lights-out."

"We've noticed," REM said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Eleven Days Awake
chapters.text:
The next room had a faded newspaper pinned to the wall, headline curling at the edges.

"**1964**," REM said. "A **seventeen-year-old** named **Randy Gardner**, from **San Diego**, stayed awake for a school science project. **About eleven days**. One of the longest stretches anybody's ever properly recorded."

"Eleven *days*?" Arjun said. "Did he feel okay?"

"Not really," REM said. "By the end, his mood, his memory, and his attention were a mess. Doctors who study this now say: interesting story, terrible idea. Nobody should try to beat it."

Arjun looked at the newspaper, then at the little cot in the corner of the room, empty and waiting. For a second he imagined staying up eleven days straight, reading every comic he owned back to back.

"I'm good," he said finally. "I'd rather read them properly. One at a time. While awake enough to enjoy them."

"Wisest thing anyone's said in this room," REM said. "Including me."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Sleepiest Animals Alive
chapters.text:
The last stop before home looked like a page ripped from a nature comic, three glowing panels side by side.

In the first, a dolphin swam in slow circles, one eye open. "Dolphins and some seals," REM said, "sleep with only half their brain resting at a time. The other half stays alert, so they can keep an eye out and keep swimming."

In the second panel, a giraffe stood very still, legs locked. "Giraffes," REM said, "are some of the shortest sleepers of any big animal — sometimes under two hours a day, in quick naps, standing up."

The third panel showed a bat hanging upside down, fast asleep. Arjun studied all three, then pointed at the bat. "That one sleeps the most. Has to. Look how comfortable it looks."

"Spot on," REM said. "Some small bats sleep up to **twenty hours a day** — among the sleepiest mammals anybody's found."

"Twenty hours," Arjun said. "My mom would have a lot to say about that."

They watched the panels glow a moment longer, three very different bedtimes, none of them wrong.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back Under the Blanket
chapters.text:
The next **WHOOOOSH** dropped Arjun straight back under his own blanket, flashlight dark, cricket-ball night-light glowing its ordinary green.

"One last thing," REM said, perched on the pillow. "While you sleep tonight, your brain sorts through everything you practiced today — your cover drive, your comic plots, all of it — and files the good stuff into memory. That's part of why sleeping well after practice actually helps you get better."

"And the other part?"

"There's a kind of nightly rinse cycle in there too," REM said, "washing the gunk out of a tired brain while you're under. You'll spend about a third of your whole life asleep. Might as well do it properly."

Arjun thought about the flickering-eyed boy in Chicago, the ninety-minute overs, the glowing melatonin bottle, Randy Gardner's eleven rough days, and the bat sleeping twenty hours upside down without a care.

"Five more minutes?" REM asked, one eyebrow — somehow — raised.

"No," Arjun said, surprising himself. "I'm good."

He clicked the night-light down to its dimmest setting and closed his eyes. Somewhere outside, the glow faded to a thin green line, then nothing at all.

story.ending_line: Practice started at nine, and for once, Arjun was going to be properly awake for it.

During **REM sleep** the brain gets almost as busy as when you're awake, but the muscles go floppy so the sleeper can't act out the dream.
The deepest, quietest stage of sleep releases the most **growth hormone**, which is one reason growing kids need extra sleep.
A tiny spot in the brain right where the eye nerves cross, called the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**, works as the body's master clock for sleeping and waking.
The word **circadian**, used for the body's roughly twenty-four-hour clock, comes from old Latin words meaning 'about a day.'
In **2017**, three scientists — **Jeffrey Hall**, **Michael Rosbash**, and **Michael Young** — won the **Nobel Prize** for finding the genes that keep that clock ticking.
The sleepy-time hormone **melatonin** was first pulled out of a tiny brain gland in **1958** by a scientist named **Aaron Lerner** and his team.
In **1964**, a **seventeen-year-old** named **Randy Gardner** from **San Diego** stayed awake for about **eleven days** for a science project.
Doctors say nobody should ever try to copy Randy Gardner's eleven sleepless days — going without sleep quickly wrecks mood, focus, and memory.

Giraffes are some of the shortest sleepers of any big animal, sometimes napping standing up for under two hours a day.
Some small bats sleep up to **twenty hours a day**, making them some of the sleepiest animals known.
People spend about a **third of their whole life** asleep, adding up all those nights over a lifetime.

story.title: Tom and the Drivewheel of Ages
story.subtitle: One garage, one glowing gear, two hundred years of bicycles.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Running Machine (1817, Germany)
chapters.text:
The garage light buzzed, flickered, and Tom barely noticed. He was elbow-deep in his mountain bike's drivetrain, trying to figure out why the chain kept skipping on the steepest gear.

His hand closed around a gear tooth that wasn't his. It was small, bronze, and warm, and it hummed like it was plugged into something.

"That wasn't in my toolbox," Tom said.

The gear **WHIRRED**, caught the shop light, and turned it green. The garage dissolved into cobbled German streets and the smell of horses.

In front of him stood a wooden two-wheeled contraption with handlebars but no pedals at all. A man in a long coat sat on it, pushing himself along with his own feet like he was running while sitting down.

"That's **1817**," the gear whirred in Tom's palm. "Karl von Drais. He calls it the running machine."

Tom crouched to look underneath. "Steering bar's basically the same as mine. But you're just... running."

"Exactly the flaw," the gear said. "Somebody has to fix that."

Tom grinned. "Give it wheels that spin themselves. You'd need something to push *for* you."

The gear spun faster, like it agreed, and the street blurred forward through fifty years in a single breath.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boneshaker (1860s, France)
chapters.text:
The blur stopped on a cobblestone road that looked like it was built entirely out of teeth.

A man wobbled past on a two-wheeler with pedals bolted straight onto the front wheel. Every bump in the road jumped straight up through the frame.

"**Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement**," the gear said, warm against Tom's fingers. "French builders. They put pedals right on the front wheel. People call it a velocipede — just a fancy word for an early pedal bike. Everybody else calls it the **boneshaker**."

"Because it shakes your bones," Tom said, watching the rider's teeth rattle over a cobble. "No suspension. No give at all."

"Lallement even patented the idea in America, in **1866**," the gear added.

Tom tried the bike himself, just a few pedal turns down the street. Every rock in the road slammed straight into his wrists.

"The problem's not the pedals," he said, pulling off to the side. "It's the wheels. Both wheels are the same size and small. You're stuck going slow *and* rough."

The gear ticked, pleased. "Somebody solved half of that next. Hang on."

The cobblestones spun away under Tom's boots.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Taking a Header (1870s, England)
chapters.text:
Tom landed on an English high street, and the first thing he saw was a wheel taller than a grown man.

A rider sat perched way up high on a seat above it, with a tiny wheel trailing behind like an afterthought.

"That's a **penny-farthing**," the gear said. "Named for two old British coins — one huge, one tiny, just like the wheels."

"One turn of the pedals on that front wheel," Tom said, doing the math out loud, "covers way more ground than a small wheel would. That's actually smart. Gear ratio, basically, just built into the wheel size."

As if to prove it, the rider suddenly jammed to a stop over a rut. He pitched forward off the seat and rolled onto the grass, hat flying.

Tom winced. "Is he—"

"He's fine," the gear said quickly, as the man sat up, laughing, and brushed off his coat. "Falling head-first like that even got its own nickname: **taking a header**. Riders sat so high, a sudden stop could tip them clean over the front."

"Great design, terrible survival rate," Tom said. "You'd want wheels that are even, low, and both the same size."

The gear practically purred. "Someone's about to agree with you."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Safety Bicycle (1885, England)
chapters.text:
The next street was quieter, and the bike leaning against a lamppost looked almost normal — two matching wheels, low to the ground, and a chain looping from the pedals back to the rear wheel.

Tom circled it twice before he said anything. "This is it. This is basically a bike."

"**John Kemp Starley**, **1885**," the gear said. "He called it the Rover Safety Bicycle. Even-sized wheels, and the chain drives the back wheel instead of the pedals sitting right on the front one."

"That's the whole trick," Tom said, tracing the chain's path with one finger. "Put the pedals wherever you want, and let the chain carry the power to the wheel. You're not stuck balancing on top of the power source anymore."

"It worked," the gear said. "This design beat the penny-farthing everywhere, fast. Nobody wanted to take headers anymore."

Tom swung a leg over, just to feel the geometry, and rolled a few slow feet down the lane. The ride was steady. Predictable. Almost boring, in the best way.

"It's still rattly, though," he said, feeling every pebble through the solid rubber tires. "Somebody still has to fix that."

The gear chuckled, a sound like a bell turning over. "Funny you'd ask."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Air Under the Wheel (1888, Scotland)
chapters.text:
A workshop in Scotland smelled like rubber and glue. A man knelt beside a small tricycle, wrapping a rubber tube around its wheel and pumping it full of air with a hand pump.

"**John Boyd Dunlop**," the gear said. "A vet here in **1888**. He built this for his son's tricycle, because solid rubber tires gave the poor kid a brutal ride over cobbles."

Tom crouched by the wheel, pressing a thumb into the inflated tube. It gave, then sprang back. "A pneumatic tire," he said. "Pneumatic just means it's full of air instead of solid. It's basically a cushion you ride on."

"Exactly that," the gear said. "Dunlop's company grew into a tire brand that's still around — you've probably seen the name on tires. Even car tires, eventually."

Tom thought about his own mountain bike tires, wide and knobby and full of air, soaking up every root and rock on the trail. "This is the missing piece," he said. "Even wheels, a chain, *and* air in the tires. Now you've basically got a real bike."

"Now," the gear agreed, spinning warmer in his hand, "everybody wanted one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Golden Age (1890s)
chapters.text:
The workshop dissolved into a street crowded with bicycles — dozens of them, gliding past storefronts, bells ringing.

"The **1890s**," the gear said. "People call it the Golden Age of Bicycles. Millions sold, across Europe and the United States."

Tom noticed something else: many of the riders were women, in shorter, looser trousers instead of long skirts.

"Long skirts used to catch in the gears and wheels," the gear explained. "So the bicycle boom helped push practical clothing — people called the baggy trousers bloomers."

"Because a skirt stuck in a chain sounds like a disaster," Tom said.

"A real one, more than once. But it did more than fix clothing," the gear said. "The American reformer **Susan B. Anthony** said cycling had done more to set women free to go where they wanted than almost anything else in the world."

Tom watched a woman pedal past, fast and sure, steering exactly where she chose. "So the bike wasn't just transportation," he said slowly. "It was independence. On two wheels."

"Now you're getting it," the gear said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Bike Shop in Dayton (1890s, Ohio)
chapters.text:
The street noise faded into the clang of tools in a small American shop. Bicycle frames hung from the ceiling; two brothers worked at a bench covered in metal tubing.

"**Wilbur and Orville Wright**," the gear said. "They ran a bicycle shop right here in **Dayton, Ohio**, in the 1890s."

Tom picked up a length of hollow metal tubing, light as a pencil. "This is why I didn't expect a bike shop in this story," he said. "Wait — the Wright brothers? The *airplane* Wright brothers?"

"Same two," the gear said. "They took what they learned building light frames and spoked wheels here, and used it building something that needed to be light and strong for a very different reason."

Tom turned the tubing over, feeling how little it weighed for how strong it felt. "You'd want exactly this for a wing frame," he said. "Strong, but not heavy. That's an engineering answer, not a flying one — it just happens to work for both."

"In **1903**," the gear said, "it did. First successful airplane. Built by two bicycle mechanics."

Tom set the tubing down carefully, like it might still matter to someone.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Garage
chapters.text:
The gear spun one last time, fast enough to blur, and rattled off names like it was running out of road: gear-shifting **derailleurs** in the 1930s, letting riders change gears for hills instead of fighting them; a race called the **Tour de France**, started in **1903**, now about 3,500 kilometers across France; **BMX** and **mountain bikes**, built in the 1970s by American riders who wanted something sturdy enough for dirt trails and jumps.

"Marin County, California," the gear said. "Riders built the first mountain bikes because regular road bikes couldn't survive the hills they wanted to ride down."

"That's basically what I'm doing right now," Tom said, "two hundred years later, with carbon fiber instead of wood."

"There are over a billion bikes in the world today," the gear said. "More than any other vehicle on Earth. Whole cities in places like the Netherlands and Denmark have more bikes than cars."

The green light folded back in on itself, and the garage light buzzed on overhead, ordinary and yellow.

Tom was kneeling by his toolbox again, the small bronze gear warm in his palm. He turned it over once, then clipped it onto his bike's chain where a worn link used to be.

It held. It spun. It didn't glow — not tonight, anyway.

Tom wiped his hands on his jeans and looked at his bike like he'd never quite seen it before: a running machine, a boneshaker, a penny-farthing, a safety bicycle, air-filled tires, a hundred years of arguments about wheels, all bolted together into something that just worked.

Tomorrow there was a hill he'd been wanting to try.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow there was a hill he'd been wanting to try.

true_facts.text: In **1817**, a German inventor named **Karl von Drais** built a wooden two-wheeler with no pedals at all — riders pushed it along with their feet.
Von Drais's invention had handlebars for steering, much like bikes today.
In the 1860s, French builders **Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement** bolted pedals straight onto the front wheel, making a rough-riding bike nicknamed the **boneshaker**.
**Pierre Lallement** patented his pedal bicycle design in the United States in **1866**.
In the 1870s, the **penny-farthing** appeared, with a giant front wheel and a tiny back one, letting one pedal turn cover much more ground.
The penny-farthing was named after two British coins — one big, one tiny, just like its wheels.
Penny-farthing riders sat so high that a sudden stop could toss them forward — a fall known as **taking a header**.
In **1885**, **John Kemp Starley** built the **Rover Safety Bicycle**, with two matching wheels and a chain driving the back wheel.
The safety bicycle's even, low wheels made it much easier and safer to ride than the penny-farthing, and it quickly became the standard bike design everywhere.
In **1888**, **John Boyd Dunlop** invented the practical air-filled, or **pneumatic**, tire — a huge improvement over solid rubber tires.
During the 1890s **Golden Age of Bicycles**, riding a bike gave women new freedom, and reformer **Susan B. Anthony** said it had done more to free women than almost anything else.
Because long skirts could catch in bike gears, the bicycle craze helped make practical clothing like **bloomers** popular.
**Wilbur and Orville Wright** ran a bicycle shop in **Dayton, Ohio** in the 1890s before building the first successful airplane in **1903**.
The Wright brothers used bicycle-building skills, like light metal tubing and spoked wheels, to help design their early flying machines.
