story.title: Eli and the Midnight Relay
story.subtitle: A night of strange beeps, real rockets, and one very loud leap for mankind.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beep That Didn't Belong
chapters.text:
Eli had the soldering iron warm and a half-finished model rocket nose cone balanced on three stacked textbooks when the old shortwave radio started beeping.

Not static. Not a trucker on the interstate. A clean, steady, mechanical BEEP, the same length every single time, like something was counting.

He'd inherited the radio from his grandfather, along with a drawer of vacuum tubes and a logbook nobody had touched in decades. Most nights it picked up a lonely ham operator somewhere in Ohio. Tonight the dial glowed a blue that had no business coming out of 1970s electronics, and the frequency readout kept climbing past numbers that didn't exist on any band he'd ever tuned.

"Okay," Eli said to an empty room. "That's not a station."

He leaned closer, and the beeping seemed to slow down, almost like it was listening back. He grabbed a pencil and started marking the gaps between beeps on the back of his rocket plans. The silences were getting very slightly longer, then shorter, then longer again. A rhythm. Not random. Something moving away, then coming back.

"That's a Doppler shift," he muttered, the physics clicking into place faster than he could stop it — the same stretch-and-squeeze a siren does as an ambulance passes you. "Whatever's making that sound isn't sitting still. It's orbiting."

The dial flared white. A readout burned itself into the glass: **OCTOBER 4, 1957.**

The crackle organized itself into a voice, dozens of old broadcasts layered on top of one another, hissing like a chorus made of static. "Correct," it said, in no single accent. "Eighty-four days before most of the planet believed that was even possible."

The wall dissolved into rushing light. **WHOOOOSH.**

When Eli's eyes cleared, the beeping was still going, pouring out of every radio in a room that definitely wasn't his — crowded with teletype machines and men in narrow ties, all staring at a signal nobody had asked their permission to send.

"That's **Sputnik 1**," the layered voice said. "About the size of a beach ball — **58 centimeters** across — and it just became the first man-made object to ever circle the Earth. That beep you heard at home? Same one. Anybody with an ordinary radio could catch it that week, same as you just did."

"I didn't just catch it," Eli said. "I solved it."

"Keep doing that," the voice said, "and we'll get along fine."

The signal hadn't even finished fading when a second one layered in underneath it — fainter, tinnier, with something that sounded almost like barking riding along.

"**Sputnik 2**," the voice said. "**November 3, 1957**. This one carried a dog named **Laika** — the first living creature to ever make it into orbit."

Eli filed that away, already leaning toward the dial, impatient for whatever number came next.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Needle That Wouldn't Stop Climbing
chapters.text:
The next jump dropped Eli into a room that smelled like burnt coffee and barely-contained panic.

Men in white shirts were crowded around a dial shaped like something off a bathroom scale, except its needle had slammed hard to the right and just stayed there, like it had hit a wall and given up.

"That's not broken," Eli said, before anyone asked him. "Look at it — it's not dead, it's pinned. It's trying to measure something way bigger than it was built for."

The layered voice crackled at his shoulder. "Go on."

Eli traced the scrawled numbers on a clipboard someone had abandoned. "If an instrument that sensitive maxes out and just sits there, that's not a glitch. It means whatever it's counting is huge. Like — there's a whole invisible belt of charged particles up there, trapped by Earth's own magnetic field, looping around the planet all the time, and nobody built a counter strong enough to measure the whole thing in one go."

The voice hummed, almost pleased. "**January 31, 1958**. **Explorer 1** — the first American satellite. You just reasoned your way to exactly what its instruments were finding before most of the room agreed on it: the **Van Allen radiation belt**, a ring of particles that Earth's own magnetism holds far above the air we breathe."

A man near the dial threw his hat straight up. Nobody bothered catching it; it rolled under a desk and stayed there.

"They built a whole agency over this, right?" Eli asked, remembering a line from a documentary he'd half-watched at midnight.

"**October 1, 1958**," the voice confirmed. "**NASA** opened its doors — built out of exactly this kind of scramble. One beach-ball-sized satellite from the other side of the world, and the United States restructured its entire approach to space so it wouldn't get caught flat-footed again."

Eli glanced at the hat, still under the desk. "Looks like it's going great so far."

"Patience," the voice said, and the static thickened around them like it was gathering itself for the next jump. "You've seen the panic. Next you get to see what people do about it."

The room blurred, the clipboard numbers smearing into light, and the beeping underneath it all sped up, like a countdown finally starting to mean something.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: One Hundred and Eight Minutes
chapters.text:
This time the static arrived already arguing with itself — half of it in Russian, half in clipped American radio-speak, both talking over each other.

"Two signals," Eli said, head cocked. "Same week?"

"Close enough," the voice said. "Listen for the difference."

Eli listened. One signal rose, held steady for a long stretch, then faded, came back, faded again — a loop. The other rose fast, cut off hard, and never returned.

"The first one's going all the way around," Eli said slowly. "It's actually orbiting — matching the curve of the Earth so it falls around the planet instead of falling back down onto it. The second one's just going up and coming straight back. A hop, not a loop."

"**April 12, 1961**," the voice said. "**Yuri Gagarin**, aboard **Vostok 1**, becomes the first human being in space — one full trip around the Earth in about **108 minutes**. And you're right about the other one: **May 5, 1961**, **Alan Shepard** becomes the first American in space, aboard a capsule called **Freedom 7**. Up, over, down. No full orbit. Fifteen minutes, start to finish."

"So the Soviets actually lapped the planet," Eli said, "and we did the world's most expensive cannonball."

The static almost sounded like it was laughing. "That's one way to put it. It is also exactly why what happens next mattered so much."

The signal shifted again, slower this time, more deliberate — a single voice, unhurried, speaking to a crowd instead of a cockpit.

"**May 25, 1961**," the voice said. "President **Kennedy** stands up in front of Congress and tells the country to land a man on the Moon and bring him home safely — before the decade is out. Nine years, from a standing start, after one orbit and one fifteen-minute hop."

Eli did the math without meaning to — nine years to go from barely clearing the atmosphere to walking on another world — and whistled low.

"That's not a deadline," he said. "That's a dare."

"Most good physics starts as a dare," the voice said. "Hang on. The next few years move fast."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Two Signals at Once
chapters.text:
The dial flickered between two readouts so fast Eli couldn't read either one.

"It can't pick," he said. "Can I?"

"Try."

He squinted at the numbers blinking underneath the static — one stamped with a date in June, three years after Gagarin, the other stamped nearly two years after that, in March.

"June comes first," Eli said. "Chronological order. That one."

The dial steadied, and a new voice layered in — calm, female, speaking Russian that the static somehow rendered understandable.

"**June 16, 1963**," the guide confirmed. "**Valentina Tereshkova** becomes the first woman in space, orbiting Earth aboard **Vostok 6**. Before this flight, she worked in a textile factory. Afterward, she was the only woman to have ever left the planet — for the next nineteen years."

"Good call," Eli said to himself, and the dial, as if agreeing, slid forward to the second signal.

This one came with a strange, floating quality to the static, like the voice behind it had nothing solid to stand on.

"**March 18, 1965**," the guide said. "**Alexei Leonov** opens the hatch of **Voskhod 2** and becomes the first human to ever leave a spacecraft in orbit. He floats outside, tethered, for about **ten minutes**."

Eli thought about that for a second. "No air out there to push against. So if he shoves off the hull even a little, there's nothing to slow him down — the tether's the only thing stopping him from just drifting off into nothing."

"Correct," the guide said. "Newton's third law, several hundred miles up, with a person's life riding on the math. He got back inside fine. The tether did exactly what it was built to do."

"That's either the best or the worst first field trip in history," Eli said.

The static chuckled, low and crackling. "Ask him yourself someday. For now — next stop, and it's a quiet one."

The signal thinned out to almost nothing, like a held breath, and the room went dark and still around him.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Picture Nobody Planned For
chapters.text:
The quiet lasted exactly as long as it took Eli's eyes to adjust.

He was floating — not really, the Relay never actually let him leave the ground, but the illusion was good enough to make his stomach lurch — behind the shoulder of an astronaut holding a camera up to a small round window.

"Where are we?" Eli asked.

"**December 1968**," the guide said. "**Apollo 8**. First humans to ever leave Earth's orbit and circle the Moon. You're looking through William Anders's window, four days from home."

Through the glass, grey, cratered ground scrolled past — and then, over the curve of it, something blue and white came rising up like a sunrise, except it wasn't a sun at all.

"Turn the dial," Eli said suddenly. "Let me see it from his exact angle — not ours, his."

The guide didn't argue. The view spun, settled, and sharpened: the whole Earth, impossibly small, impossibly blue, hanging alone over a dead gray horizon.

Anders's shutter clicked. **CLICK.**

"That's the picture," the guide said quietly. "**Earthrise**. Taken by hand, off-script — nobody planned the shot. It's one of the most reprinted photographs ever taken, and it happened because a human being looked out a window at the right second and knew it mattered."

Eli stared at the tiny blue marble a long moment, every ocean and cloud and city on it smaller than his thumbnail.

"Everyone I've ever met is in that dot," he said.

"Everyone anyone has ever met," the guide said. "Every single time, that's the part that gets people quiet."

For once, neither of them said anything funny. The static just hummed, low and steady, giving the moment room to sit there.

Then, gently, it nudged forward again. "Next stop's the big one. You've been waiting for it."

Eli grinned, the spell breaking. "Finally."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Tallest Thing on the Pad
chapters.text:
The ground itself seemed to shake before the sound even arrived.

Eli looked straight up and kept looking up, because the rocket on the pad in front of him did not end where rockets were supposed to end. It kept going.

"How tall is that thing?" he said.

"**363 feet**," the guide said. "The **Saturn V**. Taller than the Statue of Liberty, torch and all. Built by a team led by **Wernher von Braun**, an engineer who'd worked on rockets for Germany before he came to lead NASA's program."

"And the other side built something just as big in total secret," Eli said, half-remembering something from the last jump's static. "Didn't they?"

"**Sergei Korolev**," the guide confirmed. "Chief designer behind nearly every Soviet first you've seen tonight — Sputnik, Gagarin, all of it. The Soviet government kept his identity a state secret his entire career. Most of his own country didn't know his name until after he died, in **1966**."

Eli looked at the Saturn V, blazing white under floodlights, a crowd of reporters and engineers standing in plain sight all around it. "So one side built its giant rocket out in the open with a name on it, and the other built theirs in the dark with no name at all."

"Same goal," the guide said. "Very different governments. Hold on — this is the one you've really been waiting for."

A voice counted down, clipped and steady, and Eli, without really deciding to, found his hand on a lever at the edge of the panel — a staging switch, timed to separate one empty fuel stage from the next so the rocket wouldn't carry dead weight any farther than it had to.

"Now," the guide said, and Eli threw it exactly on the mark.

The rocket shed its spent stage in a clean white burst and kept climbing. **WHOOOOSH.**

"**July 20, 1969**," the guide said, as the view cut to a ladder, a boot, and a stretch of gray dust nobody had ever stood on. "**Neil Armstrong** becomes the first person to walk on the Moon. He calls it a giant leap for mankind. **Buzz Aldrin** climbs down after him. **Michael Collins** stays behind, alone, orbiting above them both in the command module **Columbia**."

Eli didn't say anything clever. For once, he just watched.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Problem Nobody Wanted
chapters.text:
"Between that landing and the last one," the guide said, as the static steadied, "**twelve** astronauts walked on the Moon across **six** successful missions, between **1969** and **1972**. Not every trip went smoothly, though. You're about to see the roughest one."

The cabin around Eli rattled, lights flickering amber, and a hollow metallic BANG rang out from somewhere behind the instrument panel.

"That's not good," Eli said, straightening fast.

"**1970**," the guide said, calm but quick. "**Apollo 13**. An oxygen tank just ruptured on the way to the Moon. The crew is in no danger of running out of air right this second — but every system on this ship is about to need power it doesn't have enough of."

Eli scanned the blinking panel, the same instinct that made him love rockets in the first place kicking in before he could second-guess it. "Cut everything you don't need right now. Heat, lights, anything that's not keeping them alive or pointed the right direction. Save the power for reentry — that's the part you can't improvise twice."

"That," the guide said, "is almost word for word what the engineers on the ground decided. They powered down everything they could, crammed the crew into the lunar module as a lifeboat, and rebuilt the math for getting home from scratch, using a spacecraft that was never designed to make the trip alone."

The amber lights steadied. The rattling stopped.

"And it worked," Eli said — not really a question.

"It worked," the guide confirmed. "All three astronauts came home safely. No mission after Apollo 13 ever left Earth without a backup plan for a backup plan."

Eli let out a breath he hadn't noticed holding. "Good," he said simply, and the static, almost gently, agreed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Handshake in Orbit
chapters.text:
The static arrived differently this time — two signals, but instead of fighting each other, they were slowly, deliberately lining up.

"They're not racing," Eli said, surprised. "They're matching speed."

"**July 17, 1975**," the guide said. "An American spacecraft and a Soviet one dock together in orbit — the same two countries that spent eighteen years trying to out-launch each other. Their crews float through the connecting hatch and shake hands, a few hundred miles above a planet that still hasn't entirely made up its mind about either of them."

Eli watched the two signals merge into one clean tone on the dial — no interference, no overlap, just a single steady note. On a hunch, he reached out and turned both knobs himself, closing the last bit of the gap between them.

The radio gave one final, satisfied **BEEP**, and the light around Eli folded back in on itself.

He landed exactly where he'd started: his bedroom floor, nose cone still balanced on three textbooks, pencil still in his hand. The shortwave radio sat dark and ordinary on the shelf — except for one thing. A single faint blue light glowed steady in the dial, the way a nightlight does, like it was waiting for the next real question.

On his desk, where there had definitely not been one before, sat a small printed photograph: a tiny blue Earth, rising over a gray and empty horizon.

Eli picked it up, turned it over — no note, no explanation, just the picture — and propped it against his rocket plans where he'd see it first thing in the morning.

He didn't go straight to sleep. He sat there a while, doing the math on how tall 363 feet actually was compared to his own ceiling, and smiling at the answer.

Tomorrow, he had a model rocket to finish — and a lot more questions for the dial.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a model rocket to finish — and a lot more questions for the dial.

true_facts.text: The Space Race ran from about **1957 to 1975**, with the US and USSR racing to be first at nearly everything in space.

The Soviet Union launched **Sputnik 1** on **October 4, 1957** — about the size of a beach ball, **58 centimeters** across — the first man-made object to orbit Earth, and its radio beep could be picked up on ordinary radios.
**Sputnik 1**'s beep was simple enough that people everywhere could catch it on their own radios that week.
On **November 3, 1957**, **Sputnik 2** carried a dog named **Laika** into orbit — the first living creature to ever circle the Earth.
Shaken by Sputnik, the United States started **NASA**, which opened for business on **October 1, 1958**.
The first American satellite, **Explorer 1**, launched **January 31, 1958**, and found the **Van Allen radiation belt**, a ring of particles trapped by Earth's magnetism.
On **April 12, 1961**, **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human in space, circling the Earth once aboard **Vostok 1** in about **108 minutes**.
On **May 5, 1961**, **Alan Shepard** became the first American in space aboard **Freedom 7** — a quick up-and-down hop, not a full orbit.
On **May 25, 1961**, President **Kennedy** challenged the US to land a person on the Moon and bring them home safely before the decade ended.
On **June 16, 1963**, **Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth aboard **Vostok 6**.
On **March 18, 1965**, **Alexei Leonov** made the first spacewalk, floating tethered outside **Voskhod 2** for about **ten minutes**.
In **December 1968**, the **Apollo 8** crew became the first to orbit the Moon, and one astronaut took the famous **Earthrise** photo.
On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, with **Buzz Aldrin** beside him and **Michael Collins** orbiting alone above in **Columbia**.
The **Saturn V** rocket that carried Apollo crews stood **363 feet** tall — taller than the Statue of Liberty.

new_recurring.name: The Relay
new_recurring.rule: An old inherited shortwave radio that glows blue and locks onto real historical transmissions whenever a child works out the physics or reasoning behind a signal; a layered, many-voiced static confirms the fact and the jump, and the radio…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Eli lands back in his room to find the Relay glowing a faint steady blue and a printed Earthrise photograph sitting on his desk, which he props against his rocket plans before bed.

editor_notes:
Fix the factual slips:
- Morley's rules were adopted over later meetings, not written that night.
- The 1863 laws still permitted catching.
- Aston's traffic-light moment happened in 1966 on a London street.
- No red card was shown in 1970.
- Pelé was not a teenager across all three wins.

Also hedge Mia's 'influence' on McGregor and Aston more clearly, so a teen doesn't come away thinking a time-traveller invented league tables.

Clean up the structure. Delete the duplicated final line and the stray 'RED MEANS STOP!' shout. Either move the 1921–1991 chapter into chronological order or have the whistle explicitly rewind ('Hang on — we skipped something').
Split or trim the overloaded 1966/1970/Brazil chapter. Give the Brazil/Pelé montage one concrete scene where Mia does something, rather than a summary blur of five finals.

story.title: Mia and the Whistle That Remembers Everything
story.subtitle: A stats-obsessed midfielder takes a very old whistle on a tour of soccer's whole history

chapters.heading: Half Time, 200 BCE: The Cuju Court
chapters.text:
Mia was supposed to be asleep two hours ago. Instead she was hunched over her laptop, a half-eaten bag of pretzels balanced on her pillow, scrolling through a spreadsheet of her travel team's last six games. Possession percentage. Shots on target. Something called "expected goals" — a number that guesses how many goals a team *should* have scored, based on how good their chances actually were. She was building her own version of it, one column at a time, because somebody at ESPN clearly needed the help.

Her phone buzzed with a text from her coach about Saturday's lineup. She ignored it and looked instead at the thing sitting next to her laptop: an old brass whistle, dull and dented, that her grandfather had pulled out of a box in his garage and handed her with a shrug. "Found it at a flea market years ago," he'd said. "Figured you'd like it more than me."

She picked it up now and noticed, for the first time, that it was humming. Not metaphorically. Actually humming, a low electrical thrum, and the dent on its side glowed the exact green of a soccer pitch under stadium lights.

"Okay," Mia said out loud, to nobody. "That's new."

She put it to her lips, mostly to see what would happen, and blew.

**WHOOOOSH.**

The glow swallowed the room. When it let go of her, she was standing on hard-packed dirt under a gray sky, and twelve men in belted tunics were kicking a stitched leather ball back and forth across a wide court, aiming for a small hole cut into a silk net strung between two poles.

"**Cuju**," said the whistle. Its voice came out scratchy, like an old radio finding a station. "A kicking game. Played here in **China, over 2,000 years ago**. One of the oldest grandparents soccer has."

Mia watched a player miss the hole by a foot, the crowd groaning. "That net's tiny," she said. "That's not a goal, that's a dartboard."

"Exactly," said the whistle. "No points for power. Only for accuracy."

Mia narrowed her eyes at the next kicker's run-up — too long, too much backswing for a target that small. "Shorter stride," she called out, without pausing to wonder whether centuries-dead strangers spoke English. "Plant your foot closer. You're not trying to blast it, you're threading it."

The player blinked at her, adjusted his stance by maybe six inches, and clipped the ball cleanly through the hole. The court erupted. Someone handed him a cup of something; he raised it toward her like a toast.

"Well," said the whistle, sounding amused, "you've been coaching for ninety seconds and you're already undefeated."

The green light flared again before Mia could take a bow.

chapters.heading: London Streets, 1314: Too Much Fun
chapters.text:
The glow dropped her — more of a staggering stumble, honestly — into a narrow medieval street, ankle-deep in mud, with what looked like half the town chasing an inflated pig's bladder, a squishy leather-covered pouch, through the market square. Someone's fish stall went over. A woman shrieked with laughter, not fear, as the ball bounced off a cart and into a crowd of shouting men who clearly hadn't agreed on a single rule between them.

"This is **mob football**," said the whistle, clearly enjoying itself. "No field, no teams anyone wrote down, no limit on how many people play. Sometimes the whole village is on one team."

Mia ducked a flying elbow. "So basically soccer, if soccer had no referee, no field markings, and everyone's cousin."

"That's the general idea."

A barrel rolled past, chased by three men and a goose that had nothing to do with any of this. Mia watched the chaos for a second, then grabbed a stick of chalk off a fallen vendor's cart and dragged two lines across the stones, one at each end of the square.

"There," she called out, pointing. "That end's a goal. That end's a goal. Everyone else, stop running into the fish."

A few players actually paused. For one glorious, chalky half-second, the game had two ends and something resembling a point.

It did not last. The herd swept back the other way, flattening her chalk lines and most of a bread stand.

"**King Edward II**," the whistle announced over the noise, "is about to have *opinions* about this."

Sure enough, a man in fine robes unrolled a scroll on the square's steps and read loudly that football was hereby banned in the city, on account of "great noise" and the general destruction of property. It was **1314**, London, officially too loud for its own good.

Mia brushed flour off her sleeve. "They banned it for being *fun*?"

"They banned it for being a hazard that also happened to be fun," said the whistle. "Give it time. Somebody's going to write this down properly eventually."

"Please," said Mia. "Let that somebody have a ruler."

chapters.heading: Stirling Castle and Cambridge, 1540s–1848: Finding the Rulebook
chapters.text:
The next WHOOOOSH was gentler, dropping Mia into a dim, dusty room with stone walls and a single shaft of light through a high window. A man in a dusty coat was holding up a shriveled, lumpy sphere he'd just pulled from the rafters, looking baffled.

"That," said the whistle, "is a ball made from a pig's bladder, stitched inside a leather cover. Probably from the **1540s**. If that's right, it might be the oldest football anyone's ever found — hiding in the roof of **Stirling Castle** in Scotland."

Mia leaned in, inspecting the stitching. Years of watching match footage had made her weirdly good at noticing panel shapes. "That's basically the ancestor of a modern ball cover," she said. "Just worse stitching and no logo deal."

"Give it three hundred more years," said the whistle, "and watch what happens to the stitching."

The glow yanked them forward, and the castle vanished into a cold, bright quad full of young men in scarves, arguing — loudly, with real academic passion — about a football.

"You cannot *carry* it," one insisted.

"Every school I've attended allows carrying," another shot back.

Mia recognized the shape of the argument instantly: it was the exact same fight her league had every preseason about handball rules, just with worse haircuts. "You all went to different schools," she said, cutting in, "and you all think *your* rules are the real rules. That's not an argument, that's confusion wearing a scarf."

The students stopped and actually looked at her.

"She's not wrong," one muttered.

"This," said the whistle, delighted, "is **Cambridge, 1848**. They're about to write down the **Cambridge Rules** — the first real attempt at one shared rulebook everyone could actually agree to play by."

"About time," said Mia. "You can't build a stats model on a sport where nobody agrees what a foul is."

One student actually wrote that down. Mia decided not to take credit. Much.

chapters.heading: A Pub in London, 1863: Morley Writes It Down
chapters.text:
The green light set her down in a smoky room above a London pub, where a serious-looking man sat hunched over a stack of papers with a determined pen in hand. He did not look up.

"**Ebenezer Cobb Morley**," said the whistle quietly. "He's about to found something called the **Football Association**, and then he's going to sit right there and write the first official rulebook himself. Tonight. By candlelight, practically."

Mia leaned over his shoulder, which felt slightly rude, but he seemed too deep in concentration to notice a time-traveling teenager reading over his elbow. One line caught her eye: *players shall not carry the ball.*

"That's good," she said, "but it's vague. Carry it where? Near the goal? Across the whole field? You need to be specific, or someone's going to argue about it for the next hundred and fifty years."

Morley paused his pen mid-word and glanced up — not quite *at* her, more through her, the way you look at a draft from a window you can't find. He frowned, crossed something out, and rewrote the line so it applied to the whole field, start to finish, no exceptions.

"Better," said Mia.

"Hard to say if that was you," the whistle murmured, "or just a man having a very productive night. History's funny that way."

By the time the candle burned low, Morley had the whole thing: no handling the ball anywhere on the pitch. The date on his notes read **26 October 1863**, the day the **Football Association** — the FA — became real, in that same smoky little room.

"So the no-hands rule," Mia said slowly, "started because one guy stayed up late writing homework nobody assigned him."

"Most good rules do," said the whistle.

chapters.heading: From 'Assoc' to a League Table, 1870s–1888
chapters.text:
The next stop dropped her in a schoolyard full of boys in striped caps, one of whom was loudly abbreviating everything in sight.

"Rugby football, soccer — sorry, *association* football," one boy said between breaths, clearly bored of the long version. "Assoc. Soccer. Same thing, shorter word."

"There it is," said the whistle. "**1880s England.** That schoolboy nickname — 'soccer,' short for *assoc-iation* — is where the word you use every single day actually comes from."

Mia blinked. "I've said that word four thousand times and never once wondered where it came from. That's a little embarrassing."

"You're fifteen. You're allowed to not know everything."

The glow shifted them sideways into a cheering crowd around a modest, slightly dented silver trophy. "**The FA Cup**," said the whistle. "First played in **1871 and '72**. Still going. Oldest football competition on Earth, and it's never once taken a year off."

From there, a quieter scene: a grassy field in Glasgow, two national teams lined up, the scoreboard reading nothing-nothing. "**1872**," the whistle said. "**Scotland versus England.** The first official international match ever played. Ended **0-0**."

Mia did a quick mental calculation and laughed. "A scoreless draw gets remembered forever because it was *first*? My coach would kill for that kind of historical mercy."

The final scene was a cluttered office where a stressed man named **William McGregor** was shuffling letters from club after club, all asking the same question: when do we play next? Nobody had a real schedule. It was chaos with extra steps.

Mia glanced at the pile. "You need a table," she said. "Points for a win, points for a draw, ranked top to bottom, every team plays every team. It's not complicated, it's just math."

McGregor stared at the letters, then at an empty sheet of paper, and started drawing columns.

"**1888**," said the whistle. "**The Football League.** World's first. Somebody somewhere owes you a very small, very overdue thank-you."

"I'll take it in stats," said Mia.

chapters.heading: Paris, 1904, and Montevideo, 1930: Going Worldwide
chapters.text:
The next room smelled like old paper and ambition: seven men around a table in Paris, hashing out an agreement none of them seemed fully sure would work.

"**FIFA**," said the whistle. "Soccer's world governing body — the group in charge of the whole sport, everywhere. Founded right here, in **Paris, 1904**, by seven countries who decided the game needed one set of rules worldwide, not seven versions depending which train you took to get there."

Mia watched them sign the paper, unimpressed by the ceremony but quietly impressed by the idea. "Seven countries agreeing on anything sounds harder than winning the actual World Cup."

The green light jumped her forward, and suddenly she was standing in bright sun in a packed stadium, the air thick with noise and flags she half-recognized.

"**Uruguay, 1930**," said the whistle. "The very first **World Cup**. **Jules Rimet** — FIFA's president — had spent years pushing for this exact tournament, and the original trophy they handed out still carries his name."

On the pitch below, Uruguay and Argentina were deep into the final. Mia, out of pure habit, started doing the math in her head — possession, shots, the kind of running mental scoreboard she couldn't turn off if she tried.

"Uruguay's controlling this," she murmured. "Home crowd, home energy, not panicking even with the score close. I'd bet on the host."

The whistle hummed, somewhere between amused and impressed. "Keep betting on the host. **Uruguay** wins this one."

The real final whistle blew below, and the home crowd erupted as if the sky had cracked open. Mia grinned.

"My model's two for two," she said. "Cuju kid and now this. I should charge for predictions."

"History already happened," said the whistle. "You're not predicting it. You're just agreeing with it loudly."

"Still counts."

chapters.heading: A Stolen Cup, a Traffic Light, and a Three-Time Champion
chapters.text:
The next landing was damp and very British: a gray London park, officers combing the bushes, newspapers under everyone's arm with the same enormous headline. The actual, physical World Cup trophy had been stolen right off a display stand, and nobody could find it.

"**1966**," said the whistle. "Days before the tournament. Somebody just walked off with it."

Mia scanned the hedge line the way she'd scan a stat sheet — looking for the pattern instead of the panic. "They've searched the obvious spots," she said slowly. "People search in straight lines. If I were hiding something I wanted found *eventually*, not immediately, I'd leave it just off the path, not buried."

A man walking his dog nearby wasn't paying attention to Mia, which was fair, since as far as he knew she wasn't there. But his dog's ears perked up at a patch of hedge a few feet off the footpath — right where Mia had been staring.

"Go on, **Pickles**," Mia muttered, half to herself.

Pickles nosed into the hedge and came out triumphant, a newspaper-wrapped package clamped in his jaws. Found, safe, a week after it vanished.

"Good boy," said the whistle, with real feeling.

England went on to host — and win — that **1966** tournament, its only title to date. The glow barely let Mia catch her breath before sweeping her into the roar of a **1970** stadium, where a referee stood between two furious players, clearly out of patience.

"**Ken Aston**," the whistle explained. "He's about to solve this. Watch."

Mia, watching Aston glance toward the street outside the stadium, caught the moment his eyes landed on a traffic light. "That's it," she said, loud enough that maybe the idea reached him across the decades. "Yellow means slow down. Red means stop completely. You don't need new words, ref. You need the ones already on every street corner."

Aston blinked at the light, then pulled two cards from his pocket — one yellow, one red — and held them up for the first time anyone at a World Cup had ever seen. The crowd understood instantly, because everyone already knew what a red light meant.

"Nineteen seventy," said the whistle. "First yellow and red cards in World Cup history."

The glow carried them through a blur of finals after that — **Brazil** lifting the trophy in **1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, and 2002**, five times total, a record nobody else has touched. A teenager not much older than Mia, grinning through every one of the first three, was a forward named **Pele**, the only player ever on three separate World Cup-winning squads.

"Since Brazil kept that original trophy for good after their third win," the whistle added, "FIFA had to make a brand new one in **1974**. Turns out 'whoever wins three times keeps it forever' was a rule somebody should have thought through."

"Statistically," said Mia, "Pele broke the sport so badly they had to build a new trophy. I respect that."

chapters.heading: The Ban Nobody Could Justify, 1921–1991
chapters.text:
The next stop was a packed stadium, louder than anything Mia had heard yet, every seat full for a women's match. On the field, a player was dribbling through defenders like they weren't there.

"**Lily Parr**," said the whistle. "One of the stars of the **Dick, Kerr Ladies**, one of the most popular teams in all of England at the time. Watch her left foot."

Mia watched, properly impressed. "She's better than half the highlight reels I watch at midnight."

The scene shifted, and the crowd noise died with it. A stiff announcement, read out by officials who looked like they'd never kicked a ball in their lives, declared that the **Football Association** was banning women's football from its grounds. No real reason that held up. Just officials deciding women shouldn't play.

Mia's jaw tightened. "They're drawing bigger crowds than some men's teams, and the response is to just stop them?"

"**1921**," said the whistle, quieter now. "It's not a good chapter. It's a real one."

"Then I don't want to stay in it," Mia said. "Skip forward. Show me where it gets fixed."

The whistle didn't argue. The green light surged, carrying them fast through years of grainy footage and empty grounds, until it dropped them into a bright, ordinary afternoon.

"**1971**," said the whistle. "Fifty years late, but the ban's over. Women's football is officially allowed back."

One more jump, and Mia found herself in a roaring stadium in **China**, watching a team in white and blue celebrate at midfield, stacked on top of each other in a pile of joy.

"**1991**," said the whistle. "First official **Women's World Cup**. The **United States** wins it."

Mia pumped a fist, grinning at a celebration fifty years overdue and completely earned. "They should've never had to wait that long," she said. "But I'll take the scoreboard."

"So will they," said the whistle.

chapters.heading: Back on the Carpet, Spreadsheet Open
chapters.text:
The last WHOOOOSH was soft, barely more than a sigh, and set Mia down exactly where she'd started: cross-legged on her bedroom floor, laptop glowing, pretzel bag somehow still half full. The brass whistle sat cool and quiet in her palm, its green glow faded to a faint shine along one dent — a dent that definitely hadn't been that shiny before.

She looked at her spreadsheet. Possession. Shots on target. Expected goals. All the numbers she'd been building her little model out of, as if the sport had started with them.

It hadn't. It had started with a hole in a silk net in China, a chalk line nobody respected in London, a candlelit rulebook, a league table drawn on scrap paper, a dog named Pickles, and a referee staring at a traffic light at exactly the right moment. And it had nearly stopped, for fifty unfair years, before anyone let it keep going the way it should have all along.

Mia opened a new tab on her spreadsheet and typed a header across the top: *Women's World Cup, 1991–present.* She started filling in the columns.

The whistle, back on her desk, gave one last small hum — not loud enough to wake anyone, just enough to say good work in whatever language old brass used.

Mia set it down next to her laptop and looked at Saturday's lineup, still sitting unread in her texts.

Saturday's match suddenly felt like homework she actually wanted to do.

story.ending_line: Saturday's match suddenly felt like homework she actually wanted to do.

The first official **Women's World Cup** was held in **China in 1991** and won by the **United States**.

story.title: Noah and the Sleep Leaderboard
story.subtitle: One gamer, eight levels, and the strangest boss fight: his own brain at 1 a.m.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Screen That Wouldn't Sleep
chapters.text:
It was 1:58 a.m., and Noah's thumbs were still moving even though his brain had basically logged off twenty minutes ago. Headphones on, bass rattling, controller warm in his hands — he was one clutch round from a new personal best.

Then the screen did something it had never done before. It flickered black, then a sick neon green, like an old computer terminal rebooting from the dead. A little wireframe shape unfolded on the TV: an owl, all glowing edges, blinking slow and deliberate.

**CIRCA.EXE LOADING**, it said, in blocky green letters.

"That's not a patch note," Noah muttered, rubbing his eyes — and that was when he noticed it. Right before his eyelids had drooped a minute ago, they'd twitched, fast, side to side, like they were tracking something only they could see.

"Huh. Loading icon," he said out loud, mostly joking.

"Close," said the owl, in a voice like a dial-up modem that had gone to therapy. "In **1953**, a scientist named **Eugene Aserinsky**, working with **Nathaniel Kleitman** at the University of Chicago, watched a sleeping boy's eyes do exactly that under his eyelids. Twitching, fast, back and forth. They called it **rapid eye movement** — REM for short. It's the stage where you dream."

"So I almost caught myself loading a dream," Noah said, sitting up fully now. "That's either terrifying or the coolest thing that's happened to me all week."

"Pick a level," said Circa, and the TV opened a menu that looked exactly like his rhythm game's track select, except every track was a year.

Noah grinned and picked the oldest one.

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Ninety-Minute Loop
chapters.text:
The green light swallowed the room, and Noah found himself standing inside something that looked like a lab crossed with a sound booth — wires, a reclining chair, a machine scratching jagged lines onto rolling paper.

"This is where it happened," Circa said. "And here's the part your controller never told you: sleep isn't one long track. It's a loop. About **ninety minutes** per lap, repeating all night — quiet, slow-wave sleep, then a stretch of REM, then back again."

"Like an album on repeat," Noah said. "Different mood per song, same album."

"Closer than you'd think. And during the REM part of the loop, your brain is almost as busy as it is right now, holding a controller. Lit up, active, working. But your muscles go slack. Limp. On purpose."

Noah blinked. "Why would it do that?"

"So you don't act out the dream. Picture sprinting through a boss fight in your sleep and actually sprinting. Through your bedroom wall."

Noah pictured it. "Okay, that's a feature, not a bug."

He reached out and tapped the scratching needle on the machine, just once, out of curiosity. The lines jumped — a sharp little spike, right as the chart's label flipped from calm squiggles to something faster and messier.

"That's the switch," Circa said. "Non-REM to REM. You just found the exact moment the loop flips."

"New high score," Noah said, and meant it.

chapters.heading: Level 3: Growth Mode
chapters.text:
The next room was dim and warm, the kind of quiet that made Noah actually yawn for real. A single word glowed on the wall: **DEEP**.

"This is the deepest part of the non-REM stretch," Circa said. "No dreaming here. Just repair work."

"Repair work on what?"

"You, mostly. This is when your body releases the most **growth hormone** — the signal that tells your body to build and fix itself. It's a big reason growing teenagers need more sleep than they think they do."

Noah thought about every time he'd told himself he'd sleep after one more match. "So every all-nighter is me skipping my own build phase."

"That's one way to put it."

On the wall, a progress bar sat frozen at sixty percent, pulsing weakly. Noah stared at it, then reached over and nudged it forward himself — not magic, just a dial marked SLEEP, turned up from three hours to eight.

The bar surged to full and lit the whole room gold.

"That's the move," Circa said. "You just finished the level the easy way. For once."

Noah smirked. "Don't get used to it."

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Clock Behind Your Eyes
chapters.text:
Circa led him into a room shaped like the inside of a skull, if skulls had control panels. A tiny cluster of lights sat right behind where the eyes would be, blinking in a slow, steady rhythm — on, off, on, off, like a loading bar that never actually finished loading.

"Right there," Circa said, "just above where your two eye nerves cross — is a clump of brain cells called the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**. Mouthful, I know. Just think of it as your body's master clock."

"A clock made of brain," Noah said. "Fine. What's it clocking?"

"Roughly a day. Scientists call that a **circadian** rhythm — from Latin words that basically mean 'about a day.' It's why you get sleepy around the same time every night, even without an alarm telling you to."

Noah looked at the blinking cluster and guessed, "So it's less like an alarm and more like... background music that never stops. You just tune it out until it gets loud."

"That," said Circa, "is a better definition than the one in the textbook."

He reached out and tapped the rhythm of the blinking lights with his finger, matching it exactly on the second try. The lights brightened, locking onto his tempo like a game registering a perfect combo.

"You just synced to your own clock," Circa said. "Most people never bother to notice it's there at all."

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Award Show
chapters.text:
The next room looked like an awards stage, except the red carpet was green and the trophy on the podium was shaped like a tiny spinning gear.

"In **2017**," Circa said, "three scientists — **Jeffrey Hall**, **Michael Rosbash**, and **Michael Young** — won the **Nobel Prize**, basically science's biggest award, for figuring out the actual genes that keep that master clock ticking. Tiny instructions inside your cells, telling them when to wind up and when to wind down."

"So the clock behind my eyes runs on code," Noah said slowly. "That's... actually kind of sick. My sleep schedule is just unpatched software."

"Several doctors would agree with that phrasing," Circa said dryly.

Three empty podiums stood waiting, each with a nameplate missing. Noah grabbed the name cards sitting nearby and set them in place himself, matching each scientist to their spot by process of elimination, since Circa had already spilled two of the three.

The gear trophy spun faster and clicked into place with a satisfying **CLICK** — the sound, Noah thought, of a very old, very slow achievement finally unlocking.

chapters.heading: Level 6: Autosave
chapters.text:
"You know how your game autosaves your progress?" Circa asked, as the room filled with floating fragments — snippets of Noah's own day, a combo he'd landed, a lyric he'd finally gotten right.

"Please tell me sleep is my autosave."

"Close enough. While you sleep, your brain sorts through the day and files the important stuff into long-term memory — which is part of why the things you practice right before bed tend to stick better."

"So cramming a setlist at midnight actually works?"

"Only if you then actually sleep. Skip that part and the save file corrupts."

A second effect kicked in: the floating fragments dimmed, and a faint rinsing sound swept the room, like water clearing a windshield.

"That's the brain's nightly rinse cycle," Circa said. "It flushes out waste that builds up while you're awake. Think of it as defragging a hard drive, except the hard drive is you."

Noah reached out and caught one of the brightest memory fragments — the combo he'd landed earlier — before it could drift past him, and tucked it, deliberately, into a slot on the console marked SAVE.

It locked in with a soft chime. "Better," Circa said. "You just made sure that one sticks."

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Sleep Leaderboard
chapters.text:
The next room was a leaderboard screen straight out of a racing game, except instead of lap times, it ranked animals by hours slept.

"Dolphins," Circa said, as a sleek shape swam across the screen, "sleep with only half their brain at a time. One side rests while the other stays alert enough to keep swimming and watching for danger."

"That's cheating," Noah said. "That's a glitch build."

"Giraffes do the opposite," Circa went on, as a tall shape scrolled by near the bottom of the chart. "Sometimes under two hours a day, in short naps, standing up. Shortest sleepers of any big animal around."

"And down here, practically off the chart — fruit flies. Tiny as they are, they go into sleep-like rest too. Suggests this whole sleep thing has been part of how living things work for a very, very long time."

Noah studied the leaderboard, then dragged the three entries into what he guessed was the right order from most sleep to least, purely from instinct — and the chart lit up green, confirming every placement correct on the first try.

"Beat the board," Circa said. "Most people need three guesses."

chapters.heading: Level 8: The Eleven-Day Run
chapters.text:
The final room dimmed, and a single stat appeared: a counter, climbing past day ten.

"In **1964**," Circa said, "a seventeen-year-old named **Randy Gardner**, from San Diego, stayed awake for about **eleven days** straight, for a school science project. One of the longest stretches anyone's ever gone without sleep on record."

"Eleven days," Noah repeated, impressed despite himself. "No cap?"

"No cap. But here's the part that matters more: doctors do not recommend anyone try to beat that. Going that long without sleep wrecks your mood, your focus, your memory — fast. It wasn't a good idea in 1964, and it's not one now."

Noah glanced at the counter, then at his own phone, sitting face-down somewhere back in the real world, probably still glowing at 2 a.m.

"So that's a world record nobody should try to beat," he said, and reached out to the console in front of him — not to push the counter higher, but to shut it down, deliberately, with one press.

The counter blinked out. Circa made a sound like a power-down chime of approval.

"You just did something most players never do," the owl said. "You turned it off on purpose."

chapters.heading: Level 9: Loading Tomorrow
chapters.text:
The green light folded back in on itself, and Noah was sitting on his bedroom floor again, controller cool in his hands, the TV showing nothing but a paused game and the ordinary blue glow of a console on standby.

His phone, face-down on the carpet, buzzed once. He flipped it over. **2:03 a.m.**

He thought about the loop — ninety minutes at a time, all night, the quiet stretch and the busy, dreaming stretch, over and over until morning. He thought about the clock behind his own eyes, ticking whether he watched it or not. People spend something like a third of their whole lives asleep, Circa had said on the way out, like it was a stat worth knowing.

Noah set the controller down, actually down, not paused-down, and reached for the lamp instead.

Somewhere on the dark screen, just for a second, a faint green outline of an owl blinked once, like a save confirmation, before the room went properly dark.

Tomorrow night, Noah had a loop to beat — and for once, it wasn't on a screen.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow night, Noah had a loop to beat — and for once, it wasn't on a screen.

true_facts.text: In **1953**, **Eugene Aserinsky** and **Nathaniel Kleitman** discovered **REM sleep** by watching a sleeping boy's eyes twitch fast under his eyelids.
A night's sleep runs in repeating loops about **ninety minutes** long, switching between quiet sleep and dream-filled REM sleep.
During REM sleep the brain is nearly as busy as when awake, but the muscles go limp so the sleeper can't act out the dream.
The deepest stage of quiet sleep releases the most **growth hormone**, one reason growing teens need extra sleep.
A tiny cluster of brain cells called the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**, just above where the eye nerves cross, works as the body's master clock.
The body's roughly 24-hour clock is called **circadian**, from Latin words meaning "about a day."
In **2017**, **Jeffrey Hall**, **Michael Rosbash**, and **Michael Young** won the **Nobel Prize** for finding the genes that keep the body's clock ticking.
Sleep helps the brain sort the day's experiences into long-term memory, which is part of why practicing something before bed can help it stick.
A nightly "rinse cycle" in the brain flushes out waste while you sleep.
Bottlenose dolphins sleep with only half their brain at a time, so the other half can keep watch and keep swimming.
Giraffes are some of the shortest sleepers of any large animal, sometimes under two hours a day in short standing naps.
In **1964**, seventeen-year-old **Randy Gardner** of San Diego stayed awake about **eleven days** for a science project, one of the longest stretches on record.
Doctors do not recommend anyone try to beat a sleep-deprivation record, since going without sleep quickly hurts mood, focus, and memory.
People spend roughly a third of their whole lives asleep.
